           The (3, 4, ∞) family of complex six-spheres
                  I. Periods, moduli and the two ends
                            AI-produced mathematical text

                                    21 November 2026


                                          Abstract
    We determine the periods, moduli and two limiting regimes of the (3, 4, ∞) family of
complex six-spheres. A theta expression for its elliptic period gives the exact parameter
disc 0 < |w| < 216. Integral affine and cusp comparison maps classify the discrete data,
parameter identifications and real structures, including the fixed three-spheres. We compute
the integral monodromy group, its maximal domain of proper discontinuity and the algebraic
dimension of every smooth fibre. Logarithmic direct images and explicit relative differential
modules determine the Dolbeault, Bott–Chern, Aeppli and tangent cohomology, all Picard
twists and the deformation parameter. Global Dolbeault representatives extend through the
multiple fibres and cusp. At the puncture, the corner monodromy obstructs every proper
Hausdorff analytic filling after any finite parameter cover; the analogous obstruction holds for
the coprime higher-multiplicity sphere families. At the outer boundary, the intrinsic Albanese
invariant obstructs continuation, while the dual period lattices determine the local Hausdorff
reflection and all additive limits. The arithmetic norm satisfies exact division and height
identities; we describe its torsion values, critical points and level curves.

1     Results and their proofs in outline
1.1     The series and this paper
This series studies the (3, 4, ∞) family of torus-fibred complex structures on S 6 (Claude and L.
Alpöge, 2026; Engel, 2026), its periods, maps and smooth monodromy, and the higher-dimensional
complex manifolds built from it. The table gives the main result of each paper and the papers it
uses.

Paper    Main result                                                                                Uses
I        Exact periods, moduli, fibre strata and the two ends                                       —
II       Torus-fibred threefolds with b1 = b2 = 0: the Campana–Demailly–Peternell argu-             I, IV
         ment and the sign theorem for all degenerations
III      Maps from the six-spheres and the manifolds they give                                      I, II, IV, V
IV       Smooth monodromy in Θ7                                                                     I, II, III, V
V        Complex fourfolds on 3HP2 #(−HP2 ) and a resolved fibre product                            I, III, IV

root generators and affine translations. Its base is B = P1t , with special values 0, 1, ∞, and
B ◦ = B \ {0, 1, ∞}. The ordered homology lattice and period matrix are

solution and cusp fan, take

The fixed-data period subgroup is 2klZ. At fixed admissible u there are exactly 2kl classes for

    For the standard family the reduced finite fibres have Albanese nomes

                            q2 = iw/216,         q1 = −w2 /483 = (27/64)q22 .

An antiholomorphic diffeomorphism Xc → Xc′ exists exactly when c′ − (1 − c̄) ∈ 2Z, equivalently
w′ = −w̄. The members with real structures are precisely ℜc ∈ 12 + Z. On each,

                                Aut± (Xc ) = C∗ ⋊ Z/2,                z 7−→ 1/z̄,

and there are two holomorphic-conjugacy classes of antiholomorphic involutions. For negative
imaginary w both fixed manifolds are S 3 , with the semifree circle action having the circle D2σc as
fixed set. For positive imaginary w one class is fixed-point free and the other has fixed manifold
S 3 with the free Hopf circle action, up to the stated circle and orientation conventions.

    Mechanism. Integral centralizers, finite norm maps and cusp winding determine the parameter
equivalence, while the marked reflection and cap-meridian maps determine the real forms.
Literature status. New classification for the displayed discrete data and real forms; the standard
2Z equivalence is known (Du et al., 2026a, Theorem 1.4, p. 3). Proof in outline.

    On D = Sp4 (R)/ U(1, 1) put qd (J) = ψ(d, Jd). The largest Γ-invariant open domain of proper

   For every smooth fibre its Néron–Severi group is the integral kernel in Z6 of

                  E12 − E13 τ + (6E23 − E14 )µ + E24 βc + E34 (6µ2 − τ βc ) = 0.

and
            a(Ft ) = 2 (t ∈ Ac ), a(Ft ) = 1 (t ∈ Ec \ Ac ), a(Ft ) = 0 (t ∈

                              (Πc KR )/Πc K ,→ Ft −→ C2 /(Πc KR + Πc Λ)

in outline.

1.6     How the paper is organized
The marked period and quotient coordinates lead to the exact norm, its admissible domain,
and the proper family. The intrinsic classification is followed by discrete logarithmic data,
the monodromy quotient and the exceptional fibres. Sections 12–15 compute the cotangent,
Bott–Chern and tangent cohomology; the complete coefficient construction precedes its use in
the Picard family. The integral circle quotient and the real structures then lead to the puncture
and outer-boundary problems. Their local models, component obstructions and topology are
developed with the specified marked comparison maps.
    The remaining main-body sections treat other multiplicities and finite covers, rational CM
heights, the critical level curves, and arithmetic periods. Appendices A–C contain the credited
proofs of parameter equivalence, tangent cohomology, local deformations and automorphisms.
The final part states the unresolved arithmetic questions. Each arrow in the diagram identifies a
particular supplying and receiving body argument in the table below it.

Proposition 2.12 (The compactness radius). [tag 01Q8]
    The exact set of nonzero parameters for which every ordinary fibre and both normalized finite
root fibres of Engel’s period-reference quotient are compact complex two-tori is

                                          0 < |u| < e−2πM .

This is the parameter domain for the compact family with both smooth finite root models. The
condition on ordinary fibres alone at equality is determined by whether a maximizing point of
Dpart is ordinary; the maximizing locus is determined in proposition 25.6. For an independent
reference, the radius is |λ0 |e−2πM .

Proof. 1. The function N (ξ, W ) = |W | exp(2π Im µ Im ξ/ Im τ ) is invariant under both line-
  bundle period identifications. The inverse lift multiplies it by e2πDc . More directly the real
  determinant of the four period columns is a nonzero sign times (Im τ )Dc . Thus the four
  columns generate a full lattice exactly when Dc ≠ 0, and then the quotient is a compact torus
  by a closed fundamental parallelepiped. At Dc = 0 their real span has dimension three; a
  rank-four lattice in R4 cannot result, so the quotient cannot be a compact complex two-torus.
  The function Dpart descends continuously to the connected base with the cusp removed and
  tends to −∞ at the cusp. Its image is therefore (−∞, M ]: the maximum is attained, and the
  intermediate value theorem fills all smaller values. Consequently Dc is nonzero at every base
  point exactly when Im c < −M . Since |u| = e2π Im c , the assertion follows, with the indicated
  reference scaling.

   our stated period-reference normalization, this scalar is one. For any independently chosen
   reference ϕref , the scalar is instead the precisely defined ratio λ0 = ϕpart /ϕref , evaluated on
   any ordinary fibre. Scaling the reference by a ∈ C∗ changes λ0 to λ0 /a.

Proposition 7.2 (The canonical bundle and anticanonical pencil). [tag 01PZ]
    For the standard marked (3, 4, ∞) family, including every admissible choice of its affine

The degree-two complete linear system has no base points and its map is the map f , followed by
a specified projective-coordinate map of B. The degree-one system consists of the single divisor
2S2 . Every biholomorphism between two such threefolds induces the identity on B.

Proof. 1. (Claude and L. Alpöge, 2026, Lemma 9.10(ii), p. 70, and Proposition 9.11, pp. 70–71)
  give the evaluation divisor 2S2 and f∗ ωX/B ≃ OB (p0 ) for these same marked fillings. Use the
  explicit base identifications

             h = (t − 1)−1 ,    div(h) = p0 − p2 ,         ηB = dt/(t − 1)2 ,       div(ηB ) = −2p2 .

    These local canonical transitions hold for every admissible affine translation and cusp collar
    with the fixed fan. A translation ζ 7→ ζ + a(s) contributes only ds terms to its differential,
    which vanish after wedging with the base differential. A cusp multiplier xj 7→ hj (tc )xj adds
    (h′j /hj )dtc to dxj /xj , with the same cancellation. Thus the determinant characters and
    evaluation divisor are unchanged. Tensoring evaluation with f ∗ ηB , and multiplying the base
    line by f ∗ h, gives (7.3), since f ∗ p2 = 4S2 .

2. Connected compact fibres give f∗ OX = OB by (Claude and L. Alpöge, 2026, Proposition 9.13,
   pp. 74–76). A section of OX (kS2 ), viewed as a meromorphic function, descends away from p2
   to a function b(t). On the finite cover t − 1 = s42 , its pullback is invariant under s2 7→ ζ2 s2 , so
   its Laurent exponents are multiples of four. The exact order condition is

                             4 ordp2 b + k ≥ 0     ⇐⇒      ordp2 b ≥ −⌊k/4⌋.

   Conversely every such b pulls back to an allowed section. This is (7.4) as an equality of
   subsheaves, and applying it to k = 2m, −2m gives (7.5).

3. Fix the isomorphism ωX     ≃ OX (2S2 ) from the first step. Let u correspond to its canonical
   divisor section and choose ℓ ∈ H 0 (B, OB (p2 )) with ℓ(p2 ) ̸= 0. Let v correspond to f ∗ ℓ, so
   u2 = f ∗ σp2 under the induced degree-two map. The map U 7→ u, V 7→ v sends the degree-m
   basis U m−2j V j , 0 ≤ j ≤ ⌊m/2⌋, to the pullback basis from (7.4), multiplied by u when

   For ℓ = A/(t − 1) + B, A ̸= 0, the specified base map is t 7→ [t − 1 : A + B(t − 1)]. Degree one
   has the single divisor 2S2 .

4. A biholomorphism preserves the anticanonical graded ring and its complete degree-two system,
   so it induces a projective automorphism of B. The reduced singular cusp fibre and the finite
   fibres of multiplicities three and four distinguish the three values: the pullback identity for a
   fibre divisor preserves its multiplicity, and smoothness of its reduction is preserved under the
   induced fibre isomorphism. Hence each of 0, 1, ∞ is fixed. A projective automorphism fixing
   these three points is the identity.

Proposition 7.4 (Normalized root covers and the finite fibres). [tag 01Q0]
                                                        m
      The normalized base change Nj ×Dj ∆j → ∆j , tj = sj j , is the original smooth torus family
Jj′ . The maps E1 × F1 → S1 and E2 × F2 → S2 described below are finite étale covers of degrees
9 and 8.

Proof. 1. On Jj′ , the deck generator is (s, ζ) 7→ (ζj s, Rj (s)ζ + Πc (gj s)vj /mj ). It has exact order
  mj . Its rth power changes the invariant circle coordinate γ by rγ(vj )/mj ; this is nonintegral
  for 0 < r < mj , so the action is free. The quotient map is therefore a local biholomorphism.
  Its local base function is smj and its fibre multiplicity is exactly mj . The map

                              Jj′ −→ Nj ×Dj ∆j ,         y 7−→ (qj (y), sj (y))

   is finite, is an isomorphism over s =
                                       ̸ 0, and has normal source. Locally at the central fibre
   the base-change ring has equation z mj − smj = 0. Its normalization is the disjoint union of
   branches z = ζjr s. The displayed map gives those branches in the covering charts. It is thus
   the normalization everywhere, with its specified root coordinate.


                                                   43
2. Put ρ = eπi/3 , µ1 = (2 − ρ)/3, µ2 = (1 − i)/2, κ1 = βc (z1 ) + 2µ1 , and κ2 = βc (z2 ) + 3µ2 .
   The fixed-point transformation laws for µ give the two displayed values directly. We have
   Im κj = Dc (zj ) < 0. Define

              Ej = C/(Z + κj Z),       F1 = C/(Z(ρ − 2) − 3Z),        F2 = C/(Z(i − 1) − 2Z).

   Let e1 = (0, 1, −2, 0)t , f1 = (0, 0, −3, 1)t , e2 = (0, 1, −1, 0)t , f2 = (0, 0, −2, 1)t . Direct solution
   of the fixed equations and inspection of the columns give

                     ΛA1 = Zε + Zd,       ΛA2 = Zε′ + Zd,       (Aj − I)Λ = Zej + Zfj .

   The image lattices are saturated: they are the integer solutions of γ = 0, 2u + w + 3δ = 0 and
   γ = 0, u + w + 2δ = 0, respectively. The determinants of the fixed-plus-moving basis matrices
   are −3, −2.

3. The complex-linear maps L1 (ξ, η) = (η, ξ − η/3) and L2 (ξ, η) = (η, ξ − η/2) carry the product
   periods to those fixed and moving sublattices. They induce isogenies to the original central
   tori, with kernel generated respectively by (2/3, ρ) and (1/2, i), of exact orders three and two.
   For example u b = 2d/3 + e1 − 2f1 /3 = d/2 + e2 − f2 /2 gives both kernel representatives.

4. The affine deck maps lift to

                     (ξ, η) 7−→ (ξ + κ1 /3, (ρ − 1)η),       (ξ, η) 7−→ (ξ − κ2 /4, −iη).

   Substitution in Lj gives exactly Rj Lj +Πc vj /mj . They commute with their kernel translations:
   the moving differences are periods, since (ρ − 2)ρ = −1 − ρ = −(ρ − 2) − 3 can equally be
   checked in the lattice basis, and (−i − 1)i = 1 − i = −(i − 1). More directly these assertions
   follow by the two-dimensional period matrices of the indicated rotations. A nonidentity
   element of either resulting product group translates the Ej coordinate by 2a/3 + bκ1 /3 or
   a/2 − bκ2 /4, respectively. Real independence of 1, κj proves that this translation vanishes
   only for the identity element. Hence the groups C3 × C3 and C2 × C4 act freely and have
   quotient precisely Sj .

  The homogeneous first-coordinate line is determined by its transition factors. Indeed the first
  diagonal entries in (7.2) are its factors −1/τ and 1/τ , and at the cusp both extensions require

  the displayed L with its fixed cusp condition. For the finite stalks in (7.25), use the full
  matrix Rg . Given an equivariant first component u(z), begin with the vector (u(z), 0)t and
  average it under the finite group action on vector-valued holomorphic functions. The resulting

  kernel is exactly the invariant second-component functions, which are holomorphic functions
      m
  of sj j = tj , multiplied by e. The ordinary and cusp stalks are immediate. This also proves
  that V is locally free of rank two: lift a local frame of L and join it to e.
  Both H 1 (B, OB ) and H 1 (B, OB (−p0 )) vanish: on the two standard affine charts of P1 , split
  a holomorphic Laurent series on their overlap into its nonnegative and negative powers. For
  OB these are the two coboundary contributions, and for OB (−p0 ) its transition factor shifts
  the second contribution by one, still leaving no missing exponent. The positive part converges
  on the full first affine chart and the transformed negative part on the full second affine chart.
  This proves the two vanishings, equivalently the usual additive Cousin calculation on these
  charts. The exact sequence (7.25) now gives

   in V . Project it to L and solve that additive cocycle, using its just proved H 1 vanishing. Lift

  The choices can be made coherently for every parameter and every even shift. Both initial

  This follows by adding the translation vectors in the first two lines of (7.28), and by multiplying

6. The local families constructed above are proper and holomorphic. The coherent 2Z action

   With κj (c) = κpart

                                           part                              part

These are convergent formulas because the displayed nome moduli are below one. Outside the

c′ − c ∈ 2Z. Thus the generic Albanese invariants recover the parameter modulo its exact period
subgroup.

Proof. 1. In the product covers of 7.4 the invariant holomorphic one-forms are exactly the
  multiples of dξ: the moving factor is multiplied by a primitive third or fourth root. Integration
  thus identifies the Albanese with the quotient of the fixed line by the fixed-coordinate
  projections of every deck translation. These are, respectively,

               Z + κ1 Z + 23 Z + κ31 Z = 13 Z + κ31 Z,    Z + κ2 Z + 21 Z + κ42 Z = 12 Z + κ42 Z.

   Multiplication by three and two gives the stated maps of complex tori. The two displayed
   lattices include both the product-isogeny kernels and the affine quotient translations. Using
   the positive-imaginary representatives −κ1 and −κ2 /2 in the standard modular j-series gives
   the formulas. At sufficiently small nome J is injective: 1/J(q) = q + O(q 2 ) has nonzero
   derivative at zero. Thus j2 alone distinguishes parameters within a sufficiently small punctured
   subdisc when both parameters lie there. For the full generic assertion put x = −κ2 (c)/2
   and d∗ = κpart
                1     − κpart

   Equality of the two elliptic invariants at c, c′ gives matrices M, N ∈ PSL2 (Z) with x′ = M (x)
   and
                                      N (2x − d∗ ) = 2M (x) − d∗ .
   Define the exceptional set to be the c ∈ P obtained from roots of these equations for all pairs
   for which the two rational functions are not identical. Each equation has at most two roots
   after clearing denominators, so this is a countable, explicitly specified set. For a pair giving
   an identity, let C(x) = 2x − d∗ . Then N = CM C −1 . The real matrix M preserves both the
   real circle R ∪ {∞} and C −1 (R ∪ {∞}), the parallel line with imaginary part Im d∗ /2 together
   with infinity. Their unique intersection is infinity, so M fixes infinity. An element of PSL2 (Z)
   fixing infinity is x 7→ x + b, b ∈ Z, and then N (y) = y + 2b. It follows that c′ − c = −2b. This
   proves parameter recovery from the two Albanese invariants outside the specified exceptional
   set. For biholomorphic total spaces, proposition A.2 gives the parameter congruence at every
   point.

Remark 7.7 (Period variation and norm comparisons). [tag 01Q5]

1. On a fixed ordinary fibre, the three last periods remain fixed and span C2 , whereas the first
   changes by δe. A marked complex-linear identification fixing those three periods must be
   the identity, so the marked period map is nonconstant. The set of integral markings of one
   torus is countable. A holomorphic nonconstant map from a disc has uncountable image; hence
   the unmarked fibre family is locally non-isotrivial. 7.2 transfers this to total spaces. This
   is the period argument of (Viaclovsky, 2026a, Proposition 4.7, pp. 14–15). A nonconstant
   classifying map gives positive dimension of its local target. It does not by itself determine the
   derivative at the base point, as the explicit holomorphic map z 7→ z 2 has nonconstant image
   and derivative zero at zero. A.3 computes the derivative here.
2. The comparison in (Yang, 2026, Lemmas 6.6–6.7 and 6.9, pp. 31–32; Remark 6.8, p. 32;
   Proposition 6.15, pp. 37–38) uses an integral commuting lattice map, an affine fibre lift,
   normalization of the root base change, and a norm-lattice defect. We have exhibited the
   respective maps and norm equations for the present matrices. His Proposition 6.15 obtains 6/r
   from the first-column scaling and its order-six norm image. Here the first-column scaling is one
   and the two computed norm images impose parity, yielding two. These matrix substitutions
   identify the commuting maps, finite norm equations and collar corrections with the ones just
   displayed. The nonzero absolute Kodaira–Spencer conclusion in (Yang, 2026, Theorem 6.18,
   p. 39) is obtained for the present family by the explicit computation and intrinsic-pencil
   transfer in proposition A.3.


7.4   The standard isomorphism classes
Theorem 7.8 (Classification of the standard family). [tag 01Q6]
     Fix the original cusp-regular period solution, the clockwise peripheral marking, the prescribed
periodic triangular cusp fan, the affine vectors (ε, −ε′ ), and the untwisted cusp collar. For every
c, c′ ∈ P, the constructed compact complex threefolds satisfy
                                 Xc ≃ Xc′     ⇐⇒      c′ − c ∈ 2Z.
Every biholomorphism is over the identity of the original P1 . The proper holomorphic family of
their isomorphism classes has parameter 0 < |w| < e−πM and nonzero Kodaira–Spencer class at
every point.

Proof. For the standard twist data, the classification of (Du et al., 2026a, Theorem 1.4, p. 3),
with the exact parameter identification of remark A.1, is re-derived in theorem C.5. It gives
Xc ≃ Xc′ exactly when c − c′ ∈ 2Z. The explicit maps on the regular, finite, and cusp charts are
those of proposition 7.5, displayed in (7.28) and satisfying (7.30).
   As a complex parameter space for the isomorphism classes represented by this marked family,
the quotient P/(2Z) has the explicit coordinate
                           w = exp(−πic),        0 < |w| < exp(−πM ).                         (7.31)
Indeed |w| = exp(π Im c), and two complex numbers have the same value of this exponential
exactly when they differ by an even integer. Every point in the displayed punctured disc has
a logarithm giving a c ∈ P. The exponential has nonzero derivative, so these local inverse
logarithms give the claimed quotient complex structure. The integer-period quotient seen by
the middle family instead has coordinate w2 ; it is covered two-to-one by (7.31). Its two lifts are
distinguished by the exact order-two summand in (A.7). The resulting parameter space classifies
the members of the marked family. Proposition 7.5 proves properness of this quotient family and
its joint holomorphic dependence. Its Kodaira–Spencer class is nonzero by Proposition A.3.

Proposition 8.2 (The two classes over a fixed linearization parameter). [tag 01QC]
    For multiplicities (3, 4) and |p| = 1, every admissible discrete member is biholomorphic to
one member of 7.8, uniquely modulo 2Z. At fixed nonzero admissible Engel parameter u there
are exactly two isomorphism classes, exchanged by a positive circuit of u about zero. In the
convention that Engel’s root generator is the inverse of our clockwise one and his circle class is
d, the identity of the middle quotient sends

                                 Xc+1 ←→ X(u; a0 − d/3, a1 + d/4).

Reversing both declared root generators reverses these two displayed signs.

Proof. 1. Take the canonical target data (r1′ , r2′ , k1′ , k2′ , l0′ ) = (1, −1, 0, 0, 0), for which p′ = −1.
  Choose a so that p′ = ap, and an integer n ≡ k2 (mod 2). 8.1 supplies the isomorphism
  to Xc+n . The uniqueness is 7.8. At fixed u = e−2πic , its logarithms differ by integers; the
  invariant e−πi(c+k2 ) takes exactly the two square roots of u. Both occur, already as Xc , Xc+1 ,
  and A.2 distinguishes them.

2. Put PE = Pmark , the integral isomorphism of proposition 2.3, and retain Engel’s Cf4 = e1 + e4 .
   Besides the intertwining identities in that proposition, multiplication gives PE d = δ0 , ψPE =
   −γ, PE ε = −e4 and PE ε′ = δ0 − Cf4 . They also agree with the complex periods: at z1 the
   complex-linear map (ζ1 , ζ2 ) 7→ (−ζ1 /(ρ + 1), ζ2 + ζ1 /3) carries Πc PE−1 to Engel’s columns
   (1, 0), (ρ − 1, 0), ((1 + ρ)/3, 1/3), (0, −κ1 ). At z2 his Cf4 has preimage d − ε′ and fixed period
   1 − κ2 . Thus the comparison fixes the positive circle class and the local complex structures,
   in addition to their monodromy matrices.

3. The inverse-generator convention of proposition 2.3 gives aj−1 = −PE vj /mj in Engel’s lattice
   marking (and its period image in the torus). Integer shift gives Πc+1 vj = Πc (vj + γ(vj )d),
   with γ(v1 ) = 1, γ(v2 ) = −1, proving the two signs. A positive u circuit changes log u by 2πi
   and hence changes c by −1, exchanging the square roots. This gives the claimed permutation
   with its orientation.

Proposition 8.3 (The double cover of the linearization parameter). [tag 01QD]
    Fix the sphere logarithmic data in (Engel, 2026, Remark 8.1, p. 22). The resulting family has
a proper holomorphic realization on every simply connected admissible u-open set and globally
over the punctured w-disc of proposition 7.5, with u = w2 . The order-two class of d in ΛA2 /N2 Λ
obstructs descent of this family to the punctured u-disc.

Proof. Local inverse logarithms of u give the proper local families of proposition 7.5; its coherent
even shifts give their global family over the punctured w-disc. Descent through u = w2 would
furnish an isomorphism between the two pulled-back fibres at w and −w, namely Xc and Xc+1 .
Proposition A.2 excludes that isomorphism by the nonzero class of d in ΛA2 /N2 Λ. This class
has exact order two on the normalized finite cover. The same obstruction applies to all sphere
logarithmic data by proposition 8.1, because r2 is odd.


8.2    Higher multiplicities
Proposition 8.4 (Classification for higher multiplicities). [tag 01QE]
   Let k, l be positive integers with gcd(3k, 4l) = 1, and put m1 = 3k, m2 = 4l. Consider
Viaclovsky’s sphere members expressed in the same clockwise marking, with wj = rj εj + sj d,
gcd(rj , mj ) = 1, cusp winding l0 , and p = m1 m2 l0 − m2 r1 − m1 r2 = ±1, where ε1 = ε, ε2 = ε′ .
Two such members are biholomorphic precisely when their multiplicity pair agrees and, for some
a ∈ {1, −1} and integer n = c′ − c,

   p′ = ap,   rj′ ≡ arj   (mod mj ),    nr1′ ≡ as1 − s′1     (mod k),    nr2′ ≡ as2 − s′2   (mod 2l).

The congruences on rj′ already follow from p′ = ap. For fixed discrete vectors and cusp collar the
identification subgroup is 2klZ. For fixed admissible u and this multiplicity pair, all the stated
sphere translation data give exactly 2kl isomorphism classes, permuted in one cycle by a circuit
of u about zero.

Proof. 1. The base is intrinsic for these sphere members. A biholomorphism F : X → X ′ gives
  g = f ′ F . Since H 2 (S 6 , R) = 0, the closed form g ∗ ωFS is exact. Restrict to a regular torus
  T and wedge with a flat Kähler form on T . Stokes’ theorem gives integral zero, while the
  integrand is nonnegative and strictly positive wherever dg|T ̸= 0. Thus g is constant on
  each regular fibre. The image of (f, g) is a compact analytic curve whose projection to B
  has degree one; its normalization gives a holomorphic h : B → B with g = hf . Apply the
  same construction to F −1 to see that h is an automorphism. The three homological local
  monodromy orders are three, four and infinity, independently of k, l; their intertwining maps
  under F therefore fix each special point. Hence h = 1. The nonreduced fibre multiplicities now
  force equal k, l. This is the base-preservation argument of (Viaclovsky, 2026a, Proposition 4.7,
  pp. 14–15), with the displayed maps.

2. The root model of degree m1 is the pullback of the degree-three model by s 7→ sk , and likewise
   at the other point. Its linear action remains A1 or A2 , while its root generator has order mj .
   The primitive invariant coordinate rj /mj proves freeness of every nonidentity power. The
   normalization and deck-commutation arguments of 7.4 and A.2 apply to these root covers,
   preserving the chosen generator. Their norms are

                                       N3k = kN1 ,         N4l = lN2 ,

   so the fixed-coordinate norm images are 3kZε + kZd and 4lZε′ + 2lZd. The norm equation
   (8.1), with mj replaced by these covering degrees, gives exactly the displayed congruences.
   On ordinary fibres the affine lift has simultaneous rational centralizer QI + QE, as in


                                                  55
   proposition A.2. Comparison of the constant period columns gives fibre-linear part aI, integer
   shift n and lattice map aSn−1 , where Sn = I + nE. Functorial normalization of the root base
   change makes the lift commute with the prescribed deck generator; summing its defect gives
   the norm equation. The explicit base norms are
           N3 v = 3γ(v)ε + (2vu + vw + 3vδ )d,          N4 v = 4γ(v)ε′ + (2vu + 2vw + 4vδ )d,

   primitive first elementary divisor because gcd(m1 , m2 ) = 1. Thus the sphere data have p = ±1.
   Reducing p′ = ap modulo m1 , m2 gives the two congruences for rj .

   k, r2′ modulo 2l, and the Chinese remainder theorem gives exactly one integer shift class

Theorem 9.4 (Classification in Viaclovsky’s coordinates). [tag 032S]
    Use a local logarithm c of the transported linearization, u = e−2πic , and the same reference

            b′ = αb,       hN0′ ≡ ρ′0 − αρ0     (mod k),       hN1′ ≡ ρ′1 − αρ1   (mod 2l).

The relation b′ = αb, reduced modulo 4l, gives N1′ ≡ αN1 (mod 4l), since gcd(3k, 4l) = 1. It

Corollary 9.5 (Holomorphic dependence of the comparisons). [tag 032T]
    For fixed discrete data in 9.4 and a fixed admissible shift h, the constructed comparisons are
holomorphic isomorphisms of families over a sufficiently small parameter disc. In particular, for
sphere data with multiplicities (3, 4) the identification with the standard family uses the parameter

                                    W = e−πi(c+s2 ) = (−1)s2 w.

The smooth monodromy conjugacy class around the positive parameter circle is unchanged by this
identification of twist data.

Proof. 1. The rational vectors bj , integral defects ℓj and toric exponents in the proof of propo-
  sition 8.4, transported through proposition 9.2, are independent of c. All period matrices,
  root comparisons, and cusp unit factors are holomorphic in c. On a small Stein parameter
  disc D, the correction sheaf is VB ⊠ OD . Its first cohomology on B × D is zero: project to
  D, use the same two-chart complex and H 1 (B, VB ) = 0, and then Stein acyclicity. Thus the
  affine correction can be chosen holomorphically in c. For (k, l) = (1, 1) the only nonvacuous
  finite congruence is h ≡ s2 − s′2 (mod 2), because the admissible r2′ is odd. Taking s′2 = 0
  gives the displayed parameter identification. Two choices of these family comparisons differ
  fibrewise by an automorphism of the standard member. The automorphism calculation in
  theorem C.4 identifies that group with C∗ ; it is connected. On overlapping parameter arcs
  the transitions are therefore isotopic to the identity. Composing around a circle changes the
  resulting diffeomorphism only by such an isotopy and by conjugation at the chosen base fibre.
  Multiplication of the parameter by (−1)s2 preserves the positive orientation.

Proposition 10.3 (The center and the Zariski closure). [tag 01RA]
    The group in (10.2) has center ⟨Z⟩ ∼    = Z and is the following explicit central extension of

  2

                     (B, x, k)(C, y, l) = (BC, x + By, k + l + κ((B, x), (C, y))),

Its real and rational Zariski closures are respectively the full real and rational symplectic stabilizers

Levi quotient SL2 .

Proof. 1. The numerator defining κ is divisible by 12, by the two congruences proved above.
  The bijection
                          (B, x, k) 7−→ g(B, x, a(B) − 6Q(x) + 12k)
   intertwines the displayed multiplication with matrix multiplication by (10.3). This proves
   associativity and identifies the central extension with the displayed cocycle. The kernel of the
   homomorphism to Z2 ⋊ SL2 (Z) is ⟨Z⟩. That affine group has trivial center: commuting with
   all translations forces its linear part to be I, and commuting with S, T forces its translation
   part to vanish. Thus the center of Γ is exactly the stated kernel.

2. The logarithms U − I, V − I, Z − I are linearly independent elements of the three-dimensional
   Heisenberg Lie algebra. The square of each is zero. A polynomial vanishing on all integral
   powers I + n(U − I) vanishes on the whole one-parameter line; the same holds for V and Z.
   Hence the Zariski closure contains the full unipotent radical. Its Levi image contains S, T ;
   the powers of T and of ST S −1 similarly supply the two opposite unipotent subgroups of SL2 .
   Their Lie algebras and their bracket span sl2 . They generate the connected algebraic group
   SL2 . A subgroup containing the entire unipotent kernel and surjecting onto this Levi quotient
   is the entire vector stabilizer. Its dimension is 3 + 3 = 6. This reasoning uses equations over
   Q, so proves the rational assertion as well as the real assertion.

Theorem 10.6 (The maximal domain of proper discontinuity). [tag 01RC]
    The set O is the largest Γ-invariant open subset of D on which the action is properly
discontinuous. It is also the largest such open subset for PZ . Each sign region is a complex
manifold in the analytic topology, and its quotient by either discrete group is a Hausdorff complex
analytic orbifold.




                                                62
Proof. 1. Let PR be the real symplectic group preserving the real line Re. For a fixed J, the form
  hJ (v, w) = ψ(v, Jw) + iψ(v, w) is a nondegenerate Hermitian form of signature (1, 1) on the
  complex vector space (ΛR , J), with the convention conjugate linear in the first entry. When
  qe (J) ̸= 0, the complex line Ce is nondegenerate and its Hermitian orthogonal complement is
  a complex line of the opposite sign. Normalize e by a positive real scalar and choose a unit
  vector in this complement. Comparing these two Hermitian bases for two complex structures
  with the same sign gives a real symplectic map preserving Re and conjugating one complex
  structure to the other. Thus PR is transitive on each sign region.

2. An element of the stabilizer of J inside PR is complex linear and sends e to re for a real
   nonzero r. Preservation of qe (J) gives r2 = 1. On the complementary complex line it acts by
   an element of U (1). The stabilizer is consequently the compact group {±1} × U (1). Each
   sign region is therefore a homogeneous space of PR with compact stabilizer L. Local sections
   of PR → PR /L, and a finite cover of a compact subset K, give a compact subset C of PR
   mapping onto K. Every element carrying a point of K back into K belongs to CLC −1 , which
   is compact. This proves properness. Restricting a proper action to a closed discrete subgroup
   gives the required finite-intersection condition. Both Γ and PZ are closed discrete matrix
   groups. The two sign regions are disjoint invariant open-and-closed subsets of O, so the same
   finite-intersection condition holds on their union. Proper actions by discrete groups have
   finite stabilizers and Hausdorff quotients; their holomorphic local finite-group quotient charts
   supply the asserted analytic orbifolds.

3. We prove maximality by exhibiting a dense set of points with infinite stabilizer in the zero
   locus of qe . The real vector stabilizer Pe,R acts transitively on D0 = {J : qe (J) = 0}. Here is
   a direct comparison map. In the Hermitian space just described, e is a nonzero null vector.
   Choose v with hJ (e, v) = 1, and replace v by v − 12 hJ (v, v)e. This preserves  hJ (e, v) = 1 and
   makes v null. The ordered complex basis (e, v) has Gram matrix 1 0 . The complex-linear
                                                                          0 1
                                                                              

   map between two such bases fixes e and preserves h, hence its imaginary part ψ. As a real
   map it belongs to Pe,R and conjugates the two complex structures.

4. The subgroup Pe,Q is dense in Pe,R . For the unipotent coordinates in (10.1) this is density of
   Q3 in R3 . For SL2 one may approximate a, b, c by rational numbers in the chart a ̸= 0 and
   set d = (1 + bc)/a; translates of that chart cover the group. Hence

                                         {rJ0 r−1 : r ∈ Pe,Q }

  is dense in D0 . Put R0 = g(T 6 , 0, −1), so R012 = R and (R0 − I)2 = 0. At rJ0 r−1 the nonzero
  rational nilpotent L = r(R0 − I)r−1 commutes with the complex structure and satisfies L2 = 0.
  Choose a positive integer d clearing its denominators. The matrix I + dL and its inverse
  I − dL are integral, symplectic, and fix e; this follows either by conjugating the identity
  (I + s(R0 − I))t Ω(I + s(R0 − I)) = Ω or by expanding it. The twelfth power of I + dL lies in
  Γ, because Pe,Z /Γ ∼= Z/12. It has infinite order and fixes rJ0 r−1 . Thus points with infinite
  Γ-stabilizer are dense in D0 .

5. Every open neighborhood in D of any point of D0 therefore contains a point with infinite
   stabilizer. An open set on which the action is proper cannot meet D0 . This proves the
   largest-open-set assertion for Γ. The same points have infinite PZ -stabilizer, so it proves that
   assertion for the full parabolic as well.

Proposition 11.2 (The torsion locus and its degrees). [tag 01QS]
    The locus on B ◦ where P (t) is torsion is countable and dense. Every fibre over this locus
is an abelian surface. The divisor on the smooth base cut out by 6kP = O has degree 3k 2 − 1,
including local intersection multiplicity, for every positive integer k.

Proof. 1. On a simply connected open subset write uniquely µ = a0 τ + b0 , a0 , b0 real. The section
  is torsion precisely when (a0 , b0 ) ∈ Q2 . In a local complex parameter z, direct differentiation
  gives
                                      ∂(a0 , b0 )      |µ′ (z) − a0 τ ′ (z)|2
                             det                  =−                          .
                                   ∂(Re z, Im z)               Im τ
  This determinant vanishes on no open set. On an open set of vanishing, the two real differential
  equations imply da0 = db0 = 0, hence µ = a0 τ + b0 with constant real coefficients. Analytic
  continuation would give this identity on the cover. The cusp law (τ, µ) ◦ g0 = (τ − 1, µ) then
  forces a0 = 0, and the g2 -law makes a constant µ impossible. Thus every open subset contains
  a point where this real map is a local diffeomorphism, and its image contains rational pairs.
  This proves density. For each integer triple (n, A, B), n ̸= 0, the function nµ − Aτ − B is
  holomorphic and not identically zero by the same argument. Its zeros are discrete; a countable
  union proves countability.

2. For N µ = Aτ + B, A, B, N ∈ Z, N > 0, use the linear coordinate change ζ2′ = ζ2 − (A/N )ζ1 .
   The four integral vectors

                            b − B δ,
                           Nu     b        b + Aδ,
                                          Nw    b       N γb − 6Au
                                                                 b − 6B w,
                                                                        b     δb

   span a sublattice of index N 3 . Its first two periods lie on ζ2′ = 0, and its last two lie on ζ1 = 0.
   Both intersections are genuine rank-two lattices because D < 0. Their product quotient is
   therefore a product of elliptic curves, and inclusion of this sublattice induces a finite surjective
   holomorphic homomorphism onto Ft . A positive integral form on the product can be summed
   over its finite translation kernel and multiplied by the index to descend an integral positive
   form to Ft . The Riemann polarization criterion proves projectivity.

                                                   67
3. For the degree statement, (Engel, 2026, Lemma 2.1, pp. 3–4, with the height computation on
   p. 4) gives ⟨P, P ⟩ = 1/6, χ(OS ) = 1, the component groups at the two reducible fibres have
   orders three and two, and the local corrections for P are 4/3 and 1/2. The application to
   6kP is as follows. The corrected divisor class of a section is its class minus O and a fibre
   multiple, plus the unique rational combination of nonidentity fibre components that makes
   it perpendicular to those components. On restriction to the generic fibre this assignment
   is additive because the divisor class [Q] − [O] is the group law in Pic0 . The perpendicular
   correction makes its self-intersection the negative of the height, so the height is quadratic.
   The element 6kP is in the identity component at both reducible fibres; its correction terms
   vanish. Hence
                                6k 2 = (6k)2 ⟨P, P ⟩ = 2 + 2((6kP ) · O),
   which gives the formula. The rational functions for 6P show that it has finite affine coordinates
   at 0, 1, so it is a nonzero point of each additive identity component; multiplication by k
   remains nonzero in C. At infinity its multiplicative coordinate is (−a)6k = a6k ̸= 1. Thus all
   intersections counted by the height occur on B ◦ , so their total degree is 3k 2 − 1.

  0 has coefficient vector

   in that ordered list. This coefficient change is invertible, with inverse (A′ , B ′ , C ′ , D′ , E ′ ) 7→
   (A′ − D′ c, B ′ + E ′ c, C ′ , D′ , E ′ ). Thus every integral class outside Zη has a nonidentically-zero

    Fix any admissible c. For each integral alternating matrix E, let ZE (c) be the zero set on the
marking cover of the explicit holomorphic function in (11.1), with β = β part + c given by (3.1).
Let π be the cover map to B ◦ , and define
                                                                                         

                    Ec = π                  ZE (c) ,         Ac = π                ZE (c) .
                                   [                                          [

                             E̸=0, Pf(E)=0                                  Pf(E)<0

These give the exact loci of all elliptic quotients and all abelian surfaces, respectively. The
algebraic dimension of every smooth fibre is
                                                  
                                                  2,       t ∈ Ac ,
                                                  
                                                  
                                       a(Ft ) =    1,       t ∈ Ec \ Ac ,
                                                  

                                                  
                                                            t∈/ Ec ∪ Ac .
Together with (11.1), these classify every smooth fibre by countable unions of explicit analytic
zero sets. The saturated null lattices in the proof determine all connected elliptic kernels and
their quotient maps.

Proof. 1. We apply the Appell–Humbert correspondence and Riemann projectivity criterion
  (Schnell, 2019, Theorem 4.1, p. 1, and Theorem 4.4, p. 3). Equation (11.1) gives J-invariance,
  so Definition 11.4 identifies the integral class E with the real Chern form − Im HE = E.     e
  The Appell–Humbert integrality condition is therefore exactly the integrality of E. The
  complex-oriented square computed in 11.5 shows that Pf(E) < 0 is equivalent to definiteness
  of this Hermitian form. Its sign can be chosen positive. The cited projectivity criterion then
  gives precisely the asserted abelian locus, in both directions.

                                                       70
2. For nonzero E with Pfaffian zero, its real rank is two. Its nullspace KR ⊂ R4 is a rational
   plane because it is the kernel of an integral matrix. J-invariance makes ΠKR a complex line,
   and K = KR ∩ Z4 is saturated. The maps

                             (ΠKR )/ΠK ,→ Ft −→ C2 /(ΠKR + ΠZ4 )

   are holomorphic group morphisms; the first is a closed embedded elliptic curve and the second
   is its quotient onto an elliptic curve, with connected kernel. A basis of the saturated K extends
   to an integral basis of Z4 . The other two periods project to real-linearly independent vectors
   in the one-dimensional complex quotient, because Π is a real isomorphism. They therefore
   form a discrete lattice there. Compactness follows by taking the image of its compact real
   fundamental parallelogram. Conversely any elliptic quotient pulls an integral positive area
   form back to a nonzero rank-two integral (1, 1) form. This proves the characterization of
   Ec . Equivalently all its kernels can be found by saturated rank-two lattices with a basis v, w
   satisfying detC (Πv, Πw) = 0 and real independence. This is a second exact integer test, with
   explicit inclusion and quotient morphisms.

3. For the algebraic-dimension assertion, an effective divisor on a torus has a semipositive
   Hermitian form: averaging its integration current under translations gives that constant form.
   A nonzero semipositive form has rank one or two. Rank two gives the abelian case. Rank one
   gives the elliptic quotient just constructed. In the absence of a definite form, there cannot
   be two different such kernel subtori. Indeed addition from their product onto Ft would be a
   surjective holomorphic homomorphism with finite kernel, and the product polarization would
   descend after multiplication by an integer, giving a definite form. Thus there is a single kernel
   Kt in this case. Every effective divisor is a sum of its translates: its intersection number with
   Kt is zero, whereas a curve mapping nonconstantly to the elliptic quotient has strictly positive
   intersection with a general quotient fibre. Every meromorphic function therefore factors
   through this quotient. One can check the last statement on a fibre avoiding its polar divisor,
   where it is a holomorphic function on a compact elliptic curve and hence constant; analytic
   continuation then gives the factorization. The quotient supplies nonconstant meromorphic
   functions, so the algebraic dimension is exactly one. If neither locus occurs, a nonconstant
   meromorphic function would have a polar divisor of one of the two forbidden ranks. This
   proves dimension zero. Finally monodromy acts by integral determinant-one changes of basis,
   preserving (11.1) and its Pfaffian. Thus the stated unions descend as the stated subsets of B ◦ .

  multiplication gives Pf(aη + bE) = 6a2 . For any further integral class F , substitution in
  its period equation gives a linear relation among 1, τ, µ, (µ + τ )2 . These four functions are
  linearly independent: applying g0 to a relation A + Bτ + Cµ + D(µ + τ )2 = 0 and subtracting
  yields −B + D(1 − 2(µ + τ )) = 0. A further cusp difference forces D = 0, and then B = 0;
  nonconstancy of µ forces A = C = 0. Comparison of coefficients now gives F34 = F12 = 0,
  F13 = −6F24 , and 6F23 − F14 = 12F24 , exactly F ∈ Zη + ZE. Every other integral class

                                                71
   therefore has a discrete zero set along this period locus. Excluding their countable union gives
   the asserted exact Neron–Severi lattice. It contains the nonzero isotropic E and no matrix of
   negative Pfaffian; 11.7 gives algebraic dimension one. Finally c = −5τ − 12µ − (β part + τ ) has
   imaginary part tending to minus infinity at the cusp. A sufficiently small cusp neighbourhood
   is therefore admissible by 3.3. The torsion locus of P is countable by 11.2, so its exclusion
   still leaves such points in every open subset of that neighbourhood.




11.2    Compact curves and surfaces
Proposition 11.9 (Vertical compact subspaces). [tag 01QY]
    For a standard-twist member Xc with underlying manifold S 6 , every compact irreducible
complex curve lies in one fibre of f , and every compact irreducible complex surface is one of the
reduced fibres.

Proof. 1. The given diffeomorphism with S 6 implies H 2 (Xc ; Z) = 0. For a compact irreducible
  curve C, let ν : Ce → C ,→ Xc be its normalization map. The holomorphic map f ν has
  deg(f ν)∗ OP1 (1) = 0, since its Chern class is pulled back from the zero class on Xc . A
  nonconstant holomorphic map of compact Riemann surfaces has positive degree: a regular
  value has a positive number of preimages, all with positive local multiplicity. Therefore f ν,
  and hence f |C , is constant.

2. An irreducible surface Z in the smooth threefold is an effective Cartier divisor. If its image
   were all of B, a general smooth fibre would meet it in a nonempty effective divisor D whose
   line bundle is OXc (Z)|Ft . Its integral Chern class is zero. Choose a flat Kähler form ω on
   the torus Ft . The equality Ft c1 (D) ∧ ω = D ω has left side zero and right side positive, a
                                R               R

   contradiction. Thus Z lies in a single fibre. Each reduced fibre is irreducible of dimension
   two, so containment forces equality.



Proposition 11.10 (Curves in the special fibres). [tag 01QZ]
    There is no rational curve in Xc \ Wc . There are elliptic curves outside all three special fibres,
in particular in each of the two smooth fibres Ft± . All curves in Wc are precisely the images of
irreducible algebraic curves in dP6 under its finite normalization map. Distinct curves have the
same image only for the three paired boundary lines. All curves in a bielliptic fibre Sj are images
of irreducible curves in its finite product cover.

Proof. 1. By 11.9 every curve is vertical. A holomorphic map from P1 into a torus lifts to its
  vector-space universal cover, since P1 is simply connected, and its coordinate functions are
  constant by compactness. Thus a smooth torus fibre contains no rational curve. A map from
  P1 into a bielliptic surface lifts through its finite unramified torus cover by the same covering
  criterion; the lifted map is constant. These arguments prove the first assertion, including
  possibly singular rational images. 11.1 gives an embedded connected elliptic kernel in each
  Ft± , proving the second.

2. For the third assertion let η : dP6 → Wc be the finite normalization morphism. Each
   component of the inverse image of a compact curve is compact and one-dimensional and
   maps onto that curve, because finite maps have zero-dimensional fibres. It is algebraic in the
   projective surface dP6 . Conversely its image is a compact analytic curve by properness. Away
   from the conductor, η is a biholomorphism, so two distinct curves can have the same image
   only when both lie in the conductor; its identifications are exactly the three opposite pairs


                                                  72
   computed in 11.16. This is also an explicit algebraic parametrization: the curves of dP6 are
   the three exceptional lines and strict transforms of irreducible plane curves under the blow-up
   of the three coordinate points. Their homogeneous equations and their three multiplicities
   specify the strict transforms. The finite-product cover statement for Sj follows from the
   identical proper-image and finite-preimage argument applied to its unramified morphism
   Ej × Fj → Sj ; curves in the product are algebraic.



Theorem 11.11 (All compact curves). [tag 01R0]
     The following descriptions give all compact irreducible curves of Xc . In Wc and Sj they are
exactly the images described in 11.10. In a smooth fibre of algebraic dimension zero there are
none. In a smooth fibre of algebraic dimension one they are exactly the translates of its unique
elliptic kernel Kt . In an abelian fibre they are exactly the translates of elliptic subtori, together
with the irreducible zero divisors of the positive Appell–Humbert theta sections described below.
These descriptions, 11.7, and 11.9 constitute a classification including every smooth exceptional
fibre and every compact irreducible surface.

Proof. 1. All curves are vertical by 11.9, so the list of fibre types is exhaustive. The dimension-
  zero and dimension-one assertions, including uniqueness, were proved in 11.7. Let now
  Ft = C2 /ΠΛ be abelian. For every positive definite Hermitian form H whose imaginary part
  takes integer values on ΠΛ, and every function α : ΠΛ → U (1) satisfying

                                   α(λ + ν) = α(λ)α(ν)eπi Im H(λ,ν) ,

   take the nonzero entire solutions θ : C2 → C of

                                θ(ζ + λ) = α(λ)eπH(ζ,λ)+πH(λ,λ)/2 θ(ζ).                        (11.2)

   The cocycle identity follows by multiplying the displayed factors; its integral imaginary
   cross-term has exponential one. It defines a holomorphic line bundle by quotienting C2 × C.
   The invariant zero set of θ descends to a compact divisor on Ft . Retain precisely those zero
   divisors that are reduced and irreducible. This is an exact parametrization, with all periods
   and multiplier equations given; multiplying θ by a nonzero scalar does not change its divisor.
2. The correspondence (Schnell, 2019, Theorem 4.1, p. 1, and equation (4.3), p. 2) proves that
   every holomorphic line bundle and every section on this quotient has this form. For the
   cohomology matrix the exact comparison is HE = E(      e · , J · ) − iE
                                                                         e from Definition 11.4; we
   choose the sign of E making HE positive. Its imaginary part is −E,     e which gives the integral
   semicharacter equation displayed above. The effective line-bundle criterion (Schnell, 2019,
   pp. 2–3) shows that a divisor class with positive Hermitian rank two gives exactly these
   positive theta sections. A divisor of Hermitian rank one is pulled back from its elliptic quotient
   and, when irreducible and reduced, is a single fibre. Thus it is a translate of an elliptic
   subtorus. The null lattice is computed by the explicit integer kernel in 11.7. No other rank is
   possible for an effective nonempty divisor, by positivity of its averaged current. This proves
   exhaustiveness on the abelian fibre.
3. The same equations give the curves in the product covers of Sj : compute them on its two-
   elliptic-curve lattice and take images under the specified finite morphism. Conversely each
   curve downstairs is the image of a component of its finite inverse image. In Wc the analogous
   procedure uses the homogeneous polynomial parametrization of the normalization in 11.10,
   with the three boundary pairings already identified. The maps used throughout are finite or
   closed embeddings, so they preserve compactness and give one-dimensional images.

Proposition 11.12 (Rank-three period quotients). [tag 01QM]
   At every point with D = 0, T > 0, the real-linear map Π : R4 → C2 has rank three. Write
µ = a0 τ + b0 , a0 , b0 ∈ R, and put

                                k = (1, −6a0 , −6b0 , 6a0 Re µ − Re β).

Its real kernel is Rk. The subgroup ΠZ4 is discrete exactly when k ∈ Q4 . In that case it is a
rank-three lattice in a real hyperplane and its quotient in C2 is a noncompact complex Lie group.
In every other case the topological quotient C2 /ΠZ4 is non-Hausdorff.

Proof. 1. The real matrix, with output order (Re ζ1 , Im ζ1 , Re ζ2 , Im ζ2 ), is

                                          6 Re µ Re τ 1       0
                                                              
                                        6 Im µ   T   0       0
                                                                .
                                                               
                                         Re β Re µ 0         1
                                        

                                           Im β Im µ 0        0

   Its last three columns are real-linearly independent because T > 0. Its determinant is T D,
   so at zero determinant the rank is exactly three. Substitution gives the displayed kernel,
   including its signs. If the image subgroup is discrete, it is a lattice of rank at most three
   in its real span. The homomorphism Z4 → ΠZ4 therefore has a nonzero kernel, forcing the
   displayed kernel vector with first coordinate one to be rational. Conversely a rational line has
   a primitive integral generator extendable to a basis of Z4 . The remaining three basis images
   are a real basis of the image hyperplane and hence generate a discrete lattice. Its quotient
   leaves one unbounded real direction. Finally a non-discrete finitely generated subgroup of this
   real hyperplane cannot be closed: a closed subgroup is a product of a real vector group and a
   discrete group, and a nonzero real vector group is uncountable. A quotient topological group
   is Hausdorff exactly when its identity subgroup is closed. This proves the last assertion.



Proposition 11.13 (The quotient at the parameter boundary). [tag 01QN]
   The unique degenerate base point at the admissibility boundary is t = 1. The boundary
constants c = x + i(3/π) log 6 give

                                   kerR Π = R(1, 3, −3, −x − 3/2).

For rational x + 3/2 = m/n in lowest terms, the quotient is a finite holomorphic quotient of

is generated by the real line R(0, 1) and the two periods (i, (1 − i)/2), (1, 0). Its Hausdorff quotient
is a real manifold homeomorphic to R × (S 1 )2 .

  while δ maps to (0, 1). For x + 3/2 = m/n in lowest terms, change coordinates by (ζ1 , ζ2 ) 7→

  sublattice of index four in the rank-three image: its two remaining generators are represented

Remark 11.14 (The local boundary obstruction). [tag 01QO]
    The only degenerate base fibre at the parameter boundary lies over t = 1. By 11.13, its
rank-three period quotient is noncompact for rational x + 3/2 and non-Hausdorff for irrational
x + 3/2; neither quotient can be a fibre of a proper family of complex spaces. Proposition 11.15
proves that the elliptic Albanese model also has no holomorphic Weierstrass continuation across
this boundary. The obstruction to a general proper holomorphic extension is proved in lemma 19.3
and theorem 19.4 by recovering the intrinsic divisor.

Proposition 11.15 (The natural boundary of the Albanese invariant). [tag 01QP]
    On its half-plane of definition, the j-invariant of Alb(S2 ) has no meromorphic continuation
across any point of the line Im c = (3/π) log 6. In particular the rank-three quotient at t = 1
cannot be replaced by a Weierstrass family of elliptic Albanese curves whose coefficients are
holomorphic in the same parameter across that line.

Proof. 1. The explicit Albanese lattice in proposition 7.6 is Z + (κ2 /2)Z, with κ2 = c + 3/2 −
  i(3/π) log 6 by 3.2. A positive-imaginary modulus is z = −κ2 /2, so the invariant is j(z). At a
  reduced rational r = a/b on the real boundary, choose an integral determinant-one modular
  matrix with bottom row (b, −a). Its value at r +iy has imaginary part 1/(b2 y). The convergent
  Fourier expansion j = q −1 + 744 + O(q) therefore gives growth of order exp(2π/(b2 y)) as
  y ↓ 0. A meromorphic function at r is bounded by a fixed power of 1/y, so continuation
  there is impossible. A meromorphic continuation near an irrational real point would also
  continue the same function near some rational real point in that neighbourhood, which has
  just been excluded. The affine change from c to z transfers this obstruction to the stated line.
  A Weierstrass family with holomorphic coefficients has a meromorphic j-invariant, expressed
  as the quotient of its cubic invariants, so it cannot supply the indicated continuation. This
  obstruction applies to continuation of the displayed elliptic Albanese family.

   coherent cohomology vanishes. This gives a holomorphic nonvanishing extension of [γ]. Thus
   Oγ ⊂ G is a subbundle; its quotient is O(−1) by the determinant just computed. Once again
   H 1 (O(1)) = 0 splits the extension. This proves every assertion in (12.3).

Proposition 12.5 (The root-to-coarse comparison maps). [tag PI10] Write GB = R1 f∗ OX and
GB = R1 f¯∗ OX . Then
                                      GB = ρ∗ GB .
On a root disc t = sm , take a frame (e1 , e2 ) in which the covariant action is (1, ζ a ), where

                               ρ∗ GB −→ GB ,      (u, v) 7−→ (u, sa v).
It is the map induced by normalization after the root base change. The covariant action on
cohomology is (g −1 )∗ : GB,s → GB,gs ; the pullback g ∗ : GB,gs → GB,s has the inverse eigenvalues
(1, ζ −a ).
     For the relative logarithmic cotangent bundle of definition 2.4, the evaluation pairing gives

                                           E = f¯∗ (E ∨ ),

where E is the vertical root bundle in proposition 12.2.

Proof. The factorization f = ρf¯ and exactness of finite-group invariants give Rq f∗ OX =
ρ∗ Rq f¯∗ OX . In the chosen root frame, invariance of h(s)e2 is exactly h(ζs) = ζ a h(s). Its
convergent series is therefore sa H(sm ). This gives both the invariant frame and the displayed
adjunction matrix. The normalization map agrees with this map on the punctured disc by its
marked torus identification, hence on the whole disc by holomorphic continuation. At s = 0 its
second component is zero; this specifies the comparison with the normalized torus fibre while the
coarse base-change theorem uses the full scheme fibre. Inverting the covariant action gives the
displayed pullback eigenvalues.
    On an ordinary chart the pairing is ⟨dζi , ∂ζj ⟩ = δij . At the cusp the exponential map sends
∂ζi to 2πixi ∂xi and dζi modulo the base differential to (2πi)−1 d log xi , preserving that pairing.
On a finite root chart, dt/t = m ds/s removes exactly the base logarithmic direction from the
quotient defining E. Thus these local perfect pairings agree under the transition maps and give
E = f¯∗ (E ∨ ).

Proposition 12.6 (Local freeness and the determinant line). [tag 01RR]
   Both A and E are locally free, of ranks three and two. The vertical vector ξ = ∂/∂ζ2 is

                                    ⟨·,ξ⟩
               0 −→ N −→ E −−→ OX −→ 0,                     N = det E = ωf (−2S1 − 3S2 ).       (12.7)

  calculation. At a double point write tc = xy with third coordinate z; then A = R d log x ⊕
  R d log y ⊕ R dz and its base subline is R(d log x + d log y). At either triple point write tc = xyz;
  then A has the three logarithmic coordinate basis vectors and its base subline is their sum.
  In each case that subline is a direct summand. These calculations apply on every one of the
  three double curves, including their endpoints.
2. At Sj we use the specified free cyclic quotient q : Jj′ → Nj , which is finite and étale on
   total spaces, and tj = smj on the base. On Jj′ the logarithmic conormal is mj ds/s, and
   its coefficient is a unit over C. It is again a direct summand of the logarithmic cotangent
   bundle. The comparison q ∗ A = Ω1J ′ (log(s = 0)) identifies the quotient bundles and their exact
                                       j
   sequence; faithful flat descent proves the claim downstairs.
3. On the marked torus family ξ is the constant second vertical vector. The linear monodromies
   fix it, and translations preserve it. On a cusp toric chart it is a nonzero constant vector in the
   relative logarithmic tangent lattice of rank two. A toric coordinate change xi 7→ ci (tc )tbci xi
   changes d log xi by a multiple of d log tc , so this constant relative vector descends and is
   nowhere zero in that bundle, including where its image in the ordinary tangent fibre vanishes.
   Hence evaluation is surjective and its kernel is the determinant line. Taking determinants of
   0 → f ∗ L → A → E → 0 gives

                                                               E4 (τ )2

Proof. 1. Consider the holomorphic quadratic differential Q = 6(dµ)2 − dτ dβ. Direct differenti-
  ation of the two affine transformation laws in (Claude and L. Alpöge, 2026, Definition 3.1,

                                   gj∗ Q = τ −2 Q (j = 1, 2).

   (Claude and L. Alpöge, 2026, Theorem 3.4(i), p. 14; Proposition 3.6, pp. 16–17). At z2 , τ − i
   has order two and Ks is holomorphic; therefore k has at most a simple pole at i. Away from

   descends to the compact modular curve X(1) = P1 , so it is constant. Its cusp value is one.
   This proves (12.12) and the exact two local orders.

Proposition 12.13 (The global rank and the period scalar). [tag 01RX]
    The map κ1 : R1 f∗ E → L ⊗ R2 f∗ O = O is surjective, and H 0 (κ1 ) : C2 → C has rank one.
Let h = a dζ1 + dζ2 be the unique global section of f∗ E with h(ξ) = 1. In an invariant target
frame normalized as below,
                               κ1 (hγ)(p2 ) = − 14 µs (0) = − 4i C4 .
The rank-one condition is equivalent to aτz + µz ̸≡ 0. The same direct-image exact sequence
expresses the two Hodge numbers in terms of the global rank r as h1,2 = 2 − r and h1,1 = 3 − r;
here r = 1.

Proof. 1. Sheaf surjectivity is proved in lemma 12.12. The lift h exists and is unique because
  f∗ E is an extension of O by O(−1). Its invariance under g2 gives a(g2 z) = τ a + µ, hence
  a(z2 ) = 1/2. In the quotient frame (γ, u) of G the connecting map is
                                          s
                               κ0 (h) =     (6aµs + βs )γ + (aτs + µs )u ℓ.
                                                                        
                                          4
   Choose the variable eigenframe b1 by Reynolds averaging so that γ ∧ b1 = v(s)γ ∧ u, v(0) = 1.
   Then s v(s)(γ ∧ u)ℓ is the invariant target frame. Cup product with γ gives at the central
   point −(aτs + µs )/4 = −µs /4, proving rank one.

2. To check the stated equivalence, there is a second global section

                                  qE = σ1 ⊗ u + 6σ2 ⊗ γ      of R1 f∗ E.

   It is the negative of the relative (1, 1) image of the invariant flat class η = u ∧ w + 6γ ∧ δ.
   It extends at the cusp because the relative logarithmic forms and γ, u extend there. At a
   finite point it is an invariant holomorphic tensor on the smooth cover, hence belongs to the
   four explicit invariant generators of lemma 12.12. Its cup-product row is zero, since the two
   terms are 6µz and −6µz . It is independent of hγ on every regular fibre (its σ1 ⊗ u coefficient
   is nonzero), so these two sections form a basis of the two-dimensional global section space.
   Consequently the global map has rank one precisely when its value on hγ, equivalently aτz +µz ,
   is not identically zero. The Hodge-number formulas follow from lemma 12.12, and the nonzero
   scalar above gives r = 1.

The nonzero direct-image scalar in proposition 12.13 determines that integer.

Proof. 1. Since B is a curve, coherent Leray has no differential and gives for F = ΩpX the exact
  sequences 0 → H 1 (B, Rq−1 f∗ F ) → H q (X, F ) → H 0 (B, Rq f∗ F ) → 0. Substitution of (12.14),
  with h0 (O) = h1 (O(−2)) = 1 and all cohomology of O(−1) zero, gives columns p = 1, 2
  directly. Cited result 12.4 gives column zero, and Serre duality gives column three. Replacing
  β by β + c leaves every derivative, finite eigencharacter, invariant lattice and logarithmic
  residue used above unchanged. The toric gluing units change, but their relative logarithmic
  derivatives still differ only by base logarithmic forms. Hence the same computations apply at
  each c in the stated open parameter domain.

Proof. 1. The isomorphism f∗ Ω1X = Ω1B in the residue sequence is the pullback map, so α gives

12.5    Ordinary relative differentials and the correction at the cusp
Proposition 12.17 (Relative differentials in the three local models). [tag 01S0]
   Let R = C{x, y, z}. For t = xy,

                              Ω1R/C{t} = R3 /R(y, x, 0) ≃ (x, y) ⊕ R,

and
                      Ω2R/C{t} ≃ (x, y) ⊕ R/(x, y),       Ω3R/C{t} ≃ R/(x, y).
For t = xyz, Ω1 = R3 /R(yz, xz, xy) is torsion-free of rank two and is not free at the triple point.
If I = (xy, xz, yz), there is an exact sequence

                              ∧dt                          Ru ⊕ Rv
                0 → T → Ω2 −−→ I → 0,          T =                       ,   IT = 0,
                                                      (xu, y(u − v), zv)

and Ω3 = R/I. Finally, for t = sm in R = C{s, y1 , y2 },

                                Ω1 = R2 ⊕ R/(sm−1 ) ds,
                                                                  2
                                Ω2 = R dy1 ∧ dy2 ⊕ R/(sm−1 ) ,
                                Ω3 = R/(sm−1 ) ds ∧ dy1 ∧ dy2 .

Proof. 1. The degree-one presentation is the quotient by dt; higher degrees are its exterior
  powers. At a double point the transverse quotient R2 /R(y, x) maps isomorphically to (x, y)
  by (a, b) 7→ xa − yb. Its kernel is exactly R(y, x): the equality xa = yb gives a = yh and
  b = xh by relative primality. In degree two, with basis A = dx ∧ dy, B = dx ∧ dz, C = dy ∧ dz,
  the relations are xA = yA = 0, yB + xC = 0. This gives the displayed torsion summand and
  the ideal (x, y); wedging once more gives R/(x, y).

2. At the triple point the map from ordinary to logarithmic relative one-forms sends (a, b, c)
   to (xa − zc, yb − zc). Its kernel is precisely R(yz, xz, xy): the two equations imply c = xyh,
   a = yzh, b = xzh by relative primality of the coordinates. Thus it injects into R2 , proving
   torsion-freeness. Its fibre at the maximal ideal has dimension three although its rank is two,
   so it is not free. The same minimal-generator argument works at the double locus.

3. In degree two, wedging with dt is the row (xy, −xz, yz) in the basis (A, B, C). Its syzygies
   are generated freely by u = (z, y, 0) and v = (0, y, x). To check generation, an equation
   xyA − xzB + yzC = 0 implies x | C, say C = xC1 ; then yA = z(B − yC1 ) implies A = zA1 ,
   B = y(A1 + C1 ). Thus the syzygy is A1 u + C1 v. The three relations from dt ∧ (dx, dy, dz)
   are −xu, y(u − v), zv, proving the stated presentation of the kernel. The ideal I kills it by
   those relations. Conversely the quotient I is torsion-free, so this kernel is exactly the torsion

                                                88
   of Ω2 . The presentation immediately gives Ω3 = R/I. For t = sm the sole degree-one relation
   is msm−1 ds = 0; m is a unit and taking exterior powers gives the three formulas.



Proposition 12.18 (The support of relative torsion). [tag 01S1]
    The torsion of Ω1X/B is supported precisely on S1 ∪ S2 . Its cusp modules inject into the free
logarithmic relative modules, and their minimal number of generators exceeds their rank at the
double locus. In degree two, the torsion also has support on the cusp double locus. This corrects
(Claude and L. Alpöge, 2026, Remark 9.21, p. 81), where degree-one torsion is asserted on
W ∪ S1 ∪ S2 ; the support statement in (Claude and L. Alpöge, 2026, Remark 1.3, p. 5) therefore
depends on the degree.

Proof. 1. The double and triple charts in proposition 12.17 exhaust the singular strata of W .
  Their injections into free logarithmic modules prove absence of degree-one cusp torsion. Their
  degree-two presentations have a nonzero torsion generator at every general point of a double
  curve. At a multiple fibre the finite étale comparison

                                         q ∗ Ω1Nj /B = Ω1J ′ /B
                                                           j


   is an isomorphism; its summand R/(smj −1 ) ds is nonzero for mj = 3, 4. Faithful flatness
   descends both the torsion and its support. There are no other critical fibres, and ordinary
   relative differentials are locally free on their complement. Thus the degree-one support is
   exactly S1 ∪ S2 , whereas degree two also has cusp torsion, as asserted.

                 rank d0,1

Proof. 1. Here E1p,q = H q (X, ΩpX ) and dr : Erp,q −→ Erp+r,q−r+1 are complex-linear. For r = 2,

Proposition 13.11 (Non-Kähler degrees and comparison maps). [tag 01SH]
   For k = 0, . . . , 6 the non-Kähler degrees are

                                (∆k ) = (0, 2, 2 + 2h, 4h, 2 + 2h, 2, 0).                            (13.9)
                                     p,q                                  p,q
If h ≥ 1, the two maps p+q=k HBC           → HdRk (X; C) →
                           L                                        L
                                                                 p+q=k HA are both isomorphisms
exactly for k = 0, 6. For the weaker assertion that a d-exact pure d-closed form of degree k is
  ¯
∂ ∂-exact, the valid degrees are k = 0, 1, 6, and also k = 3, 4 if h = 0.

Proof. 1. The totals from 13.5 are

                    (hkBC ) = (1, 0, 2, 2h, 2h, 2, 1),       (hkA ) = (1, 2, 2h, 2h, 2, 0, 1).

   Subtracting twice the Betti numbers gives (13.9). On the two endpoint dots both comparison
   maps are isomorphisms; all intermediate de Rham groups vanish. The first assertion follows
   by inspecting when both outside groups vanish. The weaker assertion is exactly injectivity
   of the first comparison map. In intermediate degree this is equivalent to vanishing of the
   Bott–Chern group alone, which gives the stated list. In degree zero there is no nonzero exact
   form, and in degree six integration identifies Bott–Chern and de Rham cohomology. In degree
   one the first comparison map is 0 → 0, while the second is 0 → C2 ; the formula gives ∆1 = 2.




                                                    95
Proposition 13.12 (Obstructions from exact positive forms). [tag 01SI]
   The threefold X admits no balanced, strongly Gauduchon, Kähler, locally conformally Kähler,
or Hermitian-symplectic metric.

Proof. 1. Let θ = f ∗ ωF S . It is a nonzero semipositive exact real (1, 1) form. If ω were balanced,
  the real four-form ω would be closed and X θ ∧ ω > 0, because the integrand is positive on
                        2                                2
                                                R

  the regular locus. Exactness of θ and Stokes’ theorem give zero, a contradiction.

2. More generally, if ω were strongly Gauduchon, write ∂ω 2 = ∂u   ¯ with u ∈ A3,1 . The real
   four-form Ω = ω − u − ū is closed. Bidegrees give θ ∧ Ω = θ ∧ ω 2 , so the same argument
                    2

   applies. Kähler metrics are balanced. If dω = ℓ ∧ ω with a closed real Lee form ℓ, then
   b1 = 0 gives ℓ = dv, and d(e−v ω) = 0, excluding locally conformally Kähler metrics. Finally
   any symplectic two-form on X is exact because b2 = 0. Its cube has nonzero integral for its
   symplectic orientation, whereas an exact cube has zero integral. Thus X is not symplectic
   and in particular admits no Hermitian-symplectic metric.

14.3    Changes of the specified coefficient gauge
Remark 14.4 (Fibre restriction of the coefficient representative). [tag 03CT]
   The formulas (14.13) and (14.14) choose global smooth forms through all three special fibres.
Their restriction statement uses the pullback map followed by the Dolbeault quotient on a
regular fibre. In particular, its translation-invariant value is the class represented in (13.13).
The specified coefficient form on that fibre can be related to the invariant representative by a
Dolbeault coboundary. The cocycle and weight formulas below describe the changes produced by
these choices.

15.1    All integral twists and the generic nonintegral twist
Proposition 15.1 (Integral Picard twists, including their torsion). [tag 01SO]
   For Mn = OX (n(S1 − S2 )), define u(n) = max{d(n) + 1, 0}, v(n) = max{−d(n) − 1, 0} and
ϵn = 0 if 3 | n, ϵn = 1 otherwise. Then

                              f∗ (TX ⊗ Mn ) = O(d(n)) ⊕ O(d(n − 1)),

                    R1 f∗ (TX ⊗ Mn ) = O(d(n)) ⊕ O(d(n − 1)) ⊕ O(d(n + 2)),                    (15.1)
                               R2 f∗ (TX ⊗ Mn ) = O(d(n + 6)) ⊕ Cϵpn1 .
In particular its cusp stalk is free of rank one. The four global dimensions, for every integer n,
are
                       h0 = u(n) + u(n − 1),
                       h1 = v(n) + v(n − 1) + u(n) + u(n − 1) + u(n + 2),
                                                                                               (15.2)
                       h2 = v(n) + v(n − 1) + v(n + 2) + u(n + 6) + ϵn ,
                       h3 = v(n + 6).

Proof. 1. The defining roots give f¯∗ R = OX (S1 − S2 ), so the projection formula applies to (B.8),
  with its coherent torsion summand. Tensoring (B.5) changes its generator character from −1
  to n − 1. There is exactly one invariant coefficient among exponents 0, 1 if n − 1 is 0 or 1
  modulo three, and none if it is 2. Multiplication by the coarse parameter t = s3 is zero on this
  module. Its invariant direct image is therefore exactly the displayed skyscraper, of length ϵn ,
  not a higher-order thickening. The two other special places contribute no torsion. Formula
  (2.4) proves (15.1), and the two-column Leray sequence proves (15.2).



Proposition 15.2 (The cusp length and the generic twist). [tag 01SP]
   Use the coordinate Mz = exp(zg) of 13.8. For every z ∈
                                                        / Z the cusp contribution is exactly

  (R0 f∗ (TX ⊗ Mz ))p0 = 0,    (R1 f∗ (TX ⊗ Mz ))p0 = 0,   (R2 f∗ (TX ⊗ Mz ))p0 = C{q}/(q). (15.3)

Outside the countable exceptional set explicitly defined in 15.3, these are the only nonzero direct-
image stalks. Hence the generic twist has (h0 , h1 , h2 , h3 ) = (0, 0, 1, 0), and the cusp nilpotence
exponent r equals one there.

Proof. 1. The map H 1 (W, C) → H 1 (W, OW ) is an isomorphism by the normalization complex
  in 12.2. The restriction of Mz has trivial pullback to P and descent character (exp(2πiz), 1)
  on the two generators of the dual torus. The normalization complex with these coefficients
  is the cellular cochain complex of that rank-one local system. It may be computed on the
  product cell structure as
                                (a−1,0)t    (0,a−1)
                              C −−−−−→ C2 −−−−→ C,          a = exp(2πiz).

   For z ∈/ Z this is acyclic. All normalization components remain rational with trivial pulled-back
   twist, so this normalization resolution computes H q (W, Mz |W ) through the displayed cellular
   complex. Analytic semicontinuity and base change make Rq f¯∗ Mz zero on a neighbourhood
   of p0 for all q. The projection formula and (12.5) imply the same vanishing for T ⊗ Mz .
   Tensoring (B.7) remains exact, and ν ∗ Mz = OP because P is rational and the topological first
   Chern class of Mz is zero. Thus the degree-two direct image is exactly the reduced skyscraper
   H 2 (P, KP ) ⊗ Cp0 . The reduced support gives annihilator (q) and proves (15.3).

                                                 106
2. If the twist is nontrivial on every smooth fibre and on both finite root-cover central tori, all
   cohomology of its fibre restriction vanishes at those places. Indeed a nontrivial topologically
   trivial line bundle on a complex torus has zero cohomology: in a unitary flat presentation its
   Dolbeault Laplacian has no zero Fourier mode. Tensoring the tangent extension by that line
   preserves acyclicity. Base change on the root charts and exact invariants then give zero direct
   images away from p0 . 15.3 proves that the excluded twists form a countable set. Leray now
   gives the asserted four dimensions.

Proposition 15.4 (Local complexes and every noncusp torsion length). [tag 01SR]
         / Z. At a regular resonance t∗ in (15.4), with A = C{t − t∗ }, the two stalks are
   Let z ∈
       (R1 f∗ (TX ⊗ Mz ))t∗ = (A/(t − t∗ ))2 ,        (R2 f∗ (TX ⊗ Mz ))t∗ = A/((t − t∗ )2 ).   (15.7)
