Proof. 1. We first give the comparison that turns the local calculation into a computation of
  the sheaves. On a simply connected disc of smooth torus fibres, including a finite root cover,
  retain the real marking and the holomorphic period matrix. Translation by Π(s)v, for fixed
  v ∈ R4 , is holomorphic on the total family. After subtracting the integer cocycle of a resonance,
  the line bundle has constant lattice multipliers. Multiplying the lifted real translation by
  its constant factor of automorphy makes the lattice act as the identity and gives a genuine
  compact real torus action on the line bundle. The same action acts on the tangent bundle by
  differentiation. It commutes with the full Dolbeault differential.
2. Averaging over this compact torus projects the relative Dolbeault complex onto its invariant
   part. Choose the lift so that the central trivial line has trivial character. On every nonzero
   Fourier character, the relative Dolbeault symbol is exterior multiplication by a nonzero
   covector; contraction by a dual covector is a contracting homotopy. After shrinking the disc,
   these nonzero covectors have a uniform positive lower bound for bounded Fourier frequency
   and grow linearly for unbounded frequency, because the real period matrices and their inverses
   stay bounded. The homotopies therefore preserve smooth Fourier series, with all derivatives,
   and are uniform on compact subsets of the disc. The tangent extension is triangular with
   respect to its vertical and horizontal parts; its nilpotent off-diagonal term is treated by the
   finite homological perturbation series, so every nonzero Fourier complex is still contractible.
   These homotopies exhibit averaging as a quasi-isomorphism.

Proposition 15.6 (Local separation and Kodaira dimension). [tag 0335]
    The multiplicity pair (3k, 4l) is constant on every sufficiently small deformation of one of the
preceding members. Distinct pairs therefore determine disjoint open loci among these isomorphism
classes. Moreover
                                             −∞, kl < 3k + 4l,

Equality kl = 3k + 4l never occurs under gcd(3k, 4l) = 1.

Proof. 1. Local miniversality identifies every small deformation with the fixed-data period family;
  9.4 makes its multiplicity pair an intrinsic biholomorphic invariant. The canonical formula of
  B.2 and connected fibres identify its pluricanonical sections with those of O(r(kl − 3k − 4l))
  on the root curve. Negative weight has no sections. Positive weight has linearly growing

  k | 4l; coprimality forces k = 1, and then l = 3 + 4l is impossible.



Proposition 15.7 (Separation in irreducible analytic families). [tag 033B]
   Suppose a proper holomorphic submersion over a connected irreducible reduced complex base
has two fibres of the type in B.2. Then their multiplicity pairs agree. For these members the
asymptotic number
                                         r ) − h0 (X, K −r )
                                 h0 (X, KX                      1   1   1
                     s(X) = lim                        X
                                                             =    −   −
                             r→∞             r                 12 3k 4l
recovers the ordered multiplicity pair uniquely.

Proof. 1. For coprime m, n, the number of nonnegative solutions of mi+nj = N is N/(mn)+O(1)
  as N → ∞: there is one permitted residue class of j modulo m, and its representatives lie
  between 0 and N/n. The canonical formula in B.2 proves the displayed limit, with a negative
  value when the anticanonical counts grow. Write 1/12 − s(X) = a/b in lowest positive terms.
  Since gcd(m + n, mn) = 1, we have a = m + n, b = mn. Thus m, n are the two roots of
  T 2 − aT + b. Their order is determined because only m is divisible by three and only n is
  divisible by four.

2. For every fixed integer r, apply the finite-free-complex theorem of (Bănică and Stănăşilă,
   1976, Chapter III, Theorem 4.1, p. 124) to the relative canonical power, which is an invertible
   flat sheaf for a holomorphic submersion. Its zeroth cohomology dimension has analytic
   jumping loci. On an irreducible base any value constant on a nonempty open set is its generic
   value: a proper analytic jumping locus has empty interior. Local miniversality in B.2 makes
   these dimensions constant near either of the two given fibres, since all nearby fibres have
   the same multiplicities and their canonical formula is independent of the period parameter.
   Consequently the two fibres have equal dimensions for every positive and negative r. Their
   limits s(X) are equal, and the preceding arithmetic recovers the same pair.

Lemma 16.5 (The cusp neighbourhood and its circle classes). [tag IP07]
  For the cusp neighbourhood N0 and the vanishing lattice K = Z⟨w, d⟩,

                                          π1 (N0 ) = Λ = Λ/K.                                      (16.5)

The punctured-cusp map to this group kills K and the base meridian. Both long-period covectors
extend in integral H 1 (N0 ; Z). The literal character on an ordinary fibre has no extension to all
of X ≃ S 6 .

Proof. The toric covering has rays (v, 1) for all v ∈ Z2 . Meridians about its toric divisors kill the
whole cocharacter lattice: (0, 1) is a ray and (ei , 1) − (0, 1) = (ei , 0). Hence the toric cover is
simply connected. Its free period deck group is Λ = Λ/K, proving the displayed isomorphism.
The base meridian bounds the disc given by a point of the dense orbit on a central component.

of θγ to all of X ≃ S 6 would give a nonzero homomorphism H1 (F ) → Z factoring through
H1 (X) = 0, which is impossible.

Proposition 16.6 (The filled three-dimensional target). [tag 02PC]
     For the original data the quotient over the complement of the cusp disc is the exterior of the
(3, 4) torus knot, with the specified Seifert structure. For general admissible (l0 , l1 , l2 ) the filled
quotient is the lens space determined by the following meridian slopes in one oriented integral
torus basis (ρ1 , h):

       µ1 = (3, −l1 ),      µ2 = (−4, 4l0 − l2 ),         det(µ1 , µ2 ) = p = 12l0 − 4l1 − 3l2 .   (16.6)

In the lens-space convention that the second meridian is −q0 µ1 + pλ1 , where det(µ1 , λ1 ) = 1, the
lens parameter satisfies 3q0 ≡ 4 (mod p). In particular the target depends only on the signed
integer p, and is a three-sphere exactly when |p| = 1.

Proof. 1. Let P be the three-holed sphere, with oriented boundary meridians ρ0 + ρ1 + ρ2 = 0
  and positive fibre h. The two finite meridian relations are 3ρ1 − l1 h = 0 and 4ρ2 − l2 h = 0;
  the cusp solid-torus meridian is ρ0 + l0 h. Eliminating ρ0 gives ρ2 = l0 h − ρ1 on the annulus
  joining the finite solid tori, which gives exactly (16.6). Since both slopes are primitive, this is
  a genus-one Heegaard splitting. Choose a, b ∈ Z with al1 + 3b = 1 and put λ1 = (a, b). Direct
  multiplication gives

                      µ2 = −q0 µ1 + pλ1 ,     q0 = a(4l0 − l2 ) + 4b,      3q0 − ap = 4.           (16.7)

   This proves the claimed lens parameter in a convention fixed by the displayed oriented
   meridians. The fundamental group of this gluing is Z/|p|. Admissibility implies gcd(p, 6) = 1,
   so the modular inverse of 3 used above exists.

2. For (l0 , l1 , l2 ) = (0, 1, −1) the two exceptional-fibre data are (3, 1), (4, −1). They are realized
   by the circle action
                                    s · (z1 , z2 ) = (e4is z1 , e3is z2 ) on S 3 ⊂ C2 .
   Its invariant map is [z13 : z24 ]; the local circle translation residues are 4−1 = 1 (mod 3) and
   3−1 = −1 (mod 4). Removing a regular orbit gives the same two Seifert solid tori and their
   product annulus as above. A regular orbit is the (3, 4) torus knot under the coordinate
   exchange (z1 , z2 ) 7→ (z2 , z1 ) when the opposite ordering is used. The displayed orbit map and
   meridian slopes identify the manifold with its peripheral structure.

16.1    The cusp replacement and its relative uniqueness
Theorem 16.7 (The cusp replacement and its relative homotopy class). [tag 02PD]
    For every admissible member, there is a smooth map eq : X → Q over B whose restriction
outside an arbitrarily small cusp neighbourhood is the literal circle quotient. For fixed quotient
gluing, its homotopy class is independent of the cusp replacement, provided the replacement maps
the cusp neighbourhood into its designated solid torus and is kept fixed on its outer collar. In
particular there is a well-defined class for the original member X ≃ S 6 .

Proof. 1. On the cusp boundary use the product coordinates (q, θγ ) after the specified collar
  shear. By (16.5), the boundary circle class extends to N0 . Since S 1 = K(Z, 1), it has a
  continuous representative θ′ : N0 → S 1 . Its restriction to the boundary is homotopic to the
  given one: the two maps induce the same homomorphism on π1 of the boundary mapping torus.
  The homotopy-extension property for a manifold with boundary changes θ′ on a collar so that
  it agrees exactly with θγ there. Relative smooth approximation gives a smooth representative,
  still equal on a smaller collar. Then (f, θ′ ) is the required map into D2 × S 1 , and agrees with
  the finite-filling maps on the overlap. Both components of (f, θ′ ) are smooth on N0 , so the
  product map is smooth at the critical points of f as well.
2. The inclusion ∂N0 → N0 surjects on π1 , as (16.5) explicitly shows. It follows that H 1 (N0 ; Z) →
   H 1 (∂N0 ; Z) is injective. Since both spaces are connected, the long exact sequence gives
   H 1 (N0 , ∂N0 ; Z) = 0. Two circle replacements agreeing on the boundary therefore have
   quotient whose relative H 1 class is zero, hence have a relative homotopy. Keeping the base
   coordinate fixed gives the required homotopy of maps into the solid torus. Different choices of
   the collar size are compared on a common smaller collar. This proves the assertion.

   final classification transfer to the original coordinates. Then log s′j = log sj on paired branches.
   Under ζ 7→ −ζ̄, conjugation of 1/(2πi) supplies the compensating sign, and the identity of
   the two logarithmic collar translations follows exactly. Two roots of the same fixed real
   coordinate differ by an mj th root of unity; this changes the comparison only by a constant
   period-coordinate translation, and the additive correction of 7.5 glues those constants. The
   preceding holomorphic-unit comparison handles a different original local base coordinate. Its
   inverse has the same construction.

5. At the cusp choose s = (2πi)−1 log tc , so s 7→ −s̄. The full holomorphic unit matrix satisfies
                                                                  !

   The integral extra matrix has trivial exponential. Hence (x, tc ) 7→ (x̄, t̄c ) intertwines the full
   cusp deck groups, with the same integral index λ. The toric fan is defined over Z, so this
   map extends antiholomorphically on every toric chart and stratum. It preserves the untwisted
   cusp collar. We have therefore constructed an antiholomorphic map to the target datum with
   parameter −c̄, r1′ = −1, k1′ = 1, r2′ = 1, k2′ = −3, l0′ = 0, whose p′ is +1.

6. Apply 8.1 to normalize this target back to the canonical p = −1 datum. Take a = −1 and
   the odd shift n = 1. This gives a holomorphic map to X1−c̄ . Every other antiholomorphic
   map, composed with the inverse of this one, is a holomorphic comparison between canonical
   members. 7.8 gives exactly the stated congruence. Exponentiating it gives w′ = −w̄.

7. We construct an involutive splitting of the group extension. For a real member, choose
   any resulting antiholomorphic self-map J. Its derivative on ordinary fibre coordinates is
   +complex conjugation: the initial reflection has derivative −complex conjugation, while the
   normalization just used has linear part −I2 . Hence it conjugates translation by b ∈ C/Z to
   translation by b̄. Its square is a holomorphic translation b0 . Commuting J with J 2 shows
   b0 = b̄0 in C/Z. This equality forces the imaginary part of a representative of b0 to vanish,
   so take b0 ∈ R. Replacing J by the composition of translation by −b0 /2 with J changes its
   square to b0 − b0 /2 − b0 /2 = 0. We have an antiholomorphic involution. Under b 7→ e2πib , its
   conjugation action is z 7→ 1/z̄. This proves the split group and specifies its antiholomorphic
   coset.



Proposition 17.3 (Two conjugacy classes of real structures). [tag 02PE]
    For a real member the antiholomorphic involutions have exactly two conjugacy classes under
holomorphic automorphisms. For any fixed involutive splitting σ they are represented by σ and
ρ(1/2)σ. Every nonempty fixed set is a closed connected orientable totally real three-manifold
with the mod-two homology of S 3 . The circle ρ preserves each such fixed set and acts semifreely
on it.

Proof. 1. Proposition 17.2 identifies the full holomorphic group with C∗ and gives the conjugation
  action z 7→ 1/z̄. Thus the square of zσ is z/z̄, and it is an involution exactly for z ∈ R∗ .
  Conjugation by y ∈ C∗ changes this coefficient to |y|2 z, giving exactly the two sign classes.



                                                 118
2. At a fixed point an antiholomorphic involution has a real three-dimensional fixed tangent space,
   and its complexification is the full tangent space. An invariant metric and its exponential
   map identify its fixed locus locally with this real subspace. It is therefore a closed totally
   real three-manifold. The smooth Z/2 action admits an equivariant triangulation by (Illman,
   1972, Theorem 3.1, p. 48); compactness and finite dimension give the finite-dimensional
   G-CW hypothesis. Smith’s theorem, in the form of (Knudson, 2004, Theorem 4.1(1), p. 10),
   applies to the smooth finite action on the sphere and gives the stated mod-two homology.
   A nonempty three-dimensional fixed set is consequently connected, and its first mod-two
   cohomology vanishes; its orientation class w1 therefore vanishes. On the unit circle 1/z̄ = z,
   so σ commutes with ρ. Its stabilizers are inherited from the semifree action on X and are
   therefore either trivial or the whole circle.

                                                 121
Theorem 17.6 (The real three-manifolds). [tag 02PG]
    Every nonempty fixed set in Theorem 17.5 is diffeomorphic to S 3 . Its fundamental group is
trivial and its integral homology is (Z, 0, 0, Z). For negative imaginary w, the restricted circle
action is the standard semifree action on S 3 with fixed circle D2σc . For positive imaginary w, the
nonempty real form has a free circle action isomorphic, up to circle and orientation conventions,
to the Hopf action.

Proof. 1. For negative imaginary w both fixed manifolds meet D2 in one circle. Their circle
  action is semifree, so the orbit space is a compact orientable surface with boundary. The local
  quotient at a fixed circle is the quotient of S 1 × C by scalar rotation on C, hence is a boundary
  collar. Over the surface interior the principal circle bundle is trivial because the surface has
  boundary and H 2 = 0. Changes of boundary trivialization extend over the attached normal
  discs by rotation. Thus the three-manifold is

                                      (B × S 1 ) ∪∂B×S 1 (∂B × D2 ).

   If B has genus gB and bB boundary components, van Kampen or its surface handle decompo-
   sition gives first homology Z2gB +bB −1 . Smith’s theorem makes this rank zero. Since bB > 0,
   we have gB = 0, bB = 1. The displayed manifold is then ∂(D2 × D2 ) = S 3 , with the indicated
   circle action. This derives the smooth recognition from an explicit surface decomposition.

2. For positive imaginary w the nonempty real manifold is free under ρ. The two real tori on
   t < 1 join at the single real torus over 1. At 0 the odd root comparison is a torus product. At
   infinity they are capped by the real neighbourhoods of D1 and D12 . These are solid tori: the
   primitive circle in the edge direction collapses and the remaining real circle is their core. In
   the outer real-fibre lattice Z⟨w, d⟩ the two cap meridians are w and w − d.

3. We check the intervening torus identification. Put B1 = A−1            −1
                                                                     2 A1 A2 and C = B1 . The two
                                                                                             2
                                                                 −1
   real-arc involutions satisfy R< Rm = B1 , Rm B1 Rm = B1 and B1 = I. Moving between the
                                                                            3

   real root lifts requires B1k Rm B1−k = B1 Rm , so 2k ≡ 1 (mod 3) and k = 2. Thus the odd-root
   transport is C. It satisfies R< = CRm C −1 , and C(u + w) = −w + d. The exchange across the
   multiplicity-four real torus is A22 ; after this odd-root transport it is CA22 C −1 , whose restriction
   to ⟨w, d⟩ is w 7→ −w, d 7→ d. Consequently the meridians, compared on one boundary torus,
   have determinant of absolute value one. The resulting genus-one Heegaard splitting is S 3 :
   primitive meridians intersecting once can be taken to the two coordinate circles by an integral
   torus automorphism, giving the usual two solid tori of S 3 . The free circle d then has Euler
   number of absolute value one, so the displayed bundle over S 2 is the Hopf bundle. This proves
   the fundamental-group and integral-homology assertions.

 f = g(−I, 0, 6). Their maps on the three coordinates are (B, x, t) 7→ (AB, Ax, t + α(A)), with

Proof. 1. The projection g(B, x, t) 7→ B maps Γ onto SL2 (Z) by 10.2. For any B ∈ SL2 (R), the
  usual modular reduction gives an integral matrix A with AB = n(u)a(v)k(θ) in the stated set.
  Choose a lift g(A, y, s) ∈ Γ and multiply on the left. For the displayed edge generators, the

  map from a general parabolic element to one over the modular set.

2. Two choices of lift over the same A differ by Γ ∩ H. The group calculation in 10.2 identifies
   this kernel with ⟨U, V, Z⟩, where U = g(I, (1, 0), −6), V = g(I, (0, 1), −6) and Z = g(I, 0, 12).

3. The multiplication law sends (x, t) under U to (x + (1, 0), t − 6 − 6x2 ), and under V to
   (x + (0, 1), t − 6 + 6x1 ). Powers of these maps first put x1 and x2 in [0, 1). A power of Z then
   puts t in [0, 12). All three are left translations in Γ, so they retain the original coset.

4. Within the interiors of these intervals equality of two reduced representatives forces their kernel
   element to have zero x-translation and then zero central translation. Modular uniqueness
   gives the same conclusion in the base interior. The usual edge and elliptic identifications,
   lifted by the specified surjection, account for the measure-zero boundary. This proves the
   fundamental-set assertion and all displayed Heisenberg identifications.

18.3    Extending the marked base map
Theorem 18.3 (Extension of the marked base map). [tag 02RE] [tag 0314]
    For every admissible (3, 4) twist, the marked map f : Xc → P1 extends meromorphically over
every proper Hausdorff analytic filling of a finite parameter cover. For a smooth given total space,
its graph is a proper projective modification carrying the marked map. In general, a smooth
proper modification carries a holomorphic marked map to P1 , and hence a proper map to P1 × ∆.

Proof. 1. Take the reduced irreducible component containing the punctured family. It is closed
  and proper; discarding other central components preserves that family. Resolve it isomorphi-
  cally over the smooth punctured family. We use analytic resolution (Bierstone and Milman,
  1997, Theorem 1.6 and the following noncompact extension, p. 215): reduced complex analytic
  spaces admit proper modifications by locally finite sequences of smooth-centre blowups with
  smooth result. It can be chosen unchanged over the nonsingular locus. Properness makes the
  neighborhoods of the central fibre relatively compact, so the stated analytic hypotheses hold.
  Write g : Z → ∆s for the smooth result. The following argument also applies directly to a
  smooth given total space.
                                                   −2
2. We shrink the disc whenever necessary. Put L = KZ/∆ s
                                                         . The relative canonical bundle here
                                  −1
   is the line bundle KZ ⊗ g ∗ K∆  s
                                     ; its restriction to a nonzero fibre is that fibre’s canonical
                                                                    −2
   bundle. The precise proposition 7.2, proposition 7.4 input is KX  s
                                                                       ≃ fs∗ OP1 (1), with connected
   fibres and no further sections. Therefore h0 (Xs , L|Xs ) = 2, and its complete linear system
   is the given map fs , up to a projective change of coordinate. The three critical values are
   intrinsically distinguished by their fibres: multiplicity three, multiplicity four, and reduced
   normal crossings, respectively.

3. Grauert’s proper direct-image theorem (Grauert, 1960, §6, Hauptsatz I, p. 59) makes F = g∗ L
   coherent. It is torsion-free: multiplication by a nonzero base germ is injective on L, because g is
   nonconstant on the smooth connected total space, and hence is injective on its direct image. A
   coherent torsion-free sheaf on the smooth disc is locally free. Its rank is two. On the punctured
   disc, constant h0 = 2 and the analytic base-change theorem of Proposition 12.1 identify its
   fibres with the complete spaces of sections. Choose a frame (σ0 , σ1 ) of F. Evaluation gives
   two global holomorphic sections of L on Z, and thus a meromorphic map F0 = [σ0 : σ1 ] to P1 .

4. Its graph is analytic and proper by the following local construction. In a local trivialization of
   L, write the sections as a, b. Remove their common divisorial factor in the regular local ring
   of the smooth space Z. The equation va − ub = 0 in Z × P1[u:v] then has a unique component
   dominating Z; it is the closure of the graph where (a, b) ̸= (0, 0). These local components glue.
   Denote the resulting reduced graph by G. The projection G → Z is proper and projective,
   and is an isomorphism over ∆∗s . The map

                                H : G −→ P1 × ∆s ,        H = (F0 , g),

   is proper. Locally G is a hypersurface in the smooth space Z × P1 . The vanishing of the
   maximal Jacobian minors for its equation and the two target coordinates defines the closed
   analytic locus C where H is not a submersion; singular points of G are included.

5. The image H(C) is a closed analytic subset of the target. One may deduce this precise
   proper-image assertion from the same direct-image theorem: the coherent sheaf H∗ OC has
   support exactly H(C), since the constant section 1 is nonzero at every nonempty proper fibre.
   Over ∆∗s this image consists exactly of three distinct critical-value sections. It cannot have
   a two-dimensional component, since such an analytic component would contain an open set
   of the connected two-dimensional target and hence meet the punctured region in dimension


                                                131
   two. Remove any component contained in P1 × {0}. The remaining reduced analytic curve is
   proper with zero-dimensional fibres over the disc, and is therefore finite over it.

6. Each of the three labelled sections on the punctured disc belongs to a degree-one branch of
   that finite curve. Indeed their labels are intrinsic and cannot be permuted by continuation.
   The normalization of a degree-d branch over a punctured disc has cyclic monodromy of
   length d; a single-valued labelled section therefore has d = 1. The normalization extends it
   holomorphically to a map from the full disc to P1 . Let these three maps be c1 (s), c2 (s), c0 (s),
   in the multiplicity-three, multiplicity-four and cusp order. They may collide at s = 0.

7. For s ̸= 0 the unique projective transformation sending (c1 , c2 , c0 ) to (0, 1, ∞) has meromorphic
   coefficients at 0. In a common affine chart its value at z is
                                             (z − c1 (s))(c2 (s) − c0 (s))
                                  As (z) =                                 ;
                                             (z − c0 (s))(c2 (s) − c1 (s))

   homogeneous brackets give the same formula if a value is infinite. The denominators are not
   identically zero, since the three values are distinct on the punctured disc. Thus As ◦ F0 is
   meromorphic on Z. On every nonzero fibre it agrees with the marked fs , because both are
   the complete bi-anticanonical map and have the same three labelled values. Thus the two
   maps agree over the punctured disc.

8. Finally the graph of As ◦ F0 is constructed by the same local two-section argument after
   clearing powers of the base coordinate in its meromorphic coefficients. Its projection to Z is the
   asserted proper projective modification, and its second projection is the required holomorphic
   marked map. Resolve this reduced graph isomorphically over the smooth punctured family
   by the same analytic resolution theorem. Composing its holomorphic marked map with the
   resolution gives the asserted smooth proper modification.

  The global monodromy on ΛQ /Qδb has no nonzero vector with finite orbit.

   integrally. This includes every multiplicity e. After a local finite root in the base, each
   horizontal component inherits this zero class from its global preimage.

Theorem 18.6 (Nonexistence of proper fillings). [tag 0313] [tag 030D] [tag 031A] [tag 02RH]
   For every admissible (3, 4) twist, the punctured family has no proper Hausdorff complex-
analytic filling at w = 0 after any finite parameter cover. This includes every sphere member
and permits arbitrary singularities, multiplicities and extra central components.

Proof. 1. A proper filling pulls back properly to a further cover w = R6n . By 18.3 we resolve
  its dominating component and marked-map graph. Near infinity take the finite base change
  q = Q12m , normalize the dominating component, and resolve it. Principalize the inverse image
  of the two axes using (Bierstone and Milman, 1997, Theorem 1.10, p. 216, with the analytic
  category in (0.1)(2), p. 208). That theorem turns a coherent ideal on a smooth analytic space
  into a locally monomial ideal after proper smooth-centre blowups. The axis ideal is coherent
  and the relevant inverse image is compact over a smaller closed bidisc, so its hypotheses hold.
  The smooth torus family over Q∗ × R∗ is unchanged.
2. The proper map to the bidisc has connected fibres. Its Stein finite factor is generically one
   sheet because its general fibre is a connected torus. A finite birational map to the normal bidisc
   is an isomorphism: its finite local algebra is integral over, and contained in the fraction field
   of, the integrally closed local ring of that bidisc. In particular the corner fibre is connected.
3. In the axis complement, the original logarithmic deck lifts have
         AQ = I − 12mE32 + 12mE41 ,            AR = I + 12nE41 ,          [Q, R] = −12mnbδ.

   The affine relation is the difference H(s + 12m) − H(s) = 12mb through n parameter turns.
   The lifts
                                      Qo = T−mbbγ Q,   Ro = R
   commute. They give a specific semidirect product Λ ⋊ Z2 ; central δ corrections do not affect
   the following coefficients.
4. For every irreducible axis component Di , put
          αi = ordDi (Q),   βi = ordDi (R),    κi = the γb coefficient of its lattice meridian.
   Its positive meridian is (λi , αi , βi ), with nonnegative orders and positive sum. Conjugation
   changes its lattice vector by a vector killed by the first-coordinate covector; thus κi is
   independent of its basing path in the complement. Meeting components have commuting

   commutator gives

   Its strict transform meets the corner by properness. Its ratio is zero by 18.5.

Definition 19.1 (Boundary coordinates and the Hausdorff reflection). [tag PT08] For the standard

Lemma 19.3 (The intrinsic anticanonical surface family). [tag 032B]
    Let V be a connected Riemann surface and π : X → V a flat proper holomorphic map of
reduced complex spaces. Suppose that over a nonempty open subset V0 , the fibres are smooth
compact threefolds whose unique anticanonical divisor is 2Sv , where Sv is a smooth connected
surface with b1 (Sv ) = 2. Then there is an open subset V good ⊂ V , with at most countable
complement, on which the reduced support of the relative anticanonical divisor is a smooth proper
surface family. Its Albanese elliptic invariant is holomorphic.

Proof. 1. Flatness and the smoothness of the fibres over V0 imply that π is a submersion there:
  the local analytic smoothness criterion applies because the base is smooth. The relative
  nonsmooth locus is a closed analytic subset, by the Jacobian criterion. Its proper image is
  analytic by the coherent direct-image argument in Theorem 18.3, applied to the structure
  sheaf of this proper analytic locus. It misses V0 , hence is discrete. We remove it and work over
  the connected remaining curve V ′ . Removing a discrete subset from a connected Riemann
  surface does not disconnect it. Thus X ′ → V ′ is a smooth proper map.

2. Write L = KX−1′ /V ′ . Grauert’s direct-image theorem (Grauert, 1960, §6, Hauptsatz I, p. 59)
   makes F = π∗ L and R1 π∗ L coherent. His erratum (Grauert, 1963, item 2, p. 36) corrects the
   assertion in §7, Satz 2 that the locus where the comparison map fails to be bijective is always

                                                137
   closed. For the present smooth curve, the following exact sequence computes the canonical
   base-change map and its torsion obstruction. For a local base parameter t vanishing at v,
                                                                     t
   smoothness and invertibility of L give an exact sequence 0 → L →  − L → i∗ Lv → 0, where
   i : Xv ,→ X is the closed embedding. Its direct-image sequence gives, at v,
              ′


                        0 −→ Fv /tFv −→ H 0 (Xv , Lv ) −→ (R1 π∗ L)v [t] −→ 0.

   The last term denotes elements annihilated by t. The support of the torsion subsheaf of the
   coherent module R1 π∗ L is closed discrete, by the structure theorem for finitely generated
   modules over the local discrete valuation rings of the smooth base curve. Outside that support
   the canonical base-change map is an isomorphism. Also F is torsion-free: multiplication by a
   nonzero base function is injective on sections of L. It is therefore locally free. Its rank is one
   by choosing an interior point outside the discrete torsion support. Locally a frame gives a
   relative section σ of L, nowhere identically zero on a fibre. Its divisor is independent of the
   frame. Let D be its reduced support. On V0 , the divisor is 2Sv and D is exactly Sv .

3. The map D → V ′ is proper, since D is closed in a proper space. There is no vertical divisor
   component: a vertical divisor in the smooth total space would contain a whole irreducible
   fibre, contrary to the nonzero restriction of σ. Every horizontal component has proper image
   all of the connected base. Since the interior fibre is irreducible, there is exactly one horizontal
   component, and its multiplicity in div σ is two. Thus div σ = 2D on this base. In the smooth
   ambient space D is Cartier. It is flat over the curve because its local rings are torsion-free
   over the base discrete valuation ring. Restriction of the Cartier identity to an interior fibre
   gives 2Dv = 2Sv , whence Dv = Sv with its reduced structure. Flatness and the smoothness of
   these fibres make D → V ′ smooth over V0 . Its analytic nonsmooth locus therefore misses V0 ;
   the proper mapping theorem once more makes its image discrete. After deleting that image,
   D → V good is a smooth proper family of connected surfaces. Each deletion is closed discrete
   in the then-current open curve. Their finite union is at most countable, and the final good
   locus is open.

4. Ehresmann’s theorem identifies the smooth fibres along every path; in particular their first
   Betti number is two. (Buchdahl, 1999, Theorem 11, p. 297) then gives a Kähler metric on
   every fibre. Hence h1,0 = 1, every holomorphic one-form is closed, and the integral period
   map has a rank-two lattice image. Constant h1,0 , properness, and analytic base change
   supply a local relative holomorphic one-form. Locally on a simply connected base disc, a
   relative one-form and a basis of the free part of H1 give two holomorphic periods. Their ratio
   lies in one half-plane after orienting the basis. To see holomorphicity directly, choose local
   primitives of the closed relative form on simply connected fibre charts; their differences are
   holomorphic functions of the base, and the finite sum around a transported cycle is its period.
   The modular invariant of the ratio is independent of all choices, so these local invariants glue
   to a holomorphic function on V good .



Theorem 19.4 (Nonextension across the parameter boundary). [tag 032C]
    For every w0 with |w0 | = 216 and every connected open neighbourhood U of w0 , there
is no flat proper holomorphic map X → U from a reduced complex space whose fibres over
U ∩ {0 < |w| < 216} are biholomorphic, fibre by fibre, to Xw . In particular an extension
isomorphic to the given family over that intersection does not exist.

Proof. 1. We may restrict a putative extension to a small disc meeting the circle, with closure
  away from zero. This is a holomorphic base restriction; properness and flatness are preserved.
  The calculation of the canonical evaluation in proposition 7.2, gives KXw = O(−2S2 (w)) and

   h0 (KX w
            ) = 1. Its sole divisor is 2S2 (w), so it is intrinsic under every fibrewise biholomorphism.
   The surface has b1 = 2: on its finite product cover the rotation kills the moving factor in
   invariant first cohomology and fixes the elliptic factor. These are the exact proposition 7.2,
   proposition 7.4 and proposition 7.6 steps required in Lemma 19.3.

2. The at most countable exceptional set in that lemma cannot contain an arc of the circle.
   Choose a boundary point outside it and then a smaller disc on which the reduced divisor is a
   smooth proper surface family. Its holomorphic Albanese invariant agrees, pointwise on the
   inner part, with J(iw/216). The pointwise agreement gives an analytic continuation through
   that point, contrary to Proposition 19.2.

Proposition 19.6 (Nonseparation beyond the rank-drop line). [tag 032E]
    At the boundary value a = 0, the central points with (η, ξ) = (0, 0) and (0, −3i) cannot be

                            λn = n2 (γb + 3u

Theorem 19.7 (The Hausdorff reflection of the boundary family). [tag 032F]
   Let T = (∆h × C2 )/Λ at the fixed boundary parameter c∗ , after shrinking ∆h . Two central
points represented by (η, ξ) and (η ′ , ξ ′ ) are nonseparated precisely when

                              Re(ξ ′ − ξ) ∈ Ga := 12 Z + aZ     (a ∈ Q),

and every pair is nonseparated when a ∈   / Q. There is no nonseparation between distinct base
fibres, or between distinct points of a noncentral fibre. The Hausdorff reflection T H → ∆h has
the original complex tori over h ̸= 0, and its central fibre is

                             R/Ga ≃ S 1     (a ∈ Q),      {∗}    (a ∈
                                                                    / Q).

If a = m/n is in lowest terms, n > 0, then Ga = lcm(2, n)−1 Z.

Proof. 1. We give the full limiting-group argument in 19.9; its formula also applies to the fixed
  boundary family with c = c∗ , h =  ̸ 0. Put d0 = lcm(2, n) in the rational case. In the dual
  lattice, the fixed integral covector whose central limit is d0 Re ξ has (p, q, r) = (0, 0, d0 ). The
  exact dual formula (19.3) below shows that it extends continuously, as a real-linear functional
  ℓh on C2 , to that limit: its last coefficient is O(h2 ), its other moving coefficients are O(h).
  Therefore
                                       (h, z) 7−→ exp(2πiℓh (z))
   is continuous, invariant under every period, and restricts at the centre to exp(2πid0 Re ξ).
   Points with different indicated central classes are separated by this map to the circle.

                                                 140
2. For the converse take a ray h = ϵω, ϵ ↓ 0, whose real and imaginary parts have irrational
   ratio. More precisely choose ω so that p Re ω + q Im ω ̸= 0 for every nonzero pair (p, q) in
   the countable half-integral lattice in 19.9. The asymptotic dual formula shows that all such
   covectors escape to infinity. For rational a, the surviving dual group is exactly Zd0 Re ξ; for
   irrational a, it is zero. Pontryagin–Chabauty duality (Cornulier, 2011, Theorem 3.1, p. 2017;
   proof, p. 2018) now gives the period-group limits

                                     {z : d0 Re ξ(z) ∈ Z},      C2 ,

   respectively. Every element of the indicated limit is the limit of period vectors. Such a
   sequence supplies intersecting images of every two prescribed central neighbourhoods, proving
   nonseparation. This includes the quadratic-scale differences of 19.6, not only first-order
   differences.

3. Collapse exactly these central classes and leave every other fibre unchanged. The resulting
   quotient is Hausdorff. The base coordinate separates different fibres. Within a noncentral
   fibre, continuous functions supported over a compact subdisc away from zero separate distinct
   points, because there the original action is properly discontinuous and gives a smooth torus
   bundle. In the rational central fibre the displayed circle-valued function separates different
   classes. These functions descend through this quotient, so it is Hausdorff. Every continuous
   map from T to a Hausdorff space identifies nonseparated pairs and therefore factors uniquely
   and continuously through this quotient. This proves the universal property, including its
   topology. The elementary greatest common divisor calculation gives the stated value of Ga .



Proposition 19.8 (The finite boundary quotient and its leaves). [tag 032G]
    At the boundary, the construction over B \ {1} is a complex manifold, since proposition 3.2,
theorem 6.6 makes every remaining finite period map invertible and the cusp completion is
unchanged. The order-four deck action descends continuously to T H . On its rational central
circle it is translation by −a/4; on the irrational central point it is trivial. Its finite quotient is
Hausdorff with central fibre a circle or a point, respectively. Neither quotient is a complex space
over the base compatible with the given holomorphic family off the centre. The linear foliation
by C(2, −1)t on the original central torus cover has compact elliptic leaves. For rational a the
leaves are closed; for irrational a the closure of a leaf is the set with its fixed value of Im ξ.

Proof. 1. The deck transformation is a biholomorphism of the original quotient, so the universal
  property extends it uniquely to a homeomorphism of the Hausdorff reflection. The action on
  the fixed product coordinate at the centre is ξ 7→ ξ − κ2 /4 = ξ − a/4. A finite group quotient
  of a Hausdorff space is Hausdorff: finite orbits are separated by intersecting finitely many
  translated open neighbourhoods. A finite rotation quotient of a circle is a circle.

2. On a closed small base disc every noncentral torus point has a representative in the image of
   [0, 1]4 under its period matrix. These representatives belong to a single compact subset of
   C2 . At the centre their images meet every class of the circle or the point. The image of that
   compact parameterized parallelepiped is therefore the full inverse image of the closed disc in
   the reflection. The reflected map is proper; the same holds after the finite quotient. If it were
   holomorphic on a compatible complex space, the central fibre would be analytic. A circle
   cannot be a complex analytic space: a positive-dimensional analytic germ has real dimension
   at least two, and a compact zero-dimensional analytic space is finite. A central point is also
   impossible here: upper semicontinuity of fibre dimension, or the local dimension inequality at
   a point in the closure of the three-dimensional smooth locus, forces a fibre dimension of at
   least two for a holomorphic map to a curve. Thus this Hausdorff reflection cannot be glued as
   a complex-space filling to the remaining constructed manifold.

                                                 141
3. For the leaf assertion, the moving line is {ξ = 0}. At the centre the projection of the period
   group to the ξ-line is Ga ⊂ R. Its intersection with the moving line is a rank-two lattice in Cη :
   the periods are p + qi with (p + q)/2 + ka + ℓ = 0 for integers p, q, k, ℓ. For irrational a this is
   the index-two lattice p + q ≡ 0 (mod 2); for rational a it is either that lattice or Z[i]. Both
   give intrinsic elliptic leaf manifolds isomorphic to Ei . In the irrational case their maps into
   the non-Hausdorff central quotient need not be topological embeddings; “leaf” here means
   the image with this intrinsic immersed topology. When Ga is discrete, the saturated leaf is
   closed. When it is dense in R, its saturation has closure Cη × (Re ξ + R), with Im ξ fixed. The
   natural map from this central quotient to the central fibre of T H is [(η, ξ)] 7→ Re ξ mod Ga
   for rational a, and the constant map for irrational a, as in Theorem 19.7. It is well defined
   because the real second coordinate of every central period belongs to Ga .




19.3        All local limiting period groups
Theorem 19.9 (All marked limiting period groups). [tag 032H]
  Let cn → c∗ with Im cn < H∗ , and let hn → 0. Set

                    La = {(p, q, r) ∈ R3 : r ∈ Z, p + r/2 ∈ Z, q + r/2 ∈ Z, ar ∈ Z}.

It has rank three for rational a, and is Z2 × {0} for irrational a. Every convergent subsequence

    Γ∞ = {(η, ξ) : p Re η + q Im η + r Re ξ + ℓ(p, q, r) Im ξ ∈ Z for every (p, q, r) ∈ K}.     (19.2)

                     K = {λ ∈ La : λ · Vn has a finite limit},         ℓ(λ) = lim λ · Vn ,

real tori of any dimension from zero to three for rational a, and from zero to two for irrational a,
with the marked groups given explicitly by (19.2).

Proof. 1. We use the fixed complex-linear coordinates of 19.5. Write h = X + iY , τ = R + iT ,

   For an integral dual label (mw , mu , md , mg ), put r = md , p = mw − r/2, q = mu − r/2. The

              q − pR − rX − tY                  mg − ra − 6pX − 6Y (q − pR − rX)/T − r Re z

   Multiplication by At proves the formula.

                                                       142
2. A bounded sequence of dual vectors has bounded integral labels, since An is bounded. After
   subselection its label is constant. Its limit must satisfy mg = ra, because At0 has that relation.
   The remaining labels are exactly La . Conversely consider a fixed label from La . Lemma 19.5
   gives
                      T = 1 + O(|h|2 ), R = O(|h|2 ), Re B = 6XY + O(|h|4 ),
                                 δn = − Im(cn − c∗ ) + 3|hn |2 + O(|hn |4 ).
   In particular δn ≥ C|hn |2 for a fixed C > 0 after shrinking the disc. The numerator in (19.3),
   with mg = ra, is

                       −6pX − 6qY − r Re(c − c∗ ) + O(|h|3 )(|p| + |q| + |r|).

   The cancellation of the quadratic real term is essential. Division by Dc = −δn makes the error
   O(|hn |). Thus
                                      tn = (p, q, r) · Vn + o(1).
  Whenever this is bounded, the other three coefficients converge to (p, q, r). This proves that
  the dual limit, if it exists, is the discrete graph {(p, q, r, ℓ(p, q, r)) : (p, q, r) ∈ K}. There can
  be no further elements from varying labels, because a bounded sequence of labels lies in a
  finite set. A convergent dual group cannot contain two different limits with the same label:
  their difference would have label zero, whose sole preimage under every Atn is zero. Nor can a
  surviving label escape along a subsequence, since an element of a Chabauty limit must be
  approximable along the whole convergent sequence. Consequently every label either has the
  indicated finite limit or escapes to infinity. Addition and integer division show that K is a
  subgroup and is primitive.

3. By (Cornulier, 2011, Theorem 3.1, p. 2017), the map from closed subgroups of a finite-
   dimensional real vector space to their Pontryagin annihilators is a homeomorphism. Applying
   it to the dual graph gives exactly (19.2). This theorem’s hypotheses are met by the real
   vector space underlying C2 and by the closed full lattices Γn ; no nonclosed group is used as a
   Chabauty point.

4. To prove realizability, extend ℓ linearly to a covector represented by a vector v0 ∈ R3 . Since
   K is primitive, La ∩ spanR K = K. Choose v orthogonal to that span and not orthogonal to
   any member of La \ K; the excluded proper hyperplanes are countably many, and cannot
   cover the orthogonal space. If K = La , take v = 0. Put Vn = nv + v0 = (A′n , Bn′ , Cn′ ). Choose
   positive dn → 0 with dn (1 + ∥Vn ∥2 ) → 0, and define

      hn = dn (A′n + iBn′ )/6,    xn = dn Cn′ ,   ϵn = dn + Dc∗ (hn ) > 0,     cn = c∗ + xn − iϵn .

   The inequality follows from Dc∗ (h) = −3|h|2 + O(|h|4 ). These choices give −Dcn (hn ) = dn
   exactly, so their vectors are the prescribed Vn . On K the scalar products converge to ℓ, and off
   K they escape. This constructs every claimed limit inside the admissible parameter domain.

5. Finally the dual graph is a discrete free group of rank rank K. Its annihilator quotient is a
   compact connected real torus of that dimension. In the fixed Euclidean metric, dn ([z], [z ′ ]) =
   dist(z − z ′ , Γn ). Chabauty convergence gives local uniform convergence of these functions:
   minimizers relevant on a bounded set can be restricted to a bounded set, and the two defining
   Chabauty approximation properties then give both inequalities. This identifies the stated
   pointed quotient limits. Their group structures and quotient metrics are the ones displayed
   above.




                                                   143
Corollary 19.10 (Path dependence of the limiting torus). [tag 032I]
    There is no path-independent limiting group at the boundary even when cn → c∗ from the
admissible side. At hn = 0 and cn = c∗ − iϵn , all of La survives, giving a three-dimensional real
torus if a is rational and a two-dimensional real torus if a is irrational. Other admissible paths
give a point. The fixed-boundary Hausdorff reflection of 19.7 therefore cannot be identified with
all pointed fibre limits.

Proof. 1. The first sequence has Vn = 0, hence K = La and ℓ = 0. For the second, take K = 0
  in the explicit realization in 19.9. The limits have different real dimensions. Away from t = 1,
  the periods stay invertible and the local complex families converge to their ordinary value
  at c∗ ; the ambiguity is at the specified root centre. Theorem 19.4 excludes a flat proper
  holomorphic extension across the parameter boundary.

Proof. 1. The Hessian of Dc∗ (h) = −3|h|2 + O(|h|4 ) is negative at zero. Its radial derivative
  is −6|h| + O(|h|3 ), uniformly in angle. Consequently each sufficiently small positive level
  of −Dc∗ has exactly one radius in each direction and is a real-analytic simple closed curve,
  with the displayed expansion. The order-four deck action preserves it, acts freely on it, and
  the coarse map t is a four-fold covering of its image. Since the punctured root quotient is
  a punctured disc, that image is again a simple closed curve. The strict global maximum in
  Theorem 6.6 gives a uniform gap on the complement of any fixed root neighbourhood; the
  cusp tends to minus infinity. Thus no other zero-locus component exists for small enough ϵ.

2. Ramanujan’s differential identities give j ′′ (i) = −2π 2 j(i)E4 (i): indeed j ′ = −2πijE6 /E4 and

Proposition 19.12 (The maximal open locus and the negative region). [tag 032K]
   For any height H = Im c > H∗ , the zero locus is the well-defined modular-norm level set
                     n                      √          o
                ZH = t : N (µ(t), τ (t)) = 2 3 e−πH/6 ,       ℘τ (t) (µ(t)) = 0.
It is compact away from the cusp, and is a real-analytic set in the finite root charts. At every
regular point it is a smooth real curve. The construction gives a complex manifold precisely
over B \ ZH , retaining the original Mumford fibre at the cusp. The open sublevel set {Dc < 0},
with the cusp adjoined, is connected. At every point of ZH , the period quotient is the rank-three

Proof. 1. The formula for D in proposition 3.2, theorem 6.6 gives the equation, and the theta
  transformation law shows that it is independent of the modular and period representatives.
  Compactness away from the cusp follows from Dpart → −∞. The analytic and regular-level
  assertions follow in each root chart from the real-analytic implicit function theorem. On the
  complement, the real period matrix is invertible. On compact subsets of that complement its
  inverse is bounded, which proves uniform discreteness and proper discontinuity of the lattice
  action. The quotient is therefore a complex manifold with compact torus fibres. The finite
  deck action is free for the same invariant-coordinate reason as proposition 7.2, proposition 7.4:
  a nontrivial power translates that circle by a noninteger fraction, regardless of the sign of D.
  Near the cusp D < 0, so its existing holomorphic Mumford completion and its overlaps remain
  available. At a zero with irrational kernel line, the fibre quotient is already non-Hausdorff.
  At a zero with rational kernel choose a primitive integral kernel vector. Its holomorphic
  period vanishes at that root point but is not identically zero nearby. Its first nonzero Taylor
  coefficient, multiplied by arbitrarily large integer multiples and approached along suitable root
  directions, yields nonseparated central points. Thus no neighbourhood of a zero in the naive
  quotient is a Hausdorff complex manifold. This justifies the asserted maximal open base locus.
2. For connectedness, in any holomorphic coordinate z with T = Im τ > 0, differentiation gives
                                                 3 ′       Im µ ′   2
                              ∂z ∂z̄ Dpart = −     µ (z) −     τ (z) ≤ 0.
                                                 T          T
   Thus the function is superharmonic on the root charts. This property and the minimum
   principle descend under the finite quotient; one can equally apply the principle on a root
   cover of a putative minimum. A component of the strict sublevel set not containing the
   cusp would have compact closure with boundary at level −H, and would attain a smaller
   interior minimum. The strong minimum principle excludes this. A sufficiently small cusp
   neighbourhood is contained in the sublevel set, so all components reaching the cusp are the
   same one. Hence the sublevel set is connected.


Proposition 19.13 (Closed period groups at a rank-three fibre). [tag 032L]
    At a zero of Dc , let A : R4 → C2 be the real period map and ker A = Rk, with the kernel
vector stated in proposition 11.12, proposition 11.13. Define
               Lk = {m ∈ Z4 : m · k = 0},           r = rank Lk ,   Vk =          ker m.

                                                   145
Proof. 1. The last three period columns are real-linearly independent, so the rank is exactly
  three. This confirms the linear algebra of proposition 11.12, proposition 11.13. The annihilator
  characters of AZ4 are the real covectors λ with At λ ∈ Z4 . Their integral labels belong exactly
  to Lk . The smallest rational subspace containing k is Vk ; the closure of the image of Z4 in
  R4 /Rk is its image after adding Vk . For an elementary verification, the two groups have the
  same annihilator characters, and characters separate closed subgroups of a real vector space
  by putting such a subgroup into the form Rd × Ze . This proves the closure formula. Inside the
  three-dimensional image hyperplane its connected part has dimension 3 − r, and its discrete
  quotient has rank r. The one transverse real direction gives the displayed group.

2. The image is discrete exactly when the kernel line has a primitive integral generator: extend
   such a generator to an integral basis for the converse; for necessity, a discrete subgroup of
   a real three-space has rank at most three, forcing a nonzero integral kernel. A nondiscrete
   finitely generated subgroup cannot be closed, since a nondiscrete closed subgroup contains an
   uncountable vector group. Finally each fixed integral period converges to its limiting period;
   a Chabauty limit is closed and therefore contains their closure.

Proposition 19.18 (The supercritical level classification). [tag 032Q]
    For every H > H∗ , the degeneracy locus ZH is exactly one embedded C 1 Jordan curve in
the finite t-plane. It is real analytic unless H = H0 = 3 log 48/(2π); at that height it is real
analytic away from t = 0 and has the regular crossing described in 19.15. There are no singular
coarse levels at any supercritical height. The bounded complementary disc contains t = 1 and has
Dc > 0; the complementary disc in P1 , containing the cusp, has Dc < 0. The point t = 0 is in
the latter disc for H < H0 , on the curve for H = H0 , and in the former disc for H > H0 .
    The bounded discs are strictly nested as H increases, shrink to {1} as H ↓ H∗ , and exhaust
the finite plane as H → ∞. Their small-height boundary shape is the expansion in 19.11. The
maximal open base locus of the complex manifold construction consists of these two complementary
discs. Approaching their common boundary, the covolume of the marked root torus lattice is

                                 covol(Πc Z4 ) = Im τ |Dc | −→ 0.

are those of 19.13.

   The maximum L(1) = log 2 corresponds exactly to H∗ = 3 log 6/π. Thus H > H∗ corre-

   one strictly star-shaped C 1 Jordan curve about 1, real analytic away from the possible point
   t = 0. Its nonzero coarse derivative there proves regularity also on that exceptional level.

2. Since L(0) = 14 log 3, its height is H0 = 3 log 48/(2π). The exact equation Dc = H − f gives
   the two signs, the position of 0, and the bounded component {f < H} containing 1. Strict
   radial monotonicity proves strict nesting. The unique minimum f (1) = H∗ and properness of
   f off 1 prove shrinking as H ↓ H∗ and exhaustion of every compact subset as H → ∞. The
   expansion at the minimum is 19.11.

3. In the ordered real coordinates and marked lattice basis of 19.13, direct expansion of the
   period determinant gives

                                det Πc = ℑτ ℑβc − 6(ℑµ)2 = ℑτ Dc .
                                 R

   Its absolute value is the covolume and tends to zero at the level curve. The same matrix
   retains three independent columns there, so its rank is exactly three. Apply the exact quotient
   and Hausdorff-reflection computation of 19.13. The local proper-action criterion of 19.12 gives
   complex manifolds on both complementary regions and excludes every point of their common
   boundary, including its discrete fixed-fibre quotients. This proves the maximality and all the
   local degeneration assertions.

20.1    The untwisted pinching and its local smoothings
Definition 20.1 (The elliptic surface and the pinching datum). [tag PT01] S is the smooth
minimal rational elliptic surface with Weierstrass equation

                                y 2 = x3 − 3t3 (t − 1)x + 2t4 (t − 1)2 ,

π : S → B is its elliptic fibration, P is the section used in the period dictionary, T = t6P : S → S,
and L = MS = OS (P − O). We use the convention that PS (O ⊕ L) contains the total space of L,
with fibre coordinate a, zero section s0 , and infinity section s∞ . The two normal bundles are
respectively L and L−1 . We write R = PS (O ⊕ L).

Proposition 20.2 (The pinching and its smoothing line). [tag 01R1]
   The quotient
                           Q = R/{s0 (x) ∼ s∞ (T x) : x ∈ S}
has a compact, reduced complex-space structure. Its normalization is the finite holomorphic map
ν : R → Q. Its singular locus is a copy of S, and its local analytic equation along that locus
is ab = 0, with two further coordinates on S. The induced map Q → B is proper. Its sheaf of
first-order local smoothing parameters is

                         TQ1 = Ext1OQ (ΩQ , OQ ) ≃ L ⊗ T ∗ L−1 ≃ π ∗ OB (1)

on the double locus.

Proof. 1. The two sections of R are disjoint closed submanifolds. The equivalence relation consists
  of their two graphs and the diagonal; it is closed in R × R. A quotient of a compact Hausdorff
  space by a closed equivalence relation is Hausdorff: for distinct equivalence classes, compactness
  gives disjoint saturated neighbourhoods by taking finite subcovers of the complements of the
  relation. Thus the displayed quotient is compact and Hausdorff.
2. For a coordinate neighbourhood U ⊂ S and frames of L|U and L−1 |T (U ) , the two tubular
   coordinate charts are (x, a) at s0 (U ) and (T x, b) at s∞ (T (U )). We give their identification
   the ring
                   {(f (x, a), g(x, b)) : f (x, 0) = g(x, 0)} = C{x1 , x2 , a, b}/(ab).
   Changes of frame are holomorphic and invertible on each branch and have the same change
   of x on their intersection. They therefore glue these hypersurface charts to the inherited
   charts off the sections. This constructs the asserted complex space. The direct sum of the two
   regular branch rings is the integral closure: an integral element in the total ring of fractions is
   integral on each smooth branch, and conversely the two branch idempotents are integral. The
   resulting map ν is proper with at most two points in each fibre, and its local ring extension is
   finite. The map to B is well defined because πT = π; its properness follows from compactness
   of Q.
3. The conormal presentation for the hypersurface ab = 0 gives Ext1 (Ω, O) = O/(a, b). A
   change of normal frames a′ = g(x)a, b′ = h(x)b changes the equation and its smoothing
   parameter by gh. Consequently these local modules glue as Ns0 /R ⊗ T ∗ Ns∞ /R = L ⊗ T ∗ L−1 .
   For this particular surface, Engel’s Lemma 2.1 states Hom(T ∗ L, L) = π ∗ OB (1) (Engel, 2026,
   Lemma 2.1, pp. 3–4). Its identification applies here with T = t6P and L = O(P − O). One
   can recover the degree in that lemma directly: the bundle has multidegree zero on every fibre,
   since T preserves every component; hence it is π ∗ OB (n). Its degree on O is

                    n = (O − P ) · 6P + (P − O) · O = (2 − 2) + (0 − (−1)) = 1.

                                                  151
   The section intersections used here are the explicit computations in the proof of that lemma.
   This derives the displayed sheaf in the normal-bundle convention of our pushout.



Definition 20.3 (The smoothing section). [tag PT06] Set J = L ⊗ T ∗ L−1 . Proposition 20.2
identifies J with π ∗ OB (1). We fix the section ϕ ∈ H 0 (S, J) with divisor S∞ from (Engel, 2026,
Corollary 2.2, p. 4). Thus ϕx is the bundle map LT x → Lx used in the plumbing equation.

Proposition 20.4 (The nodal plumbing and its small modification). [tag 01R3]
   The first simultaneous local plumbing at the nodal point of S∞ has equation

                                      xy = uzv,         q = zv,                               (20.1)

after a holomorphic change of one normal coordinate, where q is a local coordinate on B at
infinity. This hypersurface is flat over the u-disc. For each u ̸= 0, its three-dimensional fibre
has an ordinary double point at x = y = z = v = 0. The projective modification defined by the
blow-up of (x, z) resolves that point for u ̸= 0. Its two strict-transform charts are

                            x = zr,   ry = uv;         z = xa,    y = uav.                    (20.2)

The modified family remains flat over u. At u = 0, the normalization of its central fibre contains
the blow-up of one branch of (20.1) along the smooth curve x = z = 0; hence this particular
modification changes the normalization of the unmodified pinching.

Proof. 1. The surface S is smooth and its nodal elliptic fibre has local equation q = zv at its
  node. The section ϕ has a simple zero along that fibre. Thus ϕ = zv times an invertible
  holomorphic function. Absorbing the function in one normal coordinate gives (20.1). The
  convergent power-series ring C{x, y, z, v, u} is factorial, and u is coprime to xy − uzv. Hence
  uh ∈ (xy − uzv) implies h ∈ (xy − uzv). The quotient has no u-torsion. At a nonzero
  parameter the identical argument uses u − u0 . This proves flatness over the smooth parameter
  curve. For fixed u =
                     ̸ 0 the four first derivatives vanish only at the origin, and the quadratic
  form xy −uzv is nondegenerate. This proves the ordinary-double-point assertion by its defining
  equation.

2. The two standard affine charts of the blow-up give (20.2), after removing the common factors
   z and x, respectively. For u ̸= 0 the first chart solves for v and the second for y, so both are
   smooth. The map is an isomorphism away from the origin in the fixed u-fibre: where the
   ideal fails to be visibly principal, the hypersurface equation and one of y, v make it principal.
   The fibre over the origin is P1 . The modification is projective over (20.1), since it is a closed
   subspace of its product with P1 . The first strict-transform equation is coprime to u − u0 in
   its convergent power-series ring for every u0 ; the second chart is smooth with free parameter
   u. Thus flatness over u persists.

3. At u = 0 the first chart has ry = 0. The branch r = 0 maps isomorphically to x = 0 in
   the original central fibre. The branch y = 0, together with the second chart, is the ordinary
   blow-up of the branch y = 0 in coordinates (x, z, v) along (x, z). This description follows from
   the two affine substitutions defining that blow-up and identifies the normalizations. For u ̸= 0,
   the base coordinate in the first chart is q = zry/u and in the second it is q = xav. Thus the
   modification also exhibits the triple-coordinate strata that the cusp filling requires.

Proposition 20.5 (The unsubdivided cusp fan). [tag 02ZH]
    For k, l ∈ Z, let Pk,l be the cone defined by hq , hu ≥ 0, khq ≤ y1 ≤ (k + 1)hq and l(hq + hu ) ≤
y2 ≤ (l + 1)(hq + hu ). These cones and their faces form a fan. Its two period automorphisms on
the cocharacter lattice are

   G1 (y1 , y2 , hq , hu ) = (y1 + hq , y2 , hq , hu ),     G2 (y1 , y2 , hq , hu ) = (y1 , y2 + hq + hu , hq , hu ).

The affine chart of P0,0 is

                            U0,0 = Spec C[x, y, z, v, u]/(xy − uzv),               q = zv.

In particular the unsubdivided chart is not a smooth simultaneous model of the cusp.

Proof. 1. At fixed hq , hu ≥ 0, the cone Pk,l cuts out the rectangle

                       khq ≤ y1 ≤ (k + 1)hq ,             l(hq + hu ) ≤ y2 ≤ (l + 1)(hq + hu ).

   When hq = 0 the first interval is a point. These rectangles tile their support, and their
   intersections are common faces, including this collapsed boundary. This proves the fan
   assertion. The displayed integral transformations preserve the fan and have integral inverses.

2. For a character (a, b, c, d), the six inequalities of the dual cone are c, a+c, b+c, a+b+c, d, b+d ≥
   0. The characters

       x = (0, 1, 0, 0),     y = (0, −1, 1, 1),       z = (1, 0, 0, 0),    v = (−1, 0, 1, 0),      u = (0, 0, 0, 1)

   generate its integral monoid. Indeed if b ≥ 0 we subtract bx; if b < 0 we subtract (−b)y. The
   remaining character has second coordinate zero and is a nonnegative integral combination of
   z, v, u. The sole relation is x + y = u + z + v, and the character of the first base coordinate is
   z + v. This proves the coordinate-ring assertion, including normality.



Theorem 20.6 (The compact nodal plumbing). [tag 02ZI] [tag 01R2]
  There is a reduced complex space X ♭ and a proper flat holomorphic map

                                              (f, ϖ) : X ♭ −→ B × ∆u

whose central threefold is Q. For u =  ̸ 0 its fibre is the contraction of Engel’s chosen X(u) at
one rational curve of the Mumford fibre. This curve is the double curve corresponding to the
diagonal of the square in the chosen A2 triangulation; in the coordinates of the marked cusp
fan its direction is e1 − e2 . Its normal bundle in X(u) is OP1 (−1)⊕2 . Its image is the unique
ordinary double point of Xu♭ .
     Over S ◦ = S \ S∞ the total plumbing space is smooth. Its restriction over every relatively
compact disc U ⋐ B \ {∞} is proper and flat over U × ∆ϵ for sufficiently small ϵ > 0. For u ̸= 0
it is the untwisted quotient by uϕ covering T −1 . This includes discs containing 0 or 1, before the
logarithmic transformations.

Proof. 1. Here is a construction on the whole compact surface S. Choose a Hermitian metric on
  L, use the dual metric on L−1 , and choose 0 < r < 1/4. For sufficiently small ϵ > 0 we have
  |u|∥ϕx ∥ < r2 for all x ∈ S and |u| < ϵ. Take the core

                                C = {(x, a, u) : a ∈ Lx , r < ∥a∥ < r−1 , |u| < ϵ}

   and the node space

            N = {(x, a, b, u) : a ∈ Lx , b ∈ L−1
                                              T x , a ⊗ b = uϕx , ∥a∥, ∥b∥ < 2r, |u| < ϵ}.                        (20.3)

                                                          153
  On r < ∥a∥ < 2r identify a point of N with (x, a, u) ∈ C. On r < ∥b∥ < 2r identify it with
  (T x, b−1 , u) ∈ C. Both identifications are biholomorphisms between open complex spaces;
  in the first collar b = uϕx /a, and in the second a = uϕx b−1 . Their domains are disjoint
  because ∥a∥∥b∥ < r2 . Changes of frames multiply the equation by units and give the stated
  bundle-valued equation, so no choice of frame enters the gluing.

2. This gluing is Hausdorff. At either end of a collar, exactly one of its two charts contains the
   limiting circle: the core omits ∥a∥ = r, and the node chart omits ∥a∥ = 2r; the infinity collar
   has the identical property in b. Thus the graph of the identification has no unpaired pair
   of limiting points. The two collars in each chart are separated, so there are no additional
   chains of identifications. These observations give disjoint saturated neighbourhoods of any
   two inequivalent points. Properness is equally concrete. Over a compact subset of B × ∆ϵ , the
   closed core 3r/2 ≤ ∥a∥ ≤ 2/(3r) together with the closed node subspace ∥a∥, ∥b∥ ≤ 7r/4 is
   compact and maps onto the glued space. To see surjectivity, a point outside the smaller core
   lies on a node collar, and a node point outside the smaller node subspace lies on the smaller
   core. Compactness of S supplies the uniform bound used above. This proves properness of
   the joint map to (t, u).

3. The total node rings are hypersurface rings over the regular two-dimensional local rings of
   S. They are Cohen–Macaulay. Every fibre of the joint map has pure dimension two: first fix
   t, and then impose xy = uϕ on the two line coordinates over the one-dimensional fibre of S.
   Consequently t − t0 , u − u0 is a regular sequence in every total local ring. The regular-sequence
   flatness criterion over the smooth two-dimensional base proves flatness. On S ◦ , the derivative
   of ab − uϕx with respect to u is −ϕx ̸= 0, so the total node space is smooth. On the core
   the total space is an open subset of L × ∆u and is smooth; joint flatness follows from that
   of S → B. This includes the nonreduced Kodaira fibres at 0, 1, since the argument uses
   smoothness of S. At u = 0 the node equation is ab = 0, and the two collar maps recover
   precisely the specified pinching of the two sections of R.

4. For u ≠ 0 and t ̸= ∞, the equation gives aT x = ax /(uϕx ). Hence the resulting quotient is
   exactly L× /⟨uϕ⟩, where the contracting generator covers T −1 . Every orbit meets a core or a
   collar, by the uniform contraction estimate; the displayed comparison identifies exactly its
   orbit relation. It is therefore a biholomorphism.

5. At the nodal point of S∞ , write q = zv. Absorbing a unit in one line coordinate gives xy = uzv.
   At a smooth point of S∞ the equation is xy = uq. For u ̸= 0 the latter threefold is smooth;
   the former has one nondegenerate quadratic singularity at the origin. There are no other
   singularities of a nonzero u fibre.

6. In a Tate covering of a neighbourhood of the I1 fibre use the torus coordinates (Z, W ) of
   Engel (2026, Proposition 2.7, p. 6). The two periods act as

              (Z, W, q, u) 7−→ (c1 qZ, c2 W, q, u),     (Z, W, q, u) 7−→ (c3 Z, c′4 uqW, q, u),

   with holomorphic units ci . Their monomial parts are G1 , G2 . The chart indexed by (k, l)
   has z = Zq −k , v = q k+1 /Z, x = W (qu)−l , y = qu/x, with the unit changes given by the
   line frames. It is the chart of Proposition 20.5. The Tate cover unfolds the node of S∞
   into its infinite chain, and unfolding the two plumbing collars gives the additional integer
   index l. The foregoing collar identifications are exactly the two deck identifications. Thus,
   on an invariant neighbourhood over a sufficiently small bidisc, the fan space maps by a
   holomorphic covering to the plumbing, with deck group Z2 . Each core or node coordinate
   neighbourhood has disjoint lifts indexed by the two unfolded integers; this proves freeness
   and proper discontinuity, including the ρl orbits. The first period stabilizes such a ray but
   on its orbit translates the Tate coordinate by c1 q, with q ̸= 0 and |c1 q| < 1; it does not fix a

                                                  154
  point. Properness of its quotient was proved by the compact core and node representatives.
  This proves the analytic comparison of the fan quotient with the compact plumbing.

7. Subdividing the square at hu = 0 by the chosen diagonal gives the small resolution of xy = uzv
   for u ̸= 0. Put Y = y/u, so the equation is xY = zv. The resolution associated with the
   diagonal [e1 , e2 ] has charts

                    (v, Y, a) 7−→ (av, uY, aY, v),         (x, z, b) 7−→ (x, ubz, z, bx)

  in the coordinates (x, y, z, v). On their overlap, b = a−1 and (x, z) = a(v, Y ). The character
  a = x/v has valuation y1 + y2 − hq , so these are exactly the two triangles separated by [e1 , e2 ].
  The exceptional curve is the zero section in the two normal coordinates. Their transition is
  multiplication by a, giving OP1 (−1)⊕OP1 (−1). There is one diagonal edge modulo the periods,
  so there is exactly one such curve. Removing that edge contracts the paired opposite (−1)-
  curves in the normalization dP6 to the square model P1 × P1 . This identifies the contracted
  curve in the selected toric model. The fixed double curve of Proposition 16.4 has direction e2
  in the same marked lattice; the two primitive directions satisfy det(e1 − e2 , e2 ) = 1.

Remark 20.8 (The local modification and the compact central fibre). [tag 01R5] The blow-up

5. For homology, the normalization has n = 4 or 3 components, each with ranks (1, 2, 2, 2, 1), and

   because Rj has no eigenvalue one. The degree-zero incidence matrix contributes an additional
