22.2    The base-changed cusp fan
Proposition 22.3 (Period-invariant fans after base change). [tag 0302]
    For the plain base change u = rn of the untwisted cusp model, the smooth period-invariant
refinements which retain the prescribed bottom triangulation, are jointly flat over (q, r), and have
reduced r-central divisor are indexed by k = 0, . . . , n. In a fundamental prism write its four
bottom rays as A, B, C, D as in 21.1, and put ρi = (0, i, 0, 1) for 0 ≤ i ≤ n. The maximal cones
for the index k are

                  ABCρk ,    BCDρk ,      ABρi ρi+1 (i < k),     CDρi ρi+1 (i ≥ k).

There are thirteen such models for n = 12 and three for n = 2. Each has smooth total space and
a reduced normal-crossings central divisor with n components and no triple locus. Its component

                                                 181
labels over the punctured q-disc are globally Z/n; in particular their monodromy around q = 0 is
the identity.

Proof. 1. The map of cocharacter lattices for the base change is

                                    (y1 , y2 , hq , hr ) 7−→ (y1 , y2 , hq , nhr ).

   The old top ray indexed by l pulls back to (0, nl, 0, 1). Smoothness on the two-dimensional
   top face forces insertion of every primitive ray ρnl+i , 0 < i < n: a skipped interval of length
   d > 1 would retain lattice index d on that face. Joint flatness excludes any new ray with both
   base heights positive, and the fixed bottom excludes new rays of hr = 0. Reducedness permits
   only top rays of hr = 1. These are consequently all the rays.

2. On the left face ACρ0 ρn , a triangulation with these collinear top vertices has a unique triangle
   containing the bottom edge AC. Write its third vertex as ρa . The triangles on either side of
   that bridge are then forced. The analogous right face has bridge BDρb . The first period takes
   A, C to B, D and fixes every top ray, so periodicity requires a = b = k. The fixed bottom
   triangles ABC and BCD must then cone to ρk . The remaining successive top intervals force
   exactly the displayed cones, leaving no choice. Conversely those cones have determinant ±1
   and common-face intersections. Their normalized volumes sum to n + 2, the volume of the
   prism, so they cover it. For n = 2 and n = 12, the determinant, intersection and volume
   calculations use exact rational arithmetic.

3. The period actions are

                G1 : (y1 , y2 ) 7→ (y1 + hq , y2 ),       G2 : (y1 , y2 ) 7→ (y1 , y2 + hq + nhr ).

   Thus the choices propagate consistently from the fundamental prism. The proper toric
   subdivisions descend by the covering construction of 20.6. Every ray has pure q-height or
   pure r-height, so in a regular affine chart q and r are monomials in disjoint sets of coordinates.
   This proves joint flatness. All nonzero r-heights equal one, and there are at most two top
   rays in any maximal cone; this proves reduced normal crossings and absence of triple points.
   Properness follows by descent from the proper toric modification of the base-changed proper
   cusp model.

4. The central components and all their intersection maps are specified by the stars of the ρi .
   Modulo the periods their indices are i mod n; adjacent indices meet in the conductor elliptic
   surface. Away from the cusp their normalizations are the ruled bundles of the expanded
   plumbing. At the unique bridge class the star has both bottom triangles, and gives the
   nodal-curve blow-up and small resolution described in 21.2, on the corresponding ruled bundle.
   This star description also fixes the gluing when the bridge is on an inserted component. The
   endpoint choices k = 0, n are the canonical resolutions of the base changes of the two original
   models. Intermediate values are related to them by the successive side flops.

5. Finally, G1 fixes each index and G2 changes it by n. The units in the cusp periods are
   single-valued holomorphic functions of q and do not change a ray label. The toric charts
   themselves are defined over q, not a root of q. Hence these labels remain global on the
   punctured q-disc, proving the monodromy assertion. Further smooth periodic subdivisions
   with mixed rays give infinitely many models flat over r alone, as in 21.1; they are excluded by
   the stated joint-flatness condition.




                                                       182
Corollary 22.4 (Base-changed cusp refinements). [tag 0304] [tag 0303]
    For n = 2 and n = 12, 21.5–21.6 give all finite-orbit smooth invariant plain-cusp refinements,
their proper flat families, normalization charts, finite blow-up and blow-down presentations,
multiplicities and all multiple loci. 21.16–21.18 give their complete integral topology and nearby
Euler function. Reducedness is exactly the restriction ℓ = 1 on every positive-height ray.

Proof. 1. The base maps u = w2 and u = r12 induce multiplication by 2 and 12 on the integral
  parameter characteristic. Insert n = 2 and n = 12 respectively into the periodic lattice action
  and fan construction of 21.5. Its converse recovers the invariant subdivision from each such
  plain-cusp model, so the parametrization includes every stated output.

2. For each primitive ray v, the local parameter is a monomial whose exponent on its divisor is
   its integral height ℓ(v). Thus the central divisor is reduced exactly when every such height
   equals one. Smoothness, flatness, properness, the normalization charts and all intersection
   maps are those proved in 21.5; 21.6 gives the finite blow-up and blow-down presentation.
   Finally substitute the resulting orbit counts and maps into 21.16, 21.17, 21.18 for the claimed
   topology.




22.3    Component monodromy and trace obstructions
Theorem 22.5 (Peripheral component obstruction). [tag 0305]
    The finite models of 22.1 and any of the plain u = r12 cusp models of 22.2 cannot be
glued to a proper complex space over B × ∆r with the prescribed central fibres on all three base
neighbourhoods. The obstruction is the peripheral component monodromy of these prescribed
finite and plain cusp models.

Proof. 1. If a further plain cusp refinement changes the top fan, its central fibre over an ordinary
  q ̸= 0 has additional components or different multiplicities and already cannot agree with
  the twelve-cycle model of 22.1 on the overlap. We may therefore assume its top fan is the
  standard reduced twelve-cycle. Additional mixed-height rays lie over q = 0 and do not change
  the following argument over the punctured base.

2. Suppose such a gluing exists and put B ◦ = B \ {0, 1, ∞}. Normalize its reduced central fibre
   over B ◦ . In each of the prescribed plumbing charts this is a proper smooth family whose fibres
   are the disjoint union of twelve connected ruled surfaces. The charts and their transition
   isomorphisms therefore give a locally constant twelve-element set of connected components.
   Equivalently, the Stein factor of this normalization is an unramified degree-twelve cover of B ◦ :
   the algebra of fibrewise holomorphic functions is locally O12 , since each proper connected ruled
   surface has only constant holomorphic functions. This description constructs the component
   cover over B ◦ .

3. The double curves give the adjacency graph of a twelve-cycle. Thus its transition permutations
   lie in the dihedral group D12 , the automorphism group of that graph. We record a peripheral
   permutation by its deck-identification map. Holonomy defined by lifting a clockwise path and
   returning its endpoint to the initial root slice uses the inverse permutations throughout; the
   relation and the following contradiction are unchanged. At 0 the monodromy is a rotation by
   four steps; at 1 it is a rotation by minus three steps, by the explicit root deck maps in 22.2.
   Relabelling a cycle can reverse either orientation, but changes these only to ±4 and ±3. At
   the cusp the monodromy is the identity by 22.3.




                                                183
4. The peripheral relation in π1 (B ◦ ) is g1 g2 g0 = 1 with the consistently chosen clockwise loops.
   In any common labelling, the product of the two finite rotations would therefore have to be
   the identity. Its possible rotation numbers are

                     4 + 3,   4 − 3,   −4 + 3,      −4 − 3 ≡ 7, 1, 11, 5   (mod 12).

   None is zero. This contradicts the peripheral relation.



Proposition 22.6 (The marked genus-three component cover). [tag 0306]
    Let B ◦ = P1 \ {0, 1, ∞} and use the clockwise deck-identification convention of 22.5. The
peripheral rotations 4, −3, −1 in Z/12 define a connected degree-twelve cover of B ◦ . Its compact
normalization is the smooth genus-three curve obtained from

                                                      t4
                                          y 12 =            .
                                                   (t − 1)3
The ramification indices over 0, 1, ∞ are 3, 4, 12, respectively. The peripheral relation determines
the last rotation from the first two, so this is the marked cyclic component cover used in the
partial filling of 22.41.

Proof. 1. The presentation g1 g2 g0 = 1 sends the third peripheral generator to −4 + 3 = −1. The
  first two images generate Z/12, so the resulting action on the twelve sheets is transitive. This
  constructs the connected cover by its monodromy representation.

2. The rational function t4 /(t − 1)3 has orders 4, −3, −1 at the three punctures. Its twelfth-root
   equation has the same marked deck representation. The covering-space identification is the
   map which sends a chosen twelfth root at one base point to its chosen sheet and continues
   both along the same paths. Its equality of monodromy makes that map single-valued; its local
   analytic root coordinates make it holomorphic. Normalization extends this identification to
   the compact covers.

3. Locally y 12 = z a u(z) has gcd(12, a) branches of ramification index 12/ gcd(12, a), after
   absorbing the holomorphic unit in a local twelfth root. Thus the three contributions to
   ramification are 4(3 − 1), 3(4 − 1), and 12 − 1. Their sum is 28. Riemann–Hurwitz gives
   2 − 2g = 2 · 12 − 28 = −4, so g = 3. Reversing the deck convention is realized by y 7→ y −1 ,
   with the reciprocal defining equation; the compact curve and the ramification calculation are
   unchanged.



Proposition 22.7 (Cusp-root multiplicities). [tag 0307]
    Let q = sd , u = rn , and suppose a cyclic deck generator has translation d−1 (aG1 + bG2 ) in
the additive notation for the two periods. Assume its r-component shift is integral. Then its
r-component shift is nb/d mod n, whereas the multiplicity of every generic quotient q-component
is a positive multiple of
                                                d
                                                        .
                                           gcd(d, a, b)
A nonzero r-component shift therefore forces a nonreduced q-fibre. In particular a shift −1 mod 12
in this class of constructions forces multiplicity at least twelve.

Proof. 1. In the coordinates of 20.6 the two periods have q-valuation vectors (1, 0) and (0, 1);
  their r-valuation vectors are (0, 0) and (0, n). After q = sd , the period lattice on the q-central
  component indices is dZ2 . A regular toroidal resolution has indices in (Z/d)2 . The deck

                                                   184
   generator translates them by (a, b). The order of that translation is d/ gcd(d, a, b), so the
   subgroup preserving a component has order h = gcd(d, a, b). Its subgroup fixing a generic
   point has some order h0 dividing h; unit factors may make h0 smaller. That isotropy acts on
   the normal coordinate s by a primitive h0 th root of unity. The quotient normal coordinate is
   sh0 , and q = (sh0 )d/h0 has multiplicity d/h0 , a positive multiple of d/h. Unit factors cannot
   decrease this lower bound.
2. Reducedness would require h0 = d, and therefore h = d, so both a, b are divisible by d. Then
   nb/d is zero modulo n. If nb/d is relatively prime to n, its order in Z/n is n, which divides
   the order d/h of the full component translation; this gives the final lower bound.

Corollary 22.9 (Integral Mordell–Weil lattice). [tag 0309]
  In the notation of 22.8,

                       E (C(C)) = ZP ⊕ ZR ⊕ ZR′ ,               det NS(E ) = −32.

Proof. 1. The affine coordinate ring of C is C[a, b]/(b3 − a4 − 1), with unique representatives of
  degree at most two in b. The pole orders 3i + 4j of ai bj , 0 ≤ j ≤ 2, are distinct, so cancellation
  cannot create functions with pole order one or two at infinity. Consequently

                        H 0 (C, OC (2∞)) = C,        H 0 (C, OC (3∞)) = C ⊕ Ca.

                                                  187
   A section disjoint from O therefore has X = x0 , Y = y0 + y1 a for constants x0 , y0 , y1 .
   Substitution in the Weierstrass equation forces x0 = y0 = 0 and y12 = 2. Thus the only nonzero
   sections with intersection zero with O are P, −P . Every other nonzero section has intersection
   at least one with O, and hence height at least 4 − 3 = 1.

2. 22.8 proves that every section has integral coefficient along P in the rational height decom-
   position. The remaining lattice can have index only one, two or four over ZR + ZR′ . Any
   proper such overlattice contains a nonzero element of order two modulo this sublattice. After
   subtracting an integral combination of R, R′ it is one of R/2, R′ /2, (R + R′ )/2. Each has
   height 1/3, contradicting the preceding lower bound. Thus the index is one. The determinant
   already computed in 22.8 is the full Néron–Severi determinant.



Proposition 22.10 (Unramified torsors with prescribed transgression). [tag 030A]
    Put K = C(t), L = C(C), G = Gal(L/K) = ⟨σ⟩, and let E/K be the generic elliptic curve
of S → B. There is a nonzero class

         ξ ∈ Sha(EL /L)G     whose transgression in     H 2 (G, E(L)) = ZP/12ZP        is 6P.

Here Sha denotes the subgroup of genus-one torsors trivial over the henselian local fields of all
points of C. Such a class has a relatively minimal projective genus-one surface V → C, locally
isomorphic to E → C, and an affine lift A : V → V of σ with

                                             A12 = t6P .

Thus (V, A) is a genus-one normalization base with the specified affine twelfth power.

Proof. 1. We use Galois cohomology with its continuous cochains. The five-term Hochschild–Serre
  sequence gives
                                                  d
                    H 1 (K, E) −→ H 1 (L, E)G −−2→ H 2 (G, E(L)) −→ H 2 (K, E).

   The transgression sequence is (Hochschild and Serre, 1953, Chapter III, Section 4, Theorem 2
   and the following remark, pp.129–130); its continuous form follows by passing to finite Galois
   quotients for the finitely many values of each continuous cochain. For this complex function
   field, H 2 (K, E) = 0, as in (Cossec et al., 2024, Lemma 4.7.8, p. 445). One can also see this
   from cd K = 1: the torsion submodule of E(K) has no second cohomology, and its quotient is
   a rational vector space, whose positive continuous cohomology vanishes by averaging on finite
   quotients.

2. Cyclic group cohomology gives H 2 (G, E(L)) = E(K)/ Trσ E(L). By 22.8 this is Z/12, with
   generator the class of P . Hence there is a G-invariant torsor class ξ0 ∈ H 1 (L, E) with
   d2 ξ0 = 6P . We next remove all its local ramification without changing this transgression.

3. At a place v of B choose a point w of C above it and its decomposition subgroup Gw . The only
   nontrivial decomposition groups have orders 3, 4, 12, at 0, 1, ∞ respectively. The component
   groups of the original fibres are Z/3, Z/2 and zero. Thus 6P belongs to the identity component
   of the local Néron group at every ramified place. Multiplication by the ramification index
   is surjective on that identity group over the henselian local field: on the residue group it is
   surjective on Ga (C) or Gm (C), and its derivative is invertible; Hensel’s lemma lifts a division
   point. Choose such a division point over Kvh . Viewed over Lhw , it is invariant, so its local
   norm is 6P . The restriction of the transgression class to H 2 (Gw , E(Lhw )) is therefore zero. For
   unramified places the decomposition group is trivial, so the same assertion is automatic.


                                                 188
4. Naturality and exactness of the local five-term sequences now show that (ξ0 )w is the restriction
   of some ηv ∈ H 1 (Kvh , E). Only finitely many of these classes need be nonzero. The original
   elliptic surface is nontrivial, since j = 1728t. Ogg–Shafarevich localization is therefore
   surjective:
                                H 1 (K, E) −→       H 1 (Kvh , E) −→ 0.
                                                 M

                                                 v∈B

   This is the combination of exact sequence (4.7.4) and Theorem 4.7.9 in (Cossec et al., 2024,
   p. 445); the same surjectivity and its geometric fibre-twist interpretation are given in (Xiao,
   1991, Section 4, equation (4), p. 21). Take a global η with these local values and put
   ξ = ξ0 − resL/K η. It is locally trivial at every point of C, remains G-invariant, and has
   d2 ξ = 6P . It is nonzero because its transgression is nonzero.

5. The standard interpretation of the Weil–Châtelet group represents ξ by a smooth projective
   genus-one curve over L; taking its relatively minimal regular model over C gives V . Local
   triviality identifies each henselian model with that of EL . Over C the corresponding étale
   identifications yield holomorphic identifications over small base discs. Equivalently, V is
   obtained by gluing copies of E over these discs by translations by local sections. These
   translations extend over the regular I12 model. Thus V is locally isomorphic to E , has smooth
   total surface, no multiple fibres, and the same single I12 fibre. Properness and flatness hold
   locally over the base and hence globally. The local translation gluing specifies V as in (Xiao,
   1991, Theorem 3.4, pp. 14–15; Section 4, p. 21).

6. The G-invariance of ξ gives an affine isomorphism of its generic fibre covering σ. It extends to
   the relatively minimal regular surface: in this particular situation the extension can be checked
   on a common resolution. If an exceptional (−1)-curve for one projection is not contracted
   by the other, its image is a vertical rational curve and has self-intersection at least −1, since
   blowing down only increases self-intersection. On either locally trivial model all vertical
   rational curves are components of the I12 fibre, of square −2. Thus every such (−1)-curve is
   contracted by both projections and can be removed from the common resolution. Repeating
   this proves that the map is an isomorphism. The same argument gives the local comparison
   with the Jacobian model used above. Transporting the base by σ changes none of these
   facts. Write A0 for this lift. Its twelfth power is translation by a section N ∈ E(L)G = ZP .
   Choosing the powers 1, A0 , . . . , A11
                                        0 as lifts of G gives the cyclic factor set N ⌊(i + j)/12⌋. Its
   cohomology class is precisely the descent obstruction d2 ξ, so N = (6 + 12m)P for an integer
   m. Replacing A0 by A = t−mP ◦ A0 gives A12 = t6P .

7. To form the threefold filling of 18.6, the datum (V, A) must be supplemented by its normal
   line bundles, cusp charts and specified punctured-family identification.



Proposition 22.11 (Auxiliary torsor plumbing with cusp multiplicity twelve). [tag 030B]
   For the torsor and affine lift (V, A) of 22.10, there is a line bundle M on V representing the
narrow Jacobian section P , with

                            M 2 = −2,       M ⊗ (A∗ M )−1 ≃ π ∗ OC (∞).

These data give a proper flat nodal plumbing Z ♭ → ∆h and two uniform smooth-total-space
semistable modifications Z ± → ∆h , together with holomorphic maps to B. For h ̸= 0, the
nodal fibre has twelve ordinary double points and Euler number twelve; each small-resolved fibre
has Euler number twenty-four. The cusp fibre of the latter map to B has multiplicity twelve.
Consequently this auxiliary construction does not fill the prescribed S 6 family. No proper birational
modification over B can turn its multiple cusp into a reduced cusp.


                                                 189
Proof. 1. The section P determines a relative Picard class of multidegree zero on every fibre
  component of V → C. It lifts to a line bundle M because Br(C) = 0; this is the relative Picard
  consequence of (Cossec et al., 2024, Proposition 0.9.2, p. 143; Section 4.2, p. 370). In local
  trivializations of the torsor, translation acts trivially on the relative degree-zero Picard class.
  Thus the local Poincaré lines glue up to base lines, with precisely that Brauer obstruction. In
  particular we may and do retain multidegree zero on all twelve fibre components.

2. Choose a finite multisection cover of degree d which trivializes the torsor generically, and
   resolve its base change. There the pulled-back M becomes the narrow Poincaré line for
   the pulled-back P , up to a base line. Its square is −2d, by height base change (Shioda,
   1990, Proposition 8.12, equation (8.25), p. 231). Base lines do not change the square of a
   fibre-degree-zero line. The intersection pullback formula therefore gives M 2 = −2.

3. Since σP = P , the line J = M ⊗ (A∗ M )−1 is trivial on every fibre, including the I12 fibre.
   Grauert base change and the evaluation map give J = π ∗ JC for a line on C. The line
   M ⊗ (t∗6P M )−1 has base degree twelve. To check the sign and degree, pass to the same
   trivializing cover. On a Jacobian, the degree of the restriction of O(P − O) to a section Q
   minus its degree on O is −⟨P, Q⟩, by the height formula and the narrowness of P . For Q = 6P
   this is −12d. Descending the degree factor d proves the assertion. Iterating A∗ twelve times
   now gives 12 deg JC = 12, so deg JC = 1.

4. The forms da/b2 , a da/b2 and da/b form a basis of H 0 (C, KC ). Their σ-eigenvalues are
   λ7 , λ10 , λ11 . Thus the characteristic polynomial on H 1 (C, Z) is

         p(x) = Φ12 (x)Φ6 (x) = x6 − x5 + x3 − x + 1,          p(x) + (1 − x)(x5 + x2 + x) = 1.

   It follows that 1 − σ ∗ is an automorphism of Pic0 (C), with inverse (σ ∗ )5 + (σ ∗ )2 + σ ∗ . Twisting
   M by a base line changes JC by N ⊗ (σ ∗ N )−1 . The displayed inverse therefore supplies a
   base twist making JC = OC (∞). Let ϕ be its section with divisor the reduced I12 fibre F∞ .

5. Apply the plumbing maps of 20.6 to the data (V, M, A). Set RV = PV (O ⊕ M ), and identify
   its zero and infinity sections by s0 (x) ∼ s∞ (Ax). On the node neighbourhood over V use
                                                  −1
                                 a ∈ Mx ,    b ∈ MAx ,       a ⊗ b = hϕx .

   The a collar is glued to the annular core at (x, a); the b collar is glued at (Ax, b−1 ). Choose
   the Hermitian metric and collar radii as in 20.6. Compactness of V and the bounded norm
   of ϕ give disjoint collars, Hausdorffness and compact representatives by exactly the same
   inequalities. These are holomorphic gluing maps of fourfolds over ∆h . Their local hypersurface
   rings are flat over h, and the compact representatives prove properness. The map to B is well
   defined because t ◦ σ = t.

6. At a smooth point of F∞ the equation is ab = hzC ; at one of its twelve nodes, zC = uv and it is
   ab = huv. For h ̸= 0 the latter has one ordinary double point. These twelve centres are distinct
   even if A rotates the fibre components. A centre has a = b = 0 and is in neither annular collar;
   no overlap identifies it with the centre indexed by Ax. Thus the double locus is parametrized
   by V . The two uniform prism subdivisions of 21.2 extend over these charts: the affine action
   preserves the orientation of the I12 cycle, and all remaining changes are units. They give
   proper small modifications, smooth total spaces and reduced normal-crossings h-central fibres.
   Equivalently their normalizations are the blow-up of RV along F∞ in one section, followed by
   the twelve chosen small resolutions. The normal product becomes π ∗ OC (∞)(−F∞ ) = OV .

7. The nearby function of the nodal plumbing is one on F∞ and zero on its complement in the
   conductor. Since e(F∞ ) = 12, its integral is twelve. Each small resolution replaces a point by
   P1 and adds one, giving twenty-four. Independently e(RV ) = 24; above each of the twelve

                                                  190
   nodes the modified normalization replaces a point by a chain of two projective lines, of Euler
   number three. The open parts of the fibre are copies of C∗ and contribute zero. The modified
   normalization therefore has Euler number 48, its pinching has Euler number 36, and the
   semistable nearby count is 48 − 2e(V ) = 24.

8. Finally z = a/b is a coordinate on C near infinity and qB = 1/t = z 12 /c3 , with c a unit. At a
   generic point of the auxiliary cusp fibre this gives multiplicity twelve. In fact the map qB is
   locally a twelfth power throughout the smooth nearby threefold; a holomorphic root of the
   unit can be chosen locally. On any common resolution of a proper birational comparison over
   B, every divisor over that fibre consequently has qB -valuation divisible by twelve. A reduced
   fibre on another smooth model would have a strict transform of valuation one, a contradiction.



Proposition 22.12 (Hodge theory of analytic unramified torsors). [tag 030C]
   Let V → C be any compact smooth analytic genus-one surface locally isomorphic, as a torsor
over every base disc, to the Jacobian surface E → C of 22.8. Then b1 (V ) = 6, and V is Kähler.
For every holomorphic line bundle M on V , the projective bundle PV (O ⊕ M ) is Kähler. Every
                                                                         ¯
smooth compact threefold bimeromorphic to such a bundle satisfies the ∂ ∂-lemma.
    Consequently none of these projective bundles or smooth compact bimeromorphic models can
be the non-∂ ∂¯ normalization component required in 22.16.

Proof. 1. Write p : E → C for the projective Jacobian. The calculation in 22.8 gives R1 p∗ OE =
  OC (−∞), and g(C) = 3. The coherent Leray sequence therefore gives h1 (E , OE ) = 3.
  Projectivity and Hodge decomposition imply b1 (E ) = 6. The topological Leray sequence with
  rational coefficients is

          0 −→ H 1 (C; Q) −→ H 1 (E ; Q) −→ H 0 (C, R1 p∗ Q) −→ H 2 (C; Q) −→ H 2 (E ; Q).

   The last arrow is injective because p has a section. The first arrow is an isomorphism of
   six-dimensional vector spaces. Exactness thus implies H 0 (C, R1 p∗ Q) = 0.

2. The local torsor identifications differ by translations. On a smooth elliptic fibre translations
   act trivially on H 1 . On the I12 fibre they preserve the orientation of the component polygon
   and therefore act trivially on its one-dimensional H 1 as well. These identifications commute
   with the local specialization maps. Hence, for π : V → C, they glue to R1 π∗ Q ≃ R1 p∗ Q
   on the whole curve, including infinity. The same Leray edge sequence for V now gives
   H 1 (V ; Q) ≃ H 1 (C; Q). Thus b1 (V ) = 6 is even. Buchdahl’s theorem (Buchdahl, 1999,
   Theorem 11, p.297) proves that V is Kähler.

3. Choose a Hermitian metric on O ⊕ M . The induced metric on the tautological relatively
   ample line of its projectivization has a closed real (1, 1) curvature form θ positive in the
   vertical direction. If ω is a Kähler form on V , compactness implies that θ + Aπ ∗ ω is positive
   in every direction for a sufficiently large constant A. It is closed, so it is a Kähler form on the
   projective bundle. A smooth compact bimeromorphic model is therefore in Fujiki class C and
                   ¯
   satisfies the ∂ ∂-lemma;  the domination statement is recalled, with its precise reference to the
     ¯
   ∂ ∂ theorem, in (Chen, 2026, Section 2.1, p.8). Apply 22.16 for the final obstruction.

Theorem 22.14 (Fundamental-group obstruction). [tag 030O]
    Let f : Y → ∆ be a proper holomorphic map from a smooth complex manifold, with smooth
connected fibres over ∆∗ and reduced normal-crossings central fibre D. There is a continuous
specialization map from a nearby fibre Yt to D which induces a surjection
                                         π1 (Yt ) −→ π1 (D).
Hence the central fibre of any such semistable filling of S 6 is simply connected. In particular it
cannot be a simple pinching of a connected normalization along one pair of disjoint nonempty
conductor sections, whether its elliptic normalization base is split or is a genus-one torsor.

Proof. 1. The surjectivity assertion also follows from (Nakayama and Ogus, 2010, Theorem 5.1,
  p. 2226). We use the explicit neighbourhood retraction needed in theorem 21.16 and propo-
  sition 22.19. Put W = f −1 (∆ϵ ) and W ∗ = W \ D. The negative gradient of |f |2 , for a
  Hermitian metric, retracts W onto D. For completeness, in a product chart f = z1 · · · zk the
  arithmetic– geometric mean inequality gives
                                         ∥∇|f |2 ∥ ≥ c |f |2−1/k .
   A finite cover of compact D gives a common exponent α < 1 in ∥∇ρ∥ ≥ cρα , where ρ = |f |2 ;
   for a fourfold one may take α = 7/8. The remaining trajectory length is bounded by
   c−1 ρ1−α /(1 − α). Hence trajectories converge uniformly to D, and parametrization by the
   level of ρ gives a continuous strong deformation retraction fixing D. General position moves
   every loop of W off the real-codimension-two normal-crossings strata, so π1 (W ∗ ) → π1 (W ) is
   onto. The smooth proper fibration over the punctured disc gives
                                  π1 (Yt ) −→ π1 (W ∗ ) −→ Z −→ 0.
   A small transverse meridian at a smooth point of a reduced component maps to the generator
   of Z and bounds a disc in W . Thus the image of π1 (Yt ) alone generates π1 (W ) = π1 (D).
   Restricting the retraction W → D to Yt gives the asserted continuous specialization and its
   surjection on fundamental groups.
2. For the last assertion, let R be the connected normalization and D0 , D∞ its two disjoint
   conductor sections. Choose a continuous function h : R → [0, 1] equal to zero on D0 and one
   on D∞ . The function exp(2πih) descends to the pinching. A path from a point of D0 to its
   paired point in D∞ becomes a loop whose image has winding number one. Consequently the
   pinching has a surjection of its fundamental group onto Z. This contradicts the preceding
   necessary condition when Yt ≃ S 6 .

Theorem 22.15 (The Hodge obstruction to normal-crossing limits). [tag 030Z]
    Let g : Z → ∆s be a proper holomorphic map from a smooth complex fourfold, smooth over
∆s , with reduced normal-crossings central fibre D. Suppose its nearby fibres are biholomorphic to
  ∗

the six-sphere members of the specified family, after any finite base change w = sN . Then

                                H 1 (D; C) = 0,         h1 (D, OD ) ≥ 1.

Consequently the natural map H 1 (D; C) → H 1 (D, OD ) is not surjective. In particular, D cannot
be the analytification of a proper complex algebraic variety with normal-crossings singularities.
                                                                                             ¯
    If D has simple normal crossings, at least one of its nonempty closed strata fails the ∂ ∂-lemma.
In particular, no such simple normal-crossings filling can have all irreducible components Kähler
or all irreducible components Moishezon. These obstructions hold for every N ≥ 1.

Proof. Theorem 22.14 gives a surjection from the fundamental group of a nearby fibre onto
π1 (D). Since that fibre is diffeomorphic to S 6 , it follows that π1 (D) = 1 and H 1 (D; C) = 0.
    For a compact complex threefold X diffeomorphic to S 6 , the groups H 2 (X; Z) and H 4 (X; Z)
vanish, so c1 (X) = c2 (X) = 0. The analytic Riemann–Roch formula, obtained from Atiyah and
Singer (1968, Theorem 4.3, pp. 564–565), gives
                                             1
                              χ(X, OX ) =       ⟨c1 (X)c2 (X), [X]⟩ = 0.
                                             24
EveryRholomorphic three-form Ω is closed and is exact because H 3 (X; C) = 0. Stokes’ theorem
gives X iΩ ∧ Ω = 0. The integrand is pointwise nonnegative for the complex orientation, so
Ω = 0. Serre duality therefore gives h3 (X, OX ) = 0, and connectedness gives h0 (X, OX ) = 1.
Hence
                              h1 (X, OX ) = 1 + h2 (X, OX ) ≥ 1.
Locally along the reduced normal-crossing divisor, g has the form s = z1 · · · zk after absorbing a
holomorphic unit. This makes OZ torsion-free over the local discrete valuation ring of the disc
and hence flat over it. Upper semicontinuity for the proper flat map gives h1 (D, OD ) ≥ 1; see
Grauert (1960, §7, Satz 5, pp. 63–64).
    For a proper complex algebraic variety with Du Bois singularities, the canonical map from
singular cohomology to coherent cohomology is surjective in every degree; see Graf and Kovács
(2014, §1.D, p. 120). Normal-crossing singularities are Du Bois, including self-intersections of a
global component. Thus algebraicity and properness of D would make H 1 (D; C) → H 1 (D, OD )
surjective, contradicting the two groups just computed.
    Now suppose D is simple normal crossing and each nonempty closed stratum satisfies the
  ¯
∂ ∂-lemma.   These are exactly the strata in condition (K1) of Chen (2026, Definition 2.3, p. 9).
For a proper semistable degeneration with smooth total space and this condition, Chen (2026,
Theorem 2.4(4), p. 10) gives E1 degeneration of the Hodge–de Rham spectral sequence on a
nearby fibre. In total degree one this yields

                          0 = b1 (Xs ) = h0 (Xs , Ω1Xs ) + h1 (Xs , OXs ) ≥ 1,

a contradiction.
    A closed smooth submanifold of a compact Kähler manifold is Kähler. A closed stratum of a
Moishezon component is also Moishezon: choose a projective modification, take a component of
the inverse image dominating the stratum, and intersect with general relative hyperplanes until
the induced proper map is generically finite. This gives a generically finite projective cover and
hence maximal algebraic dimension for the stratum. Smooth Moishezon manifolds satisfy the
  ¯
∂ ∂-lemma,  as recalled in Chen (2026, §2.1, p. 8). Either stated hypothesis on the irreducible

                                                  193
components therefore gives condition (K1), proving the last assertion. A finite parameter cover
preserves the biholomorphism type of every nonzero fibre, so the argument applies for every
N ≥ 1.

Theorem 22.16 (The obstruction on normalization components). [tag 0315]
    Let D be a compact reduced complex space with normal-crossings singularities, allowing
self-intersections of global components. Suppose that every connected component of its smooth
                               ¯
normalization satisfies the ∂ ∂-lemma. Then the natural map

                                    H 1 (D; C) −→ H 1 (D, OD )

is surjective.
    Consequently every smooth-total-space reduced normal-crossings filling of the specified six-
                                                                                              ¯
sphere family, after any finite base change, has a normalization component which fails the ∂ ∂-
lemma. In particular its normalization cannot consist entirely of compact Kähler or Moishezon
manifolds. This conclusion includes normal crossings which are not simple.

Proof. 1. Let D[p] be the smooth compact branch space whose points are ordered (p + 1)-tuples of
  distinct local branches through one point of D. Equivalently, we normalize the loci where these
  branches meet, retaining their ordering. These are distinct local branches, even when they
  belong to one global irreducible component. The finite holomorphic maps πp : D[p] → D and
  their face maps are specified by forgetting one branch. The symmetric group acts by reordering;
  we take the alternating summand, with the sign character, in each degree. Averaging over
  this finite group is exact over C. Write δ for the alternating sum of the face pullbacks.

2. Both augmented complexes
                                            alt                            alt
                       CD −→ (πp )∗ CD[p] p≥0 ,          OD −→ (πp )∗ OD[p] p≥0

   are resolutions. This can be checked locally without a global ordering. In a chart z1 · · · zk = 0,
   the constant complex is the augmented cochain complex of the simplex on the k branches.
   For the holomorphic complex, fix a monomial in the convergent power series ring. It survives
   on exactly the intersections indexed by subsets of those i for which its zi -exponent is zero. If
   there are no such indices it already vanishes on D; otherwise its coefficient complex is again
   an augmented simplex complex. The usual contraction is a finite combination of coordinate
   restrictions, so preserves convergence. This proves exactness in the convergent analytic local
   rings. The descriptions agree under permutations of the local branches.

3. Resolve the holomorphic terms by smooth Dolbeault forms and the constant terms by smooth
   de Rham forms on the branch spaces. These compute the respective hypercohomologies.
   Indeed finite pushforward is exact here, and partitions of unity from local ambient smooth
   functions pull back to make the resulting sheaves fine. The ordinary de Rham lemma and
   Dolbeault lemma apply on each smooth branch space. Projection to the (0, •) part defines the
   natural comparison between the two total complexes and induces H 1 (D; C) → H 1 (D, OD ).

4. Represent a coherent degree-one class by a total cocycle (α, f ), where α is a smooth (0, 1)-form
   on D[0] and f is an alternating smooth function on D[1] . Choose the total-complex signs so
   that its equations are
                                 ¯ = 0,
                                ∂α                   ¯
                                              δα = ∂f,       δf = 0.
                                                                         ¯
   On a normalization component, ∂α is of type (1, 1), is ∂-exact and is ∂-closed.       ¯
                                                                                   The ∂ ∂-lemma
                                         ¯
   gives a smooth function h with ∂α = ∂ ∂h. Do this on every component, and put
                                             ¯
                                    α′ = α − ∂h,         f ′ = f − δh.

                                                   194
   The pair represents the same coherent class and still satisfies the displayed cocycle equations;
   now dα′ = 0. Holomorphic face maps commute with both differential operators, so
                                         ¯ ′ = ∂δα′ = δ∂α′ = 0.
                                       ∂ ∂f

   A smooth complex-valued pluriharmonic function on a compact connected complex manifold
   is constant: apply the maximum principle to its real and imaginary parts in local complex
   coordinates. Therefore f ′ is constant on each connected component of D[1] . It follows that
   df ′ = 0 and δα′ = 0.

5. Thus the same pair (α′ , f ′ ), with α′ viewed as a complex-valued smooth one-form, is a
   cocycle of the total de Rham branch complex. Its image is the original coherent class. This
   proves surjectivity. The argument on D[1] uses its compactness through the constancy of
   pluriharmonic functions.

6. For the asserted application, 22.14 and 22.15 give H 1 (D; C) = 0 and h1 (D, OD ) ≥ 1. Sur-
   jectivity is impossible, so some normalization component fails the lemma. Compact Kähler
   and smooth Moishezon manifolds satisfy it, as in the primary comparison checked in 22.15.
   The same argument applies after every finite base change, since its smooth fibres are still the
   specified six-spheres.



Proposition 22.17 (A restricted non-Kähler cap obstruction). [tag 0316]
   Let D be a compact reduced normal-crossings complex space. Suppose its irreducible compo-
nents have been partitioned into closed unions D0 , . . . , Ds , with their reduced induced structures.
Assume that
                      H 1 (Di , C) −→ H 1 (Di , O) is surjective for every i,                    (22.1)
and that the analogous map is injective for every pairwise intersection Di ∩ Dj . Then

                             H 1 (D, C) −→ H 1 (D, OD )    is surjective.                       (22.2)

    In particular these hypotheses hold for the following specified cap assembly. The horizontal
block D0 is a two-section pinching of a ruled bundle over an analytic locally trivial torsor V → C
of 22.12, with conductor map A covering σ and A12 = t6P . The normalization may undergo the
modifications of 22.11, or any smooth bimeromorphic modifications for which the two conductor
restriction maps on H 1 are the same pullbacks as before. The other blocks are smooth hyperbolic
toric Kato threefolds or compact smooth spaces satisfying (22.1), for example class-C spaces.
Assume every pairwise overlap is either a reduced union of invariant divisors of a hyperbolic
toric Kato threefold, or a compact normal-crossings surface whose normalized components and
normalized double curves are rational. No such assembly can be a semistable central fibre of the
S 6 family.

Proof. 1. Write D[p] for the disjoint union of intersections of p+1 distinct blocks. The augmented
  closed-cover complexes resolve both CD and OD . For the coherent assertion this can be checked
  in a normal-crossings coordinate chart. The local equation of D is a product of distinct
  coordinates, and each block groups a disjoint subset of those factors. The corresponding ideals
  are generated by products in disjoint sets of variables. The ordinary alternating intersection
  complex is exact, as one sees on each monomial, where it is the augmented complex of a
  simplex. The same contraction acts coefficientwise on convergent power series. For constant
  sheaves, small intersections are contractible unions of coordinate subspaces, and the same
  stalkwise simplex complex is exact. This proves both resolutions also when the global blocks
  are self-crossing.


                                                 195
2. Their hypercohomology spectral sequences have

                              E1p,q (F) = H q (D[p] , F),    F = C or O.

   Every connected compact reduced branch intersection has only constant holomorphic functions.
   Thus the comparison maps in the entire q = 0 row are isomorphisms. They induce isomorphisms
   on E21,0 and E22,0 . Surjectivity in (22.1) and injectivity on pairwise intersections imply
   surjectivity on E20,1 : lift a coherent degree-one class on the blocks, then its topological
   restriction difference vanishes because its coherent image vanishes and the pairwise comparison
   is injective.

3. Now use the natural five-term exact sequences
                                                                   d
                            0 −→ E21,0 −→ H 1 (D, F) −→ E20,1 −→
                                                               2
                                                                 E22,0 .

   The isomorphism on the last term makes a lift of a coherent d2 -closed element topologically
   d2 -closed. The isomorphism on the first term then gives (22.2). If the block comparisons
   are isomorphisms, the same argument also proves injectivity, provided the map on E20,1 is
   injective.

4. The horizontal-block comparison follows from the cohomology of its base curve. By 22.12,
   H 1 (V, C) = H 1 (C, C) and H 1 (V, O) = H 1 (C, OC ). The first equality is the Leray calculation
   there; the second also follows from R1 π∗ OV = OC (−∞), which has no global section. The
   action of A on these groups is σ ∗ , since it covers σ and the displayed maps are pullbacks from
   the base. The characteristic polynomial

                                 p(x) = Φ12 (x)Φ6 (x),        p(1) = 1,

   shows that 1 − A∗ is invertible on both groups. The normalization sequence of the two-section
   pinching, for constants and for holomorphic functions, therefore gives

                                H 1 (D0 , C) = C,       H 1 (D0 , O) = C.

   Both classes come from the same difference map on constant functions of the conductor. Their
   natural comparison is an isomorphism. Projective-bundle pullback identifies the normalization
   groups with those of V . The stipulated modifications preserve these groups and both restriction
   maps; in particular the explicit modifications of 22.11 have this property. This grouped
   computation is essential: on an individual conductor V , the comparison has dimensions six
   and three and is not injective.

5. For a hyperbolic toric Kato manifold Z, its fundamental group is Z, as in (Istrati et al., 2022,
   Section 2, p.1352); (Istrati et al., 2022, Proposition 8.4, p. 1377, and Theorem 8.5, p. 1378)
                                                                                    d
   give H 0 (Z, Ω1Z ) = 0 and H 1 (Z, OZ ) = C. The exact sequence 0 → C → O −     → dO → 0 shows
   that H 1 (Z, C) → H 1 (Z, O) is injective, because a global section of dO is a closed holomorphic
   one-form. The two dimensions are one, so it is an isomorphism. The same reasoning applies
   to hyperbolic toric Kato surfaces. Compact smooth rational varieties have both groups zero.
   Class-C blocks satisfy (22.1) by their ∂ ∂¯ property.

6. Finally let F be a reduced union of invariant divisors in a hyperbolic toric Kato threefold. Its
   normalized components are compact toric surfaces or hyperbolic toric Kato surfaces (Istrati
   et al., 2022, proof of Theorem 8.8, p.1380). Its normalized double curves are rational, since
   every invariant curve is rational in the hyperbolic case (Istrati et al., 2022, Theorem 5.2,
   pp. 1366–1367). Use the ordered-local-branch resolution from 22.16. The comparisons on
   component H 1 are isomorphisms, and the groups on normalized double curves vanish. The
   same five-term argument shows that H 1 (F, C) → H 1 (F, OF ) is an isomorphism. For an

                                                  196
   overlap with rational normalized components and double curves, the argument is identical
   with zero component H 1 . Thus every pairwise overlap in the statement has the required
   injective comparison, proving (22.2) for the specified assembly.

7. For a semistable S 6 centre, 22.14 gives H 1 (D, C) = 0, while upper semicontinuity and the
   nearby lower bound h1 (O) ≥ 1 in 22.15 give h1 (D, OD ) ≥ 1. This contradicts (22.2). The
   obstruction is the stated surjectivity comparison on the blocks and injectivity comparison on
   their pairwise overlaps.



Remark 22.18 (A punctured isomorphism with an essential singularity). [tag PT03] The auto-
morphism
                           (s, [z0 : z1 ]) 7−→ (s, [e1/s z0 : z1 ])
of ∆∗ × P1 has no meromorphic extension across zero, although the two product families extend
properly over the disc. Its restriction to the constant section [1 : 1] is [e1/s : 1], which has an
essential singularity. The proper graph of a meromorphic extension, pulled back to this section
and normalized in its dominating component, would give a holomorphic extension from the disc,
a contradiction.

Proposition 22.19 (A Hopf surface degeneration and its comparison map). [tag 0317]
   There is a proper semistable analytic family of compact complex surfaces p : H → ∆ with
smooth total space such that:

  1. its punctured restriction is a holomorphic product with the scalar primary Hopf surface

     over the two total spaces near the central fibres.

Consequently H × P1 → ∆ is a semistable family of compact threefolds with simply connected
centre and h1 (O) = 1, whose normalized components fail the ∂ ∂¯ lemma. Its smooth fibres have
Euler number zero and fundamental group Z.

  transformation (Fujimoto, 1990, Definition 1.1, pp. 85–86). Let

                                  b : B = Bl(p,0) (P1 × ∆) −→ P1 × ∆.

   does not change its group. The resulting surface is the scalar Hopf surface Hαc . For the three
   vectors in the construction we may take

                                   (c, d) = (1, i),    (i, −1),       (1 + i, i),

   giving respectively

                         α1 = αi = e−2π ,      α1+i = exp 2πi(1 + i)/2 = −e−π .
                                                                                    


   On B|∆∗ = P1 × ∆∗ , A has the canonical nowhere-zero section of its exceptional divisor. Its
   cocycle is therefore a coboundary there, while L is the constant O(1) bundle. The cocycle
   coboundary therefore gives a holomorphic product isomorphism with H− × ∆∗ .

4. Each central Hi → Fi is a principal elliptic bundle. Its intersection with the other component
   is a smooth fibre, so a local trivialization over a base disc gives NE/Hi = OE exactly. Thus
   the product of the two normal lines is trivial, with the smoothing section supplied by the
   coordinate u = xy.


                                                      198
5. Here are the integral topology maps. A scalar Hopf surface is diffeomorphic to S 1 × S 3 : divide
   the radial coordinate by multiplication by |α| and untwist its constant phase rotation along
   the radial interval. Its fibre inclusion has fundamental-group map
                                          Λ = Z2 −→ Λ/Zci .
   For c1 = (1, 0) and c2 = (0, 1), these are the two coordinate quotients. The van Kampen
   pushout kills both generators of Λ, and hence π1 (Y ) = 0. In the normalization Mayer–Vietoris
   sequence the degree-one map, with the second inclusion negated, is
                                                                              !
                                                                         0 1
                        H1 (E; Z) −→ H1 (H1 ; Z) ⊕ H1 (H2 ; Z),              .
                                                                        −1 0

   It is unimodular. The degree-zero map is the primitive column (1, −1)t , the degree-two target
   is zero, and H3 (E) = 0. The exact sequence now gives
                 H1 Y = H2 Y = 0,      0 −→ Z2 −→ H3 Y −→ Z −→ 0,           H4 Y = Z2 .
   All groups displayed in the proposition are therefore free.
6. For coherent cohomology, translations act trivially on H 1 (E, OE ), so for either central principal
   bundle the sheaf R1 π∗ O on P1 is the constant line bundle. Its Leray sequence shows that
   restriction
                                   H 1 (Hi , OHi ) −→ H 1 (E, OE )
   is an isomorphism. The normalization exact sequence therefore has degree-one map (s, t) 7→
   s − t from C2 to C. The preceding degree-zero map is surjective. Its kernel has dimension
   one, proving h1 (Y, OY ) = 1. This also displays exactly why the overlap-injectivity hypothesis
   in 22.17 fails: H 1 (E; C) → H 1 (E, OE ) has a one-dimensional kernel.
7. For completeness, the two scalar Hopf surfaces used above are not biholomorphic. An
   isomorphism lifts to an automorphism of C2 \ {0} that intertwines the two cyclic generators
   or their inverses. Hartogs extension applies to the lift and its inverse; both fix zero and have
   invertible derivative there. Differentiating the intertwining identity gives e−2π = (−e−π )±1 ,
   which is false. They have no rational curves, since a map P1 → Hα lifts to C2 \ {0} and is
   constant. The usual resolution of a bimeromorphic map of smooth compact surfaces therefore
   also shows that these two Hopf surfaces are not bimeromorphic. This agrees with the explicit
   scalar case of Abasheva and Déev (2024, arXiv version 1, Section 2.2, pp. 4–5).
8. The fundamental groups also exclude a meromorphic extension of the punctured product
   comparison. A sufficiently small closed semistable neighbourhood in H retracts onto Y ,
   by the monomial-gradient argument of 22.14. Its fundamental group is zero. The product
   neighbourhood H− × ∆ has fundamental group Z. If the punctured comparison had a proper
   meromorphic graph, resolving that graph would give a common smooth proper modification
   of the two neighbourhoods. A proper bimeromorphic map between smooth complex manifolds
   preserves π1 , by the codimension-two avoidance argument in 21.16. This is a contradiction.
   Both models already have the indicated holomorphic map to the same P1 ; the example
   therefore retains an extended base map while the total-space comparison fails.
9. Finally take the product with P1 . Its central integral Betti numbers are
                                            (1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 3, 2),
   and h1 (O) remains one. The nearby fibre is H− × P1 , of fundamental group Z and Euler
   number zero. The resulting fundamental group and Euler number are the stated invariants of
   these smooth fibres.

Remark 22.20 (Elliptic-bundle and Hopf degeneration inputs). [tag PT10] The Cartier-divisor
construction used in Proposition 22.19 is the construction of Fujimoto (1990, construction, p. 85;
Definition 1.1, p. 86). His Remark 1.4 attributes non-Kähler torus degenerations to Ueno. His
Proposition 1.14, pp. 92–93, extends principal elliptic bundles across subsets of codimension at
least three; Example 1.15, pp. 93–94, gives a principal-bundle extension failure in codimension two.
Hopf components occur in the semistable degenerations of Nishiguchi (1988, Theorem 1.4, preprint
p. 7, and Example 2.1, p. 13). The diagonal Hopf quotients, elliptic-conductor identifications and
normal lines in Schröer and Siebert (2002, Propositions 3.1–3.4, preprint pp. 6–9) provide related
explicit models. Proposition 22.19 proves its own proper family using the stated Cartier-divisor
cocycle.

Remark 22.21 (Normal degrees along the exceptional ruling). [tag PT11] For the divisor D =
E × P1 in Hi × P1 , the normal line is pulled back from E and has degree zero on every ruling fibre.
For the exceptional divisor obtained by blowing up a smooth elliptic curve in a threefold, the
tautological normal restricts to OP1 (−1) on that fibre. Restricting the normal-crossing identity

                                  ND/A ⊗ ND/B ⊗ OD (T ) ≃ OD

to the ruling therefore gives −1 + 0 + deg(T |P1 ) = 0. In particular an empty triple divisor has
the wrong degree, whereas the section T = E × {p} contributes exactly +1. Proposition 22.27
computes the full line bundles, including their elliptic factors.

Proposition 22.22 (Generic simplicity and the distinguished orbit). [tag PT12] Fix an ordinary
base point at which µ ∈/ Qτ + Q. Such base points exist. Outside a countable set of admissible
values of the parameter β, the corresponding two-dimensional complex torus is simple. For every
admissible β at this base point, the distinguished line Ce, with e = Πδb = (0, 1)t , meets the period
lattice in Ze. The induced orbit map is the injective holomorphic group map

                              ι : C∗ −→ C2 /ΠΛ,        ι(e2πiz ) = [ze].

Here [z] 7→ e2πiz identifies C/Z with the source.

Proof. On an ordinary uniformizing chart the equations µ = rτ + s, for (r, s) ∈ Q2 , define
countably many analytic loci. If they covered the chart, Baire’s theorem would force one equation
on an open set and hence identically. The marked elliptic section would then be torsion, contrary
to the construction. Thus the required base point exists.
    For integral vectors v = (a, b, c, d) and v ′ = (A, B, C, D),

                                Πv = (6aµ + bτ + c, aβ + bµ + d).

The determinant det(Πv, Πv ′ ) is affine in β, with coefficient

                                     (Ab − aB)τ + (Ac − aC).

If the coefficient vanishes and a ̸= 0, the nonreal number τ gives B = Ab/a and C = Ac/a. The
remaining determinant is (6aµ + bτ + c)(D − Ad/a). Its first factor is nonzero by the rational
independence of 1, τ, µ, and its second factor vanishes only when v, v ′ are rationally dependent.
The case a = 0, A ̸= 0 follows by exchanging the vectors. For a = A = 0, the determinant is

                             (bD − Bd)τ + (cB − Cb)µ + (cD − Cd).

Rational independence makes this zero only when all the two-by-two minors vanish, again giving
dependence. Therefore an independent integral pair has zero determinant for at most one value
of β. There are countably many such pairs.

                                                200
    A complex line defining an elliptic subtorus contains two real-linearly independent periods.
Conversely, any such period pair spans a complex line with a rank-two lattice; admissibility
makes the real period map an isomorphism. Avoiding the countable exceptional values therefore
gives simplicity. The equation 6aµ + bτ + c = 0 forces a = b = c = 0, which proves Ce ∩ ΠΛ = Ze
and the claimed orbit map.
     For comparison with an elliptic-bundle fibre, every holomorphic map from an elliptic curve to
a complex torus lifts to a map C → C2 whose derivative is doubly periodic. Compactness makes
that derivative constant. A nonconstant such map consequently has image a translate of an
elliptic subtorus. Thus a simple torus obtained above has no elliptic-curve fibre of this kind.

Remark 22.23 (The distinguished orbit on an ordinary torus). [tag PT04] The distinguished
nonconstant orbit map C∗ → T 2 on an ordinary torus has no meromorphic extension to P1 . A
meromorphic map from a smooth curve to a compact complex manifold extends holomorphically
at its isolated indeterminacies, by normalization of its proper graph. A holomorphic map P1 → T 2
lifts to C2 and is constant. This contradicts the nonconstant orbit map.

Proposition 22.24 (Normal-line obstruction at good reduction). [tag 0318]
    Let a, b be holomorphic units on a disc ∆q , with 0 < |a(q)| < 1, and let m ̸= 0 be an integer.
Put
                              Ea = (C∗ × ∆q )/ (z, q) ∼ (a(q)z, q) .
                                                                  

This is a smooth proper elliptic family over the full disc. Over ∆∗q define a line bundle Lm by

                                   (z, v, q) ∼ a(q)z, q m b(q)v, q .
                                                                      


Its restriction to each elliptic fibre has degree zero. After any finite base change q = sN ε(s), where
N > 0 and ε is a holomorphic unit, the following extension is impossible: a proper semistable
family p : C → ∆s of connected curves, with smooth total surface, an isomorphism C|∆∗s ≃ Ea |∆∗s ,
and a line bundle on C restricting to Lm under that isomorphism.
     The assertion allows any finite collection of rational tails in the central curve and arbitrary
translations in the punctured isomorphism. It remains true after tensoring Lm by the restriction
of a line bundle extending on the interface.
     In particular the axis z1 = 0 in the diagonal Hopf surfaces

                           Hq,a(q) = (C2 \ {0})/⟨(z1 , z2 ) 7→ (qz1 , a(q)z2 )⟩

cannot acquire such a semistable completion together with its normal line, after any finite base
change.

Proof. 1. Choose a logarithm of a on the disc and set τa = log a/(2πi). Then ℑτa > 0, and

                                         Ea ≃ (C × ∆q )/(Z + τa (q)Z).

   The real coordinates z = exp(2πi(x + τa (q)y)) give a smooth trivialization by the marked
   torus (x, y) ∈ R2 /Z2 . In particular its monodromy on H1 is the identity. The line factors in
   this marking are 1 along the x cycle and q m b(q) along the y cycle. On a positive parameter
   circle, the latter factor has winding m. Equivalently, the clutching calculation gives

                ⟨c1 (Lm ), [Tx ]⟩ = 0,       ⟨c1 (Lm ), [Ty ]⟩ = m,       ⟨c1 (Lm ), [Ea,q ]⟩ = 0.

   Here Tx , Ty sweep the indicated cycles around the parameter circle; the orientation of Ty is
   chosen to agree with the clutching convention in the displayed line factor. Reversing that
   convention changes both sides’ sign and has no effect on nonvanishing. One can also compute
   the integer on the square [0, 1]y × Sq1 : the two y edges are glued by q m b(q), whose degree is m.

                                                     201
2. Under q = sN ε(s) the degree becomes mN . The unit ε(s)m b(q(s)) has zero winding. Thus
   the mixed Chern class is the nonzero covector

                                 (0, mN ) ∈ H 1 (Ea,q ; Z) ⊗ H 1 (Ss1 ; Z).

3. Suppose an extension C existed. Its central fibre is connected. Flatness and properness give
   arithmetic genus one, and the normalization exact sequence gives

                                         1=        g(Ci ) + b1 (Γ),
                                              X

                                               i

   where Ci are the smooth normalization components and Γ is the dual graph, including a loop
   for a self-node. Consequently either there is a unique elliptic component and Γ is a tree, or all
   components are rational and Γ has one cycle.

4. The second case has nontrivial monodromy. This can be seen directly in the local plumbing
   uv = s. Transport around s = 0 is a positive Dehn twist on its neck annulus. An edge outside
   the unique graph cycle gives a separating neck and acts trivially on H1 . Each of the k ≥ 1
   edges in the graph cycle gives a nonseparating neck. These disjoint necks represent the same
   primitive class up to sign on the smoothed genus-one surface. The transvection is unchanged
   by reversing that class. Their product therefore has, in a symplectic basis, the matrix
                                                          !
                                                    1 k
                                                    0 1

   or its inverse under the opposite monodromy convention. It is not the identity. The given
   punctured elliptic family has identity monodromy, so this case is impossible.

5. There is therefore an elliptic core C0 with rational trees attached at finitely many points.
   Choose two oriented loops on C0 avoiding those points and with intersection number one. The
   map p is a submersion near their union. Compactness of the loops and a smooth horizontal
   distribution provide, after shrinking the disc, families of loops over the full disc. Each swept
   torus on its boundary bounds the resulting solid torus in C. Hence the first Chern class of
   every line bundle on C evaluates to zero on both such swept tori.

6. The two transported loops form a basis of the nearby elliptic fibre’s H1 : cutting off the rational
   trees adds only genus-zero pieces along separating necks, and their intersection number remains
   one. Under the given punctured isomorphism, their swept tori therefore project to a basis
   of the mixed group H1 (Ea,q ; Z) ⊗ H1 (Ss1 ; Z). They may differ from the marked swept tori by
   integral fibre classes. This accounts in particular for an arbitrary loop of fibre translations
   in the isomorphism. The fibre degree of Lm is zero, so these additional fibre classes do not
   change either pairing. The nonzero covector (0, mN ) cannot vanish on both basis vectors.
   This contradicts the bounding-solid-torus calculation and proves the assertion.

7. Finally an extending tensor factor has zero pairing on both bounding tori by the same
   argument. It cannot cancel the obstruction. Vertical divisors and any Cartier triple divisor
   on such an extended interface are included among these harmless tensor factors.

8. For the stated Hopf consequence, the axis is precisely Ea,q . The derivative of the deck
   transformation in the z1 direction multiplies a normal vector by q; its action on the axis
   coordinate is multiplication by a(q). These are exactly the two factors defining L1 . This is also
   the explicit diagonal-Hopf normal-line convention of Abasheva and Déev (2024, arXiv version 1,
   Section 2.2, pp. 4–5). The assertion just proved applies with m = 1 and b = 1. It also applies
   to the first multiplier q m b(q) for any positive m. At the cusp the nonzero unit e2πiµ(q) has
   absolute value different from one at q = 0. Indeed the nodal cubic is Y 2 = (X − 1)2 (X + 2); its

                                                   202
                                                                                   √        √
   normalization X = h2 − 2, Y = h(h2 − 3) and the √ multiplicative coordinate (h − √3)/(h + 3)
   show that the marked section at (X, Y ) = (0, ± 2) has multiplier one of −(5 ± 2 6). Choose
   that multiplier or its inverse to obtain such a contracting a(q). This proves good reduction
   for this axis.



Remark 22.25 (The individual mixed Chern class). [tag PT13] The evaluation isomorphism
Lm ⊗L−1 m ≃ O cancels the two mixed first Chern classes. Individually, Proposition 22.24 computes
the nonzero covector (0, mN ) on the two swept tori after a parameter cover of order N . Both
swept tori bound solid tori on an extending semistable good-reduction interface. Hence the
restriction of the first Chern class of every extending line evaluates to zero on both, whereas
c1 (Lm ) does not. This is the explicit restriction map relating the individual obstruction to
the tensor-product normal equation. In the constant elliptic family of Proposition 22.19, the
corresponding mixed class is zero.

Proposition 22.27 (Parabolic families and exceptional divisors). [tag 030E]
    Fix an integer n ≥ 1 and holomorphic units a(s), κ(s) on a disc, with 0 < |a(s)| < 1. After
shrinking the disc there is a proper holomorphic submersion K → ∆s , with an embedded smooth
proper elliptic family
                               E = (C∗ × ∆s )/((v, s) ∼ (a(s)v, s)).
Its central surface is a parabolic Inoue surface Sn , with π1 (Sn ) = Z, b2 (Sn ) = n, and elliptic axis
of square −n. For s =  ̸ 0, the surface Ks is obtained from the diagonal Hopf surface Hκ(s)sn ,a(s)
by n successive blow-ups at one axis point and its indicated infinitely near strict-axis points. In a
fixed annulus marking of E, its normal line has factor

                                      gs (v) = κ(s)(a(s)v + s)n .

This line extends across s = 0 and is isomorphic to the holomorphic family with factor κ(s)a(s)n v n .
For constant a, κ it is a constant family of degree −n lines.
    The relation with the normal line of the unmodified Hopf axis is

                            NEs /Ks = Lκ(s)sn ⊗ OEs (−n[−s]),         s ̸= 0.

Here n[−s] is the total exceptional correction, with the multiplicity of each successive blow-up
retained. It has no Cartier extension on E, even after a finite base change or the addition of
a vertical component. The marked divisor used to change the normal line therefore fails the
extension condition in Proposition 22.24.
    For n = 8, the degree −8 axis normal can be chosen to be the inverse of OE (2) on any chosen
smooth elliptic complete intersection E = (2, 2) ⊂ P3 . This supplies the normal-line matching
with BlE P3 described below, including one positive triple section. The matching is the displayed
isomorphism of the two normal lines, with the stated triple-curve factor.

Proof. 1. Let BR ⊂ C2 be a ball, and let πn : BbR → BR be the following modification. Blow up
  the origin, then successively the intersection of the newest exceptional curve with the strict
  transform of the axis x = 0. In the last chart,

                                          πn (z, w) = (zwn , w).



                                                  205
   Define the parameter-dependent embedding in that chart by

                              σs (z, w) = κ(s)z, a(s)w + (1 − a(s))s .
                                                                         


   Choose constants A < ρ < 1 and K > 0 with |a(s)| ≤ A and |κ(s)| ≤ K on a closed smaller
   disc. Shrink it further so that |a(s)w + (1 − a(s))s| ≤ ρR on B R . Then

                             |πn σs (z, w)|2 ≤ K 2 R2 (ρR)2n + ρ2 R2 < R2

  when R is small enough. The last-chart coordinates of these images are bounded, so this is
  compact containment of σs (B R ) in B
                                      bR , uniformly in s. For each finite bound on |κ|, these
  inequalities give such a radius R.

2. Remove the embedded ball and identify the outer and inner collars by σs πn . The outer collar
   avoids the exceptional locus, and πn is a biholomorphism there; thus the collar identification is
   a biholomorphism. Carry out the same construction over the parameter disc. The embeddings
   and the identifications are holomorphic and preserve s. Uniformly disjoint collars give a
   Hausdorff smooth threefold, and the projection is a holomorphic submersion in every chart.
   Uniform compact fundamental regions over compact parameter sets prove properness. This
   is the usual Kato construction, with the explicit moving embedding above; see Istrati et al.
   (2022, Section 2, pp.1351–1353). The general occurrence of deformations from Kato surfaces
   to blown-up Hopf surfaces is classical; see Teleman (2010, Introduction, pp.1750–1751). We
   use explicit formulas here to retain the elliptic marking and its exceptional correction.

3. The contracted map πn σs fixes (0, s). In the coordinate v = w − s it becomes

                               fs (x, v) = κ(s)x(a(s)v + s)n , a(s)v .
                                                                     


  At s = 0 this is the parabolic monomial germ with exponent matrix ( 10 n1 ). The chosen
  modification is exactly the n-fold modification in Istrati et al. (2022, Example 9.10, p.1386).
  Consequently the central surface is the stated parabolic Inoue surface; its elliptic axis is
  disjoint from the rational cycle. The construction gives π1 = Z and b2 = n, or equivalently
  one can use the cited description of this surface.

4. The strict axis is preserved in the collar gluing. Its coordinate v is multiplied by a(s). To see
   its full quotient, the axis disc in the blowdown coordinates is

                                       Ds = {v : |v + s| < R}.

   For small s, it contains 0 and satisfies a(s)Ds ⋐ Ds . Its dilates have union C and shrinking
   intersection {0}. Thus Ds \ a(s)Ds , with the two boundary collars glued, is a fundamental
   annulus for C∗ /a(s)Z . This proves the exact elliptic marking throughout the parameter disc.

5. There are two normal frames, whose distinction is essential. In the last blow-up chart the
   collar map σs πn has factor
                                   gz (v) = κ(s)(v + s)n .
   On a fixed annulus avoiding v = 0, shrink s so that both v + s and a(s)v + s are nonzero. The
   blowdown normal coordinate is x = z(v + s)n , and in that frame the factor is

                                      gx (v) = κ(s)(a(s)v + s)n .

  The change between the frames is a nonzero gauge on these annuli. The central factor is
  κ(0)a(0)n v n and has degree −n, with the factor-of-automorphy convention of Istrati et al.
  (2022, Proposition 5.6, pp.1369–1370).

8. Each blow-up of a point on the strict elliptic curve subtracts that point from its normal line.
   Following all n stages gives

                                     Ns = Lκ(s)sn ⊗ OEs (−n[−s]).

   The multiplicity n records total exceptional transforms. The reduced final exceptional locus
   meets the strict axis only once. One may check the formula directly: the standard theta factor
   θa (av) = −v −1 θa (v) shows that O([p]) has factor −p/v. At p = −s the tensor product above
   has factor
                                       κ(s)sn (v/s)n = κ(s)v n ,
