   degrees independently of the successive-blow-up formula.

9. The divisor n[−s] cannot extend. For constant a, choose two distinct classes [v1 ], [v2 ] ∈ C∗ /aZ .
   The sequences sj = −aj vi tend to zero, whereas the corresponding divisors are constantly n[vi ]
   and have different limits in Symn (Ea ). For varying a(s), choose the holomorphic logarithm
   τa (s) = log a(s)/(2πi) on the disc. The Abel–Jacobi coordinate of n[−s] is n log(−s)/(2πi)
   modulo Z + τa (s)Z. On a positive parameter loop it winds n times around a primitive cycle

                                                 207
    in the smooth elliptic family. An extending section over the disc would have zero winding.
    A finite base change of order N multiplies this nonzero integer by N . After removing a
    vertical Cartier elliptic component, an extending divisor would still have a proper horizontal
    part of degree n, finite over the disc, defining a continuous section of the relative symmetric
    power, which has just been ruled out. Nonproper exceptional divisors in deformations of Kato
    surfaces are a classical phenomenon, studied by Dloussky and Teleman (2012, arXiv version 2,
    Section 1.2, PDF pp. 3–5); the calculation here identifies the precise weighted divisor in this
    marked family.
10. This also explains the scope of ordinary elementary modifications. If a degree-zero line Lm
    from 22.24 is changed by point blow-ups, then its new normal is Lm ⊗ O(−Dexc ). If both
    that normal and the weighted Cartier correction extended on a semistable good-reduction
    interface, their tensor product would extend Lm , contradicting 22.24. In this Kato family the
    correction is exactly Dexc = n[−s], whose nonextension was proved above.
11. Finally let E = (2, 2) ⊂ P3 be smooth and set L = OE (2), of degree eight. Its normal in P3 is
    L ⊕ L. For A = BlE P3 , the exceptional divisor is D = E × P1 and, in the lines convention,
                                          ND/A = L ⊠ OP1 (−1).
    A bare Hopf-product cap has normal M ⊠ O with deg M = 0. The required triple-divisor line
    would then be (L ⊗ M )−1 ⊠ O(1), which has no nonzero section because its elliptic degree is
    −8. Thus the required triple-divisor line has no effective section on this interface.
12. For the parabolic surface with n = 8, changing κ varies the flat factor through all of Pic0 (E):
    constant factors are parametrized by C∗ /aZ . Choose its axis normal to equal L−1 . In
    B = S8 × P1 the divisor D = E × P1 then has normal L−1 ⊠ O. With triple section
    T = E × {p},
              ND/A ⊗ ND/B ⊗ OD (T ) = (L ⊠ O(−1)) ⊗ (L−1 ⊠ O) ⊗ (O ⊠ O(1)) ≃ OD .
    This proves precisely the first-order matching claimed.


 Proposition 22.28 (Globalization at the contracted parabolic elliptic axis). [tag 030F]
     Let S = S8 (a, κ) be the central parabolic surface in 22.27, let E ⊂ S be its elliptic axis, and
 put N = NE/S , so deg N = −8. The contraction π : S → Y of E is a compact normal surface
 with a single isolated singular point p. Its germ at p is the vertex of the affine cone over (E, N −1 ).
 In particular,
                                             H 2 (Y, ΘY ) = 0.
The restriction morphism from a semiuniversal deformation of Y to a semiuniversal deformation
of (Y, p) is regular. Consequently every prescribed analytic one-parameter deformation of this
isolated singularity is induced, after shrinking its parameter disc, by a proper deformation of
the compact surface Y . If the prescribed local deformation smooths the singularity, the global
deformation has smooth fibres away from the central value.

 Proof. 1. We first identify the analytic neighbourhood. At the central parameter the Kato gluing
   of 22.27 is
                                        (x, v) 7−→ (κa8 xv 8 , av).
    It is exactly linear in x. Thus a neighbourhood of E is a neighbourhood of the zero section in
    the negative line bundle N , with the indicated factor of automorphy. Its contraction is the
    cone associated with the section ring
                                     R(E, N −1 ) =         H 0 (E, N −m ).
                                                     M

                                                     m≥0


                                                   208
  A line bundle of degree eight on an elliptic curve is very ample and normally generated. The
  cone is normal, its only singularity is its vertex, and the blow-up of the vertex maximal ideal
  is Tot(N ) near its zero section. One can see the last assertion directly: the degree-one sections
  generate the section ring and have no common zero on E; their ratios on the blow-up recover
  the projective embedding of E, and their common radial coordinate is the coordinate in N .
  In particular, with I = OS (−E) and mp the vertex maximal ideal,

                                               mp OS = I.

  The local contraction glues to the identity on S \ E, giving the stated proper contraction of
  the compact surface.

2. Write C for the disjoint rational cycle of the parabolic surface. The meromorphic two-form
   d log x ∧ d log v is invariant under the displayed monomial gluing. In the toric blow-up charts
   it has simple poles along precisely the axis and the rational cycle, and no zeros. Consequently

                                        KS = OS (−E − C).

  Also b1 (S) = 1, by 22.27. Put F = ΘS (− log E), the locally free sheaf of vector fields tangent
  to E. Serre duality and the displayed canonical divisor give

                             H 2 (S, F)∗ = H 0 S, Ω1S (log E) ⊗ KS = 0.
                                                                  


   Indeed there are sheaf injections

                            Ω1S (log E)(−E − C) ,−→ Ω1S (−C) ,−→ Ω1S .

   Locally the first sends the logarithmic generators dx/x, dy, multiplied by x, to the ordinary
   forms dx, xdy. Finally H 0 (S, Ω1S ) = 0 follows already from b1 (S) = 1. For completeness, a
   holomorphic one-form α on a compact complex surface is closed: Stokes’ theorem applied
   to α ∧ dα makes the integral of the positive volume form associated with dα ∧ dα vanish. If
   α ̸= 0, its real and imaginary parts give independent real de Rham classes. An exact real
   linear combination would be the differential of a global real pluriharmonic function, which is
   constant on the compact surface. This would give b1 (S) ≥ 2, a contradiction.

3. We compute the one possible local higher direct image explicitly. The restriction of F to E is
   the Atiyah extension of N :

                             0 −→ OE −→ AN := F|E −→ ΘE −→ 0.

   In normal coordinates related by xj = gij (v)xi , the vertical Euler field is xi ∂xi , and the
   changes of horizontal lifts have cocycle d log gij . Thus this extension has class c1 (N ) in
   H 1 (E, Ω1E ), which is nonzero because deg N = −8. Since ΘE ≃ OE , the connecting map
   H 0 (E, ΘE ) → H 1 (E, OE ) is an isomorphism. The same cohomology sequence therefore gives
   the natural isomorphism
                                                 ∼
                                   H 1 (E, AN ) −−→ H 1 (E, ΘE ) ≃ C.

4. The successive quotients for the formal neighbourhood of E are

                             I m F/I m+1 F = AN ⊗ N −m         (m ≥ 0).

   For m ≥ 1 both line bundles in the induced extension have degree 8m > 0 on the elliptic
   curve, so their first cohomology vanishes. It follows that all restriction maps

                         H 1 E, F/I m+1 F −→ H 1 (E, F/I m F)         (m ≥ 1)
                                           



                                                 209
   are isomorphisms. Their common value is H 1 (E, AN ) ≃ C. The analytic theorem on formal
   functions (Grauert, 1960, Section 6, Hauptsatz IIa, p. 59) identifies this inverse limit with the
   completed stalk of R1 π∗ F at p. This coherent sheaf is supported at the single point p, so its
   stalk is a finite-length module and equals its completion. We have proved
                                                             ∼
                         R 1 π ∗ F ≃ Cp ,   H 0 (Y, R1 π∗ F) −−→ H 1 (E, ΘE ).

  The second map is the natural restriction followed by the Atiyah-extension map just computed.

5. There is also an equality of sheaves
                                             π∗ F = ΘY .
  To check it at p, a holomorphic derivation of the cone integrates locally to a holomorphic flow:
  embed the cone in a polydisc, lift its coefficient functions, and use the ordinary holomorphic
  vector-field flow, which preserves the defining ideal. The flow preserves the unique singular
  point, hence its maximal ideal. Functoriality of the blow-up of that ideal lifts the flow to
  the resolution, preserving the exceptional curve. Its derivative is therefore a section of F.
  Conversely a section of F differentiates pullbacks of holomorphic functions on Y and descends
  to a derivation, because π∗ OS = OY . Both operations agree off E and are inverse there;
  uniqueness extends the equality over E.

6. The global-to-local cohomology map is surjective for a concrete reason. Write a = e2πiτ
   with Im τ > 0, and vary τ to τ + u in the explicit Kato construction, keeping its translation
   parameter zero. The same uniform collar argument as in 22.27 gives a proper holomorphic
   deformation of the pair (S, E). Its Kodaira–Spencer class belongs to H 1 (S, F). Under the
   natural composite
                                                          ∼
                          H 1 (S, F) −→ H 0 (Y, R1 π∗ F) −−→ H 1 (E, ΘE )
  it is the Kodaira–Spencer class of C/(Z + (τ + u)Z), which is nonzero. For example, differenti-
  ating its second deck transformation z 7→ z + τ + u gives the usual nonzero period cocycle.
  This argument works also at the elliptic curves with extra automorphisms. The target is one
  dimensional, so the first arrow is onto.

7. The degree-two part of the Leray sequence is

                    H 1 (S, F) −→ H 0 (Y, R1 π∗ F) −→ H 2 (Y, π∗ F) −→ H 2 (S, F).

  The first map is surjective and the last group is zero. Using π∗ F = ΘY proves H 2 (Y, ΘY ) = 0.

8. For a compact complex space with isolated singularities, H 2 (Θ) = 0 makes the restriction
   from global to local deformations formally smooth. Take a finite Stein cover with one small
   neighbourhood of p and all other members smooth. For a small extension of Artinian bases,
   prescribe the lifted deformation on the singular member and take smooth local lifts on the
   other members. Their pairwise identifications lift on the smooth Stein intersections. The
   failure of the cocycle identity on triple intersections is a Čech two-cocycle in ΘY tensored
   with the square-zero kernel. Its class vanishes by the proved H 2 -vanishing; correcting the
   identifications by a one-cochain glues the desired lift. This proves the relative infinitesimal
   lifting property.

9. The analytic semiuniversal deformation theory turns this property into regularity of the
   induced morphism of analytic base germs. The general criterion is Manetti (1991, Lemma 1,
   p. 93), stated for reduced compact complex spaces with isolated singularities and proved by
   the local-to-global spectral sequence of the cotangent complex. It is also used in Dloussky
   and Teleman (2020, arXiv version 2, Section 3.2, Proposition 3.3 and the following discussion,
   p. 11). A regular morphism of analytic germs is locally a projection from a product with a


                                                210
   smooth germ. Consequently a specified analytic disc in the local deformation base lifts to
   the global base. The global family is proper by the compact deformation construction. Away
   from p its central fibre is smooth, and smoothness is open; compactness permits one common
   shrinking of the disc. A local smoothing at p therefore gives smooth global noncentral fibres,
   as asserted.



Proposition 22.29 (A proper quadric–parabolic surface smoothing). [tag 030G]
    Let S = S8 (a, κ) be as in 22.28, with elliptic axis E and normal line N of degree −8. There
is an embedding E ,→ Q = P1 × P1 as a smooth divisor of bidegree (2, 2) with NE/Q ≃ N −1 .
There is a proper flat map from a smooth complex threefold

                                             ϖ : V −→ ∆

with smooth noncentral fibres and reduced simple normal-crossings central fibre exactly S ∪E Q.
Its two normal lines are

                        NS/V = OS (−E),          NQ/V = KQ = OQ (−2, −2).

The family is obtained by globalizing a specified cone smoothing and blowing up its vertex over
the original parameter disc.
    For the elliptic-quartic configuration of 22.27, the three pairwise normal-line products, includ-
ing the triple-curve factors, can consequently all be made trivial using

                            A = BlE P3 ,        B = S × P1 ,    C = V.

Here C is the constructed proper surface family over an open disc. Its continuous surjection onto
that disc proves that C is noncompact.

Proof. 1. Put L = N −1 , of degree eight. Multiplication by two on the elliptic Picard variety
  is surjective, so choose a degree-four line bundle M with M ⊗2 = L. Choose degree-two
  line bundles M1 , M2 with M1 ⊗ M2 = M and M1 ̸≃ M2 . Each complete linear system is a
  basepoint-free double cover of P1 . The product of the two maps is an embedding in Q. Indeed
  two distinct points identified by both maps would give M1 ≃ OE (p + q) ≃ M2 . A common
  ramification point would similarly give M1 ≃ OE (2p) ≃ M2 . Thus the product is injective
  and immersive; properness makes it a closed embedding. Its image has bidegree (2, 2), and

                                   OQ (E)|E = (M1 ⊗ M2 )⊗2 = L.

   This also allows us to start with the fixed quadric and elliptic quartic in 22.27: the normal
   line there was chosen to be the inverse of this same L.
2. Use the anticanonical embedding of Q in P8 and write

                          RQ =         H 0 (Q, OQ (2d, 2d)),   Z = Spec RQ .
                                 M

                                 d≥0

   The ring is generated in degree one and is normal. One direct verification uses the bihomoge-
   neous monomials: every monomial of bidegree (2d, 2d) is a product of d monomials of bidegree
   (2, 2), and the associated monoid is the intersection of a rational polyhedral cone with its
   full lattice. The punctured cone is the complement of the zero section in OQ (−2, −2), hence
   is smooth. Choose the section e ∈ H 0 (Q, OQ (2, 2)) cutting out E. The degree-one function
   t = e on Z defines a flat map Z → A1 : its coordinate ring is torsion-free over C[t], a principal
   ideal domain. For every d ≥ 0, the sequence
                                                     e
                      0 −→ OQ (2d − 2, 2d − 2) −−→ OQ (2d, 2d) −→ L⊗d −→ 0

                                                  211
  has vanishing first cohomology in its left term. For d = 0 this follows from the Künneth
  formula for OQ (−2, −2); for d ≥ 1 it follows from the same formula and nonnegative degrees.
  Taking sections identifies
                                   RQ /(e) =       H 0 (E, L⊗d ).
                                               M

                                               d≥0

  The central surface is therefore exactly the affine cone over (E, L), including its scheme
  structure. For t ̸= 0, projection from the cone vertex identifies the fibre with Q \ E: over
  each point where e is nonzero there is exactly one radial coordinate on which e has value t.
  In particular this is an explicit smoothing of the isolated singularity of 22.28. It is the affine
  version of Pinkham’s cone construction (Pinkham, 1974, Remark 7.6(iii), p. 46; Section 9,
  pp. 63–65).

3. Blowing up the vertex of Z gives Tot(OQ (−2, −2)) = Tot(KQ ). This can be checked on the
   blow-up charts given by ratios of the degree-one homogeneous coordinates; these recover a
   point of Q, with the remaining common factor the tautological fibre coordinate ξ. The map
   to the parameter line is precisely
                                             t = ξe.
  Its central divisor is the union of the zero section Q and the restriction Tot(KQ |E ), each with
  multiplicity one. Near E the equation is t = ξz, where z is a local defining function of E in Q.
  Thus the total space is smooth and the central divisor has simple normal crossings.

4. Now contract E in the compact surface S as in 22.28. The regular global-to-local deformation
   map in that proposition lifts the specified analytic germ Z → A1 to a proper deformation
   Y → ∆ of Y = S/E. The lifted deformation agrees analytically with this cone smoothing in a
   neighbourhood of its singular point. Away from that neighbourhood the central surface is
   smooth; openness of smoothness and properness allow a common shrinking of ∆ for which
   the family there is a submersion. Blow up the single cone vertex in Y. The resulting map
   V → ∆ remains proper. Near the exceptional divisor its local model is the smooth space just
   computed; elsewhere it is unchanged and smooth. Its central strict transform is exactly S,
   because the maximal-ideal blow-up of the degree-eight elliptic cone is its given resolution
   Tot(N ) near E. The other component is Q, and their intersection is the original marked
   elliptic curve. The local equation t = ξz proves flatness and reducedness near the intersection;
   at a smooth point of either component t is a local coordinate. The noncentral fibres are the
   smooth compact fibres of Y. This proves every asserted properness and smoothness property
   for the surface family.

5. The exceptional zero section has normal KQ in its local total-space model. Since S + Q is the
   principal divisor of t, restriction to S gives

                                 OV (S)|S = OV (−Q)|S = OS (−E).

  These are the two asserted normal lines. They also show directly that the two branch normals
  along E multiply to the trivial line.

6. Realize Q as a smooth quadric in P3 and E as its intersection with a second quadric. Put
   L = OE (2). Then NE/P3 = L ⊕ L, so the exceptional divisor of A = BlE P3 is DAB = E × P1 ,
   with normal L ⊠ OP1 (−1). The strict transform of Q is still Q, because the centre is Cartier
   on it, and its normal in A is

                                 NQ/A = OQ (2) ⊗ OQ (−E) = OQ .

   It meets DAB in the constant section E × {p} corresponding to that member of the pencil of
   quadrics. In B = S × P1 , use the divisors DBA = E × P1 and DBC = S × {p}. Their normals


                                               212
   are L−1 ⊠ O and OS . In C = V, use its central divisors Q and S. The three normal products
   with the triple contribution are then

                double surface ND/first branch ⊗ ND/second branch ⊗ OD (triple curve)
                   E × P1       (L ⊠ O(−1)) ⊗ (L−1 ⊠ O) ⊗ (OE ⊠ O(1)) = O
                      Q                      OQ ⊗ KQ ⊗ OQ (E) = OQ
                      S                    OS ⊗ OS (−E) ⊗ OS (E) = OS .

   The three displayed evaluation maps are the required pairwise normal-line trivializations. The
   third space maps surjectively and properly to an open disc, which proves its noncompactness.

7. The affine smooth fibre Q \ E has

                           H1 (Q \ E; Z) = Z/2,        H2 (Q \ E; Z) = Z3 .

   Indeed the Thom sequence of the pair (Q, Q \ E) has intersection map H2 (Q; Z) → H0 (E; Z)
   given by (a, b) 7→ 2a + 2b. Its cokernel is Z/2 and its kernel is Z; the preceding term
   H1 (E; Z) = Z2 injects into H2 (Q \ E; Z). This exact extension of free groups splits abstractly.
   The map H4 (Q; Z) → H2 (E; Z) is an isomorphism, so H3 (Q \ E; Z) = 0, and its Euler number
   is four. The Euler number is also obtained independently by projection to either ruling of Q:
   away from the four branch values of E → P1 , the fibre is C∗ and has Euler number zero; at
   each branch value it is C and has Euler number one. The compact noncentral surface has
   Euler number χ(S) + χ(Q) − 2χ(E) = 8 + 4 = 12 by the local ξz = t retraction.



Remark 22.30 (Euler characteristics of the quadric–parabolic smoothing). [tag PT14] For the
compact noncentral surface Vt of Proposition 22.29,

                χ(Vt ) = χ(S8 ) + χ(Q) − 2χ(E) = 8 + 4 = 12,        χ(Vt , OVt ) = 1.

The first formula is the local ξz = t smoothing formula proved there. Mayer–Vietoris for the two
spherical boundaries in the Kato construction identifies the middle homology and its intersection
form with the eight negative exceptional classes. Thus χ(S8 ) = 8 and the signature is −8,
so c1 (S8 )2 = 2χ(S8 ) + 3σ(S8 ) = −8 and analytic Riemann–Roch gives χ(S8 , OS8 ) = 0. Since
χ(Q, OQ ) = 1 and χ(E, OE ) = 0, the normalization sequence for S8 ∪E Q and flatness give
the second formula. The three pairwise normal-line products are the explicit identities in the
proof of Proposition 22.29. Its third space V maps surjectively to an open disc and is therefore
noncompact.

Proposition 22.31 (The obstruction to a marked period lift). [tag 030H]
   Fix 0 < |α|, |a| < 1, and put

                H = (C2 \ {0})/⟨(x, v) 7→ (αx, av)⟩,       E = {x = 0} ≃ C∗ /aZ .

Let h be the automorphism induced by (x, v) 7→ (cx, bv), where b, c ∈ C∗ . Suppose p : Y → H is
a finite composition of point blow-ups, allowing infinitely near centres, and at least one point of
E is an image of its exceptional locus. If [b] ∈ C∗ /aZ has infinite order, there is no holomorphic
automorphism of Y which agrees, on the dense unmodified core, with the marked automorphism
h.
    The same obstruction holds for a finite collection of such marked modifications if the period
permutes the collection and acts as h on each marked core. More generally, if a compact
smooth surface contains a preserved marked elliptic curve E of nonzero normal degree d, every
holomorphic automorphism restricting to translation by b on E must satisfy d b = 0 in E. The

                                               213
latter assertion also excludes a finite cycle of such preserved marked cap axes when the cycle
composite is an infinite-order translation. These assertions apply to the extension of the second
cusp period to the finite Hopf modifications in 22.27, for generic nonzero parameters, after every
finite base change. The period action in these assertions is a holomorphic action on the full finite
modifications with the specified marked core.

Proof. 1. Let S ⊂ H be the image of the exceptional curves of p. It is finite. Repeated infinitely
  near blow-ups change the curves over a point but do not make S infinite. If h e were a lift, the
  maps
                                        e hp : Y −→ H
                                       ph,
   would agree on the dense core and hence everywhere, by the identity principle for holomorphic
   maps to the separated complex surface H. The image under h   e of a curve contracted by p is
   therefore again contracted by p. Applying the same argument to h   e −1 proves that the total
   exceptional locus is preserved. Thus h(S) = S.
2. The automorphism h preserves E, where it is translation by [b]. Consequently the nonempty
   finite set S ∩ E would be invariant under that translation. The orbit of any one of its points
   is finite, so for some k > 0,
                                [bk v] = [v],     equivalently bk ∈ aZ .
   This says exactly that [b] is torsion, a contradiction. In particular, no choice of multiplicities
   or infinitely near centres changes the obstruction: only their nonempty finite support on E is
   needed.
3. For finitely many modifications pi : Yi → H, a deck map has biholomorphisms Yi → Yσ(i)
   satisfying the same core comparison. The identity principle again gives equivariance everywhere.
   The union of the finitely many exceptional image sets is h-invariant; its intersection with E
   gives the same contradiction. Equivalently, around a cycle of length ℓ the map hℓ would lift
   to a single modification, while [bℓ ] still has infinite order.
4. For the more general assertion, an automorphism preserving E induces through its derivative
   in the normal direction an isomorphism
                                            t∗b NE/S ≃ NE/S .
   For a line bundle N of degree d on an elliptic curve, the homomorphism b 7→ t∗b N ⊗ N −1
   is multiplication by −d under the usual identification Pic0 (E) = E. Indeed write N =
   OE ( j nj [pj ]) with j nj = d; the Abel–Jacobi class of its translated divisor minus the
        P                P

   original one is −db. Thus preservation of N forces db = 0. Taking a power proves the finite-
   cycle version, since its composite preserves one axis and its nonzero-degree normal line. In
   particular a nonzero-degree parabolic axis cannot carry the marked generic period translation
   even if no finite Hopf modification is specified. The original finite-support argument also
   covers modifications where that normal-degree test alone would give no information.
5. The infinite-order translation at the cusp is computed as follows. The periods of 20.6 have
   the form
                 g1 : (Z, W ) 7−→ (qc1 Z, c2 W ),  g2 : (Z, W ) 7−→ (c3 Z, r12 qc4 W ),
  where the ci are nonvanishing holomorphic units near the cusp. Choose W or W −1 so that
  a = cε2 has modulus less than one, ε ∈ {1, −1}. This is possible at the marked cusp because
  its limiting unit has modulus different from one, as computed in 22.24. For q ≠ 0 small, the
  partial g1 quotient of (C∗ )2 is the dense core of the diagonal Hopf surface with multipliers
  (qc1 , a). The second period induces the above h, with
                                       b(q, r) = (r12 qc4 (q, r))ε .

                                                 214
   Fix a sufficiently small nonzero q. For each k > 0 and j ∈ Z, the equation b(q, r)k = a(q)j
   has a discrete solution set in the punctured r-disc: its left-hand side has a zero or pole of
   nonzero order at r = 0, while the right-hand side is a nonzero constant in r. Hence outside a
   countable union of discrete sets, [b(q, r)] has infinite order. Under a finite base change in r
   the nonzero order is multiplied by its ramification index and the same conclusion holds. A
   finite base change in q does not affect this fixed-nonzero-q argument.

6. To compare with 22.27, write qc1 = κ(s)sn after the chosen finite cover in the cusp variable.
   Its generic Kato fibre is precisely a finite Hopf modification with nonempty axis centre [−s]. A
   holomorphic extension of the second period to that whole fibre would therefore contradict the
   result just proved. Allowing finitely many translated copies does not remove the contradiction,
   by the finite-collection assertion.



Lemma 22.32 (The quotient of indexed cores). [tag PT15] Let h be an automorphism of H, and
let modifications pj : Yj → H, indexed by j ∈ Z, have isomorphisms h     e j : Yj → Yj+1 satisfying
     e j = hpj . On an h-invariant open set H ◦ over which every pj is an isomorphism, the shift
pj+1 h

                                             [(j, y)] 7−→ h−j pj (y).

Under this isomorphism, its natural map to the orbit space H ◦ /⟨h⟩ is the ordinary quotient map.
Moreover, two embedded compact subspaces of a Hausdorff space that share a subset open and
dense in both have the same image.

Proof. The displayed map is invariant under (j, y) 7→ (j + 1, h e j y) because h−j−1 pj+1 h
                                                                                          e j = h−j pj .
Every shift orbit meets the zeroth core exactly once, so the inverse is x 7→ [(0, p−1
                                                                                   0 x)]. These maps
are holomorphic on the component charts. Composing with H ◦ → H ◦ /⟨h⟩ gives the asserted

the two images is consequently the closure of their shared dense subset.

22.6    A local insertion into the prescribed simple-torus family
Proposition 22.34 (Local insertion of vertical Hopf bundles). [tag 030J]
    Let q0 be a regular point of the elliptic base, and let ∆z , z = q − q0 , be a simply connected
disc avoiding 0, 1, ∞. After w = r6 , take the standard twelve-cycle model
                                          X −→ ∆z × ∆r
of the prescribed local two-torus family. There is a proper replacement X ′ → ∆z × ∆r , with a
specified isomorphism to X off (z, r) = (0, 0), whose total fourfold is smooth and whose divisor
r = 0 is reduced normal crossings. The composite map to ∆r is flat.
     The replacement has twelve new compact vertical normalization components. Six are P1 -
bundles over a scalar Hopf surface; the other six are the blow-ups of those bundles along two
disjoint elliptic curves. Every new component has fundamental group Z, and therefore fails the
∂ ∂¯ lemma. The punctured family is the prescribed family, so its generic simplicity is preserved.
     The map is proper over the bidisc and flat over the degeneration parameter. Its vertical
threefolds have the dimensions stated above. All twelve component labels, and hence the obstruction
of 22.5, are unchanged.

Proof. 1. The action. Use the rank-three period subsystem
                         u(z) = (τ (z), µ(z)),         w = (1, 0),      δ = (0, 1).
   It defines the analytic semiabelian group
    Gz = C2 /(Zu(z) + Zw + Zδ),          1 −→ C∗δ −→ Gz −→ Ez −→ 0,              Ez = C/(Z + τ (z)Z).
   This is the punctured degree-zero line bundle determined by µ(z). The formula
                                                  log t
                                                           
                                   χz (t) =             u(z)    (t ∈ C∗ )                        (22.3)
                                                   2πi
   is a single-valued holomorphic homomorphism: a logarithm change adds a lattice period.
   It varies holomorphically with z. The r-monodromy fixes u, and the z-disc has no period
   monodromy.

2. The action extends to the entire twelve-cycle model. Each unfolded normalization is
                                              ∗
                                 Rz = Gz ×Cδ P1 = PEz (O ⊕ Lz ).

  Translation in Gz preserves both conductor sections. More explicitly, a class represented by
  (a, b) acts before the closing quotient by

                                   (ξ, W ) 7−→ (ξ + a, e−2πib W ).                          (22.4)

  It commutes exactly with the closing period, which is another translation of the same
  commutative group and whose scalar factor contains r12 . The adjacent line directions are
  paired dually in the local equation xy = r; the two scalar factors cancel. Scalar multiplication
  also preserves the one-dimensional toric subdivision producing the twelve components. Thus
  (22.4) extends over every node, preserves each branch, and changes a branch equation x by a
  unit times x. This checks the required action using the semiabelian marking of Proposition 22.1.

3. The affine family itself admits the necessary local punctured comparison. On U = ∆z × ∆∗r
   its lattice local system Λ has H 2 (U, Λ) = 0, since U retracts onto a circle, also for local
   coefficients. Its relative Lie algebra V is a coherent vector bundle. The exponential sequence

                                    0 −→ Λ −→ V −→ T −→ 0

  and Cartan’s theorem B on the Stein base give H 1 (U, T ) = 0 (Cartan, 1952, exposé 19, §5,
  pp. 14–15). Consequently the affine torsor has a holomorphic section on U , which supplies

    These are exactly the blow-up charts of (y, s). Thus Vx is blown up along its elliptic curve
    over y = s = 0; Vy is unchanged. Similarly Hy is blown up along the corresponding elliptic
    curve and Hx is unchanged. Each even vertical component is therefore blown up at its two
    disjoint conductor curves, whereas each odd vertical component is unchanged. The horizontal
    parities are reversed.
 7. The Cartier logarithm and properness. Set M = OBe (F ). On a trivializing cover write
    its transition units as gij . Glue the resolved pullbacks by χz (gij ). These are genuine
    automorphisms satisfying the cocycle identity. This is the Cartier-logarithm construction of
    Fujimoto (1990, construction, p. 85; Definition 1.1, p. 86); the explicit semiabelian action

    resolutions; equivalently one may twist first and then resolve the descended ideals.
 8. Over every base chart the glued space is a copy of the proper resolved pullback. It is Hausdorff:
    two points over the same base point are separated in such a chart, and points over distinct
    base points are separated in the base. Properness is local on the target, and composition with
    the proper β proves properness over the original bidisc. The canonical divisor section of M is
    nonzero off F and trivializes the twist there. The base blow-up and the resolutions are also
    isomorphisms off the origin. This gives the specified isomorphism with the original family
    there, in particular over every r ̸= 0.
 9. The construction can be inserted into any larger model which is standard near q0 : the preceding
    trivialization supplies the overlap map outside the origin. The cocharacter u is defined on this
    disc. Since the local rings of the total space are regular and r is a nonzero divisor, they are
    torsion-free, hence flat, over the one-dimensional regular parameter ring. This proves flatness
    over r. The new vertical threefolds rule out joint flatness over the bidisc. Properness over the
    r-disc alone follows only when this local replacement is inserted into a model with compact
    elliptic base.

    with its two global conductor sections. On each elliptic fibre of H → P1 , the line MH retains

 Remark 22.35 (Pullback along a lifted ordinary arc). [tag PT16] Let β : B      e → ∆z × ∆r be the
 blow-up used in Proposition 22.34, with exceptional curve F . An arc ιk (r) = (kr, r) has strict
 lift eιk meeting F at [k : 1]. Choose this point away from the distinguished resolution centres.
 Pulling the constructed model over B  e back along e
                                                    ιk gives a central cycle of twelve ruled surfaces
 over Eq0 . Indeed the pullback of OBe (F ) is a line bundle on a disc and is trivial, and the arc
 misses the additional resolution centres. The new vertical threefolds of (22.6) instead lie over
 the whole exceptional curve F under the map to the original bidisc. The maps being compared
 are the strict-lift pullback and the composite with β, respectively.

Proposition 22.36 (The dual complex under local insertions). [tag 030K]
     The local operation 22.34 attaches a triangulated cylinder to the original twelve-cycle in the
dual complex and admits an elementary collapse back to that cycle. In a compact normal-crossings
model, performing it at a regular place consequently preserves the homotopy type of the global
dual complex.
     The same conclusion holds for finite sequences of these insertions, twists by a connected holo-
morphic group action preserving the prescribed normal-crossings model, and toroidal subdivisions
of its central cone complex. In particular, starting with a model whose dual complex has a nonzero
first integral cohomology class, these operations cannot produce a semistable S 6 centre. They also
cannot change the component rotations in 22.5.

 Proof. 1. Write Hi , i ∈ Z/12, for the original component vertices and Vi for the new vertical
   ones. At a node between an even component i and its odd neighbour j, the two charts (22.5)
   have triple strata
                                    {Vi , Vj , Hj }, {Vi , Hi , Hj }.                    (22.7)
    The square with horizontal edges Hi Hj and Vi Vj is thus divided by the diagonal Vi Hj . Over all
    twelve nodes, (22.7) is exactly a triangulation of C12 × [0, 1], attached along the old horizontal
    cycle C12 × {0}.

 2. There is a literal elementary collapse relative to the old cycle. First remove each triangle
    containing a top edge Vi Vj , paired with that free edge. Next remove each remaining triangle,
    paired with its now free diagonal Vi Hj . Finally remove each vertical edge Hi Vi , paired with
    its free vertex Vi . What remains is precisely the original twelve-cycle. These are 36 elementary
    collapses. Equivalently, the retraction sends Vi to Hi and is the identity on all old vertices
    and edges.

 3. This description is valid inside a larger dual complex K. The only new strata lie over the
    base origin, so the new complex is the mapping-cylinder attachment

                                      K ∪ f :C12 →K (C12 × [0, 1]).

    It retracts onto K, regardless of possible global identifications among the local horizontal
    branches. For self-crossings the ordered local-branch dual complex records every local branch
    and its global identifications.

 4. A connected group acts trivially on the finite sets of component labels and connected compo-
    nents of every stratum: its permutation is locally constant and is the identity at the identity
    element. Cartier twists by such an action therefore keep this same incidence complex. Toroidal
    subdivisions subdivide the corresponding central polyhedral complex and hence preserve its

                                                 220
   underlying homotopy type. These arguments apply successively, proving the assertion for
   finite compositions. Around each regular insertion point the relative component monodromy
   is still the identity; no peripheral rotation is added to 22.5.

5. For completeness, a compact normal-crossings space D has a natural injection

                                     H 1 (∆(D), C) ,−→ H 1 (D, C),                                (22.8)

   where ∆(D) denotes its local-branch dual complex with connected strata. Use the ordered
   finite branch spaces D[p] and take the alternating summand for the branch-permutation
   action. Over C this is an exact direct-summand operation. Resolve the constant sheaf by this
   augmented alternating branch complex. At a point its row is the augmented simplex complex,
   so it is exact, including for self-crossings. The associated first-quadrant spectral sequence has

                           E1p,q = H q (D[p] , C)alt ,      E21,0 = H 1 (∆(D), C).

   No higher differential enters or leaves (1, 0). Its filtration piece in total degree one gives (22.8).
   Equivalently one can use the orientation local system on each unordered branch stratum; an
   ordinary constant sheaf there would be incorrect if branches permute. A nonzero integral first
   cohomology class of the finite dual complex remains nonzero over C, because first integral
   cohomology is torsion-free. Thus a surviving circle class forces H 1 (D, C) ̸= 0. By 22.14 every
   semistable centre of a simply connected nearby S 6 is simply connected, which is incompatible
   with this conclusion.

6. For the twelve-cycle, use the oriented edge-to-vertex and triangle-to-edge incidence maps of
   the triangulated cylinder in Step 1. Their chain ranks are 24, 48, 24, and their nonzero Smith
   entries are 123 and 124 , respectively. Hence its integral homology is (Z, Z, 0). The explicit
   retraction pulls the integral angular cocycle back with winding one.



Proposition 22.37 (Trivial monodromy does not force equality of first Betti numbers). [tag 030L]
    There is a compact connected complex threefold Z and a proper holomorphic map f : Z → P1
with connected fibres, with precisely one singular fibre Y , such that

                 f −1 (P1 \ {0}) ≃ H− × (P1 \ {0}),           b1 (Y ) = 0 < 1 = b1 (H− ).

Here H− is the scalar Hopf surface with multiplier −e−π , and Y = H+ ∪E H+ is a reduced
simple-normal-crossings union with E = C/(Z + iZ) and H+ of multiplier e−2π . In particular,
trivial local monodromy on H 1 does not imply b1 (Y ) = b1 (H− ), even with compact smooth total
space.

Proof. 1. This is the compact-base version of the explicit Cartier cocycle of 22.19. Put

               b : B = Bl(p,0) (P1 × P1 ) −→ P1 × P1 ,        L = b∗ pr∗1 O(1),   A = O(F2 ),

   where F2 is the exceptional curve and F1 the strict transform of P1 × {0}. Given transition
   units lab , aab , the formula

   is independent of logarithm choices and satisfies the cocycle identity. Glue the products
   Ua × E by these translations. This gives a holomorphic principal elliptic bundle π : Z → B.
   Its total space is smooth and Hausdorff; it is compact because B and the fibre are compact
   and π is locally a proper product. Let f = pr2 ◦b ◦ π.

                                                      221
2. The restrictions of the Chern vector (1 + i)c1 (L) − ic1 (A) to F1 , F2 and a smooth ruling fibre
   are 1, i, 1 + i, respectively. As checked directly in 22.19, the corresponding principal elliptic

                               Λ = Z + iZ −→ Λ/Z,               Λ −→ Λ/Zi.

Remark 22.38 (The invariant-cycle equality in the Hopf degeneration). [tag PT17] The compact
fibration of Proposition 22.37 has identity local monodromy T on H 1 (F ; R), but b1 (Y ) = 0 and
b1 (F ) = 1. It therefore refutes the converse equality clause in Honda and Viaclovsky (2025,
Theorem 1.1, p. 553), also stated as Theorems 1.2 and 3.2 in arXiv version 1, pp. 1 and 8. The
relative-homology and circle-bundle sequences in that proof give

                                 b1 (Y ) ≤ dim H 1 (F ; R)T ≤ b1 (F )

(Honda and Viaclovsky, 2025, arXiv version 1, equation (3.9), p. 9). Identity of T is equivalent
to equality in the second inequality. In the present example the first inequality is 0 < 1. Equality
of the endpoint Betti numbers still forces T to be the identity by this same chain of inequalities.
For an irreducible central fibre, the top-dimensional homology in the displayed relative sequence
has rank one, giving b1 (Y ) = dim H 1 (F ; R)T , as proved in Honda and Viaclovsky (2025, arXiv
version 1, Corollary 3.7, p. 11). The example here has two central components, with the inclusion
maps on H1 (E) computed in Proposition 22.37.

5. Use the unit-square cusp triangulation, with twelve consecutive bottom cells in the y1 direction
   and the same bridge choice in every unit prism. Its translates have bottom cell indices (i, j)
   and top interval [j, j + 1]. Thus H increases the bottom second index and the top index by
   one, while G1 shifts the first index by twelve. The fan is invariant under both, and therefore
   under G2 . For each bottom cell its three maximal cones are the determinant-one cones of
   21.1. The usual compact-core construction of 20.6, now on the I12 elliptic root model and
   with twelve plumbing intervals before the G2 quotient, gives a proper model on the root
   cover. Its unfolded charts are precisely this fan. The compact core and collars therefore prove
   properness and proper discontinuity.

6. The affine deck extends to this model because its unit multiplication preserves every toric
   chart and its shear preserves the fan. It is free. On the r-central divisor a point lies on at
   most two adjacent component labels in Z/12; no nonidentity translation can preserve that set.
   This covers their intersection over the common base origin as well. On the q-central divisor
   with r ̸= 0, the bottom triangle has second component indices contained in {j, j + 1}, again
   not preserved by a nonzero translation modulo twelve. Off both axes the root-base action is
   free. Its finite quotient is therefore smooth, proper over (q, r), flat over r, and has a reduced
   normal-crossings r-central divisor.

7. Keeping the same positive root-base rotation and using translation −b gives valuation shear
   H −1 and twelfth iterate G−1 2 . This action preserves the same fan and has the same freeness
   properties. For the family in the statement we use translation by b and the clockwise cusp
   generator g0 : s 7→ s − 1. Thus the positive fractional deck b has shift +1 for s 7→ s + 1 and
   shift −1 for g0 , exactly as required by 22.6. The finite shifts 4, −3 and this cusp shift all refer
   to the same clockwise deck-identification convention.

8. Denote this rotating model by R. Its q-fibre for r ̸= 0 has multiplicity twelve. Indeed the
   original z-central divisor is reduced and the finite action has trivial generic isotropy there,
   while q = z 12 . This is the q-multiplicity computed in 22.7.

9. The two-open gluing. On the base open set q ̸= 0 use R with the positive fractional deck b. On
   the base open set r ̸= 0 use the reduced Mumford cusp family. Their common base is U , where
   (22.11)– (22.12), composed with 22.26, give the specified holomorphic isomorphism. These
   two open sets cover B × , and there is no additional triple overlap. Glue by that isomorphism.

 Remark 22.40 (The two axial models and their overlap). [tag PT18] Proposition 22.39 uses the
 rotating model R on q ̸= 0 and the reduced Mumford family on r =        ̸ 0. On their overlap the
 exact isomorphism is ζ 7→ ζ − σ + F , with F given by (22.11). The larger rotating model has
 local equation q = z 12 at its q-boundary for r ̸= 0, so every q-vertical divisorial valuation there
 has order in 12Z. The reduced Mumford boundary has a divisor of q-order one. A common
 proper modification over q would identify the function q and the associated divisorial valuations;
 Proposition 22.11 gives the resulting contradiction. Thus the overlap isomorphism specifies
 precisely the two-open gluing on B × . Its noncompletion at the missing origin is Proposition 22.54,
 and the obstruction for the full global family is Theorem 18.6.

Proposition 22.42 (The other Kato axis). [tag 030P]
    In the proper smooth Kato family K → ∆s of 22.27 there is a second relative effective Cartier
divisor D ⊂ K, disjoint from the persistent elliptic divisor E. The surface D is smooth and proper
over ∆s . Its general fibre and central fibre are
              Ds = C∗ /(κ(s)sn )Z   (s ̸= 0),     D0 = the reduced rational n-cycle.
At its nodes the relative local equation is uv = s. Its normal line in K is the multidegree-zero
Tate line whose factor on the closing collar is a(s). In particular it has degree zero on every
component of the central cycle. Scaling the first blowdown coordinate gives a holomorphic C∗
action on the pair (K, D) over the base.
    For n = 12 this constructs an embedded proper copy of the cusp’s elliptic root interface, with
its degree-zero normal line, after choosing the units κ, a to be the Tate and normal multipliers.
In the additive period convention u = (τ, µ), W = e−2πiζ2 , these multipliers are κ(s)s12 = e2πiτ
and a(s) = e−2πiµ . The elliptic translation by 6P is realized by first-coordinate scaling a(s)−6 .
    The comparison identifies the embedded Cartier divisor and its normal line. At each central
node the ambient base map has the local form s = uv − h computed below.

Proof. 1. Use the modification, embedding and compact collar domains of 22.27. Write w for
  the second blowdown coordinate and set, on the modified fundamental region,
                                            hs = πn∗ w − s.
   The collar identification is σs πn , where σs (z, w) = (κ(s)z, a(s)w + (1 − a(s))s) in the last
   chart. Consequently
                                         hs ◦ (σs πn ) = a(s)hs .                          (22.19)
   Its zeros therefore glue to a relative effective Cartier divisor, and (22.19) is simultaneously
   the normal-line transition. The divisor is closed in the proper family K → ∆s , so it is proper.
2. For s =
         ̸ 0, the line w = s misses every blow-up centre. In the coordinate v = w − s the
   contracting germ is
                             (x, v) 7−→ (κ(s)x(a(s)v + s)n , a(s)v).
   Its restriction to v = 0 is x 7→ κ(s)sn x. The generic developing map of 22.27 restricts to the
   identity in this coordinate, since its product Gs (v) has Gs (0) = 1. Thus this is precisely the
   unmodified other Hopf axis, with the stated Tate multiplier and normal multiplier a(s).
3. The divisor of πn∗ w is reduced. After the first blow-up, both the strict horizontal axis and
   the exceptional curve have coefficient one. Every later centre is the intersection of the newest
   exceptional curve with the strict vertical axis. It lies on no other component of the divisor
   of πn∗ w. The new exceptional coefficient is therefore again one. Before the end collars are
   identified, the divisor is a chain comprising the strict horizontal axis and the n exceptional
   pieces. The end annuli join the two endpoint pieces, leaving the familiar rational n-cycle of
   the parabolic surface. It is disjoint from its elliptic curve, as also described in the parabolic
   model of (Istrati et al., 2022, Example 9.10, p. 1386).
4. At a crossing of two adjacent pieces, ordinary blow-up coordinates give πn∗ w = uv up to a
   holomorphic unit, which can be absorbed in u. Hence D has equation uv = s. It is smooth,
   and its central fibre is reduced nodal. Away from these nodes its defining equation is a
   coordinate minus s. This proves smoothness of the whole divisor and semistability over the
   disc. The monomial transition charts are those of the unit-interval Tate model, and the closing
   on the nonzero axis is exactly x 7→ κ(s)sn x. They identify the marked family with that Tate
   model over ∆s .

 5. The same local defining functions trivialize the normal line. Their only nontrivial closing
    factor is (22.19), namely the holomorphic unit a(s). On each rational component the line has
    degree zero; equivalently its two adjacent-node degree corrections cancel its self-intersection
    −2. For n = 1 the same statement uses the two branches of the self-node. The factor a(s)
    gives the gluing parameter around the cycle. This is exactly the multidegree-zero extension of
    the line with factor a(s) on the smooth Tate curves.

 6. The first-coordinate scaling commutes with the modification and the collar maps and preserves
    hs . One may equivalently descend the vector field x∂x and its local flow. Properness over the

    period yields the stated holomorphic C∗ action. On the Tate axis it is ordinary multiplication
    of x, so a holomorphic unit a(s)−6 realizes the marked translation by 6P .

                                     (Z, W ) 7−→ (e2πiτ Z, e−2πiµ W ).

                                                                12 for a holomorphic unit. The second

    multiplier tends to the contracting inverse of −(5 + 2 6), so after shrinking 0 < |a(s)| < 1

 8. At a central node, the smooth Kato total space has coordinates (u, v, s) with divisor h =
    uv − s = 0. In coordinates (u, v, h) its map to the base is

                                               s = uv − h.                                    (22.20)

    It is a submersion. The total space of the normal line, with the inherited map from D, has

    the map to s on this local nonzero-r fibre is a submersion at the displayed locus.

10. There is also a concrete obstruction to the most direct global use of this plumbing. For fixed
    s ̸= 0, all the n blow-up centres lie on the first Hopf axis x = 0, at [v = −s] and its infinitely
    near strict-axis points. The other axis Ds is v = 0, x ̸= 0. The axes are disjoint, and hence
    every exceptional rational curve misses Ds . A plumbing that leaves the complement of a small
    tubular neighbourhood of Ds unchanged retains these compact curves in its r ̸= 0 fibres over
    the same s. A complex torus has no rational curve: a holomorphic map from P1 lifts to its
    vector-space universal cover and is constant. Thus this fixed-base localized plumbing of the
    entire Kato surface cannot produce the prescribed ordinary two-tori.

 9. Label the exceptional chain so that the orders of u, V, s on Ci are i, 12 − i, 1, respectively, with
    the two end branches at indices 0, 12. These are the values in the explicit surface resolution
    above. Along any ambient vertical divisor meeting Ci , the orders of u and V sum to twelve,

    the restricted orders already sum to twelve, the ambient orders are exactly i, 12 − i. No other
    zero or pole of either character occurs near D, because their product is s12 .

                               Xi = u/si ,       Yi = si+1 /u,      Xi Yi = s                   (22.31)

    invertible differential along D. Thus (22.31) and H are biholomorphic product charts near D.
    Their character identities give the standard transitions of the minimal resolution of A11 .

11. The closing and the uniform linear collar. The Kato formula determines the global closing. In

12. Every ambient modification used above is a blow-up of a smooth closed centre and is proper.
    The total space remains smooth, and its map to the parameter disc is flat because a nonzero

    punctured family is unchanged. All centres are disjoint from the persistent elliptic axis, so its

 22.10    A local resolution retaining the cusp factor
 Proposition 22.44 (The local plumbing model). [tag 030R]
    Let
                   Xn = {f uv = gsn } ⊂ C5 ,    r = g − f,                q = sn .
There is a proper bimeromorphic local modification X   e n → Xn with smooth total fourfold and
reduced normal-crossings divisor r = 0. For fixed r = ̸ 0 it resolves the cyclic base change of a
three-branch q-normal-crossings chart. The divisor s = 0 after the displayed cyclic base change is
reduced; the divisor of the original function q = sn has multiplicity n.

 Proof. 1. For n = 1 first blow up (u, q) and then the pullback of (f, g). The charts of the
   resulting modification are

                         coordinates          map to X1             r
                          (q, U, v, f )    u = qU, g = f U v   f (U v − 1)
                         (u, Q, G, f ) q = uQ, v = GQ, g = f G f (G − 1)
                          (u, v, F, g)     q = uvF, f = gF     g(1 − F ).

    To derive them, the q chart of the first blow-up has u = qU , hence g = f U v; the ideal (f, g) is
    already principal there. Its other chart has q = uQ and equation f v = gQ. Blowing up (f, g)
    gives the last two charts. These are the blow-up charts, with the common factors cancelled
    on the closure of the dense torus. They are smooth. In the first chart U v − 1 is a smooth
    coordinate along its zero set, and in the others G − 1 or 1 − F is a coordinate. Thus the
    displayed products prove the reduced NC assertion for r.

 2. For arbitrary n, pull back this proper modification by q = sn . The first chart remains smooth.
    The second is uQ = sn times the two coordinates G, f . Resolve its An−1 factor by the
    unit-interval fan. The third chart is
                                              uvF = sn
   times the independent coordinate g. Its cone lattice may be written as N = Z3 with coordinates
   (a, b, d), where the valuations of u, v, F, s are a, b, nd − a − b, d. The cone is the cone over n∆2 .
   Insert all rays (i, j, 1) with i, j ≥ 0 and i + j ≤ n, and triangulate by the unit triangles

                      (i, j), (i + 1, j), (i, j + 1)         (i, j ≥ 0, i + j ≤ n − 1),
                      (i + 1, j), (i, j + 1), (i + 1, j + 1) (i, j ≥ 0, i + j ≤ n − 2).

    Every determinant is one in absolute value; the triangles partition the large triangle and give
    a proper smooth toric subdivision. Their number is n2 . All new rays have s-height one.

Proposition 22.45 (Exceptional-curve nonclosure and persistence in a semistable cap). [tag 030S]
    Let K∗ → ∆s be the modified degree-one Kato family of 22.43, with q = s12 , and let E → ∆s
be its unchanged persistent elliptic axis. For s ̸= 0 let Cs ≃ P1 be the exceptional curve of the
single Hopf blow-up.
    The union of the Cs has no proper analytic divisor closure in K∗ . Further finite proper
modifications cannot give these curves a proper analytic divisor closure: any such closure would

                                                 234
push forward to a forbidden one. In particular, the generic Hopf blowdown does not extend as a
relative proper holomorphic modification, or as a relative meromorphic contraction represented
by a proper analytic graph, across s = 0.
    For the deformation obstruction, suppose a smooth complex fourfold Y has holomorphic
functions (Q, r), its divisor r = 0 is reduced normal crossings, and one component K contains a
neighbourhood of some Cs0 , s0 = ̸ 0, agreeing with the complementary Kato region and its ordinary
base coordinate Q. Suppose this curve is disjoint from every conductor branch of r = 0. Then
every sufficiently nearby fibre (Q, r) = (Q0 , r0 ) contains an embedded rational curve. Consequently
such a cap cannot have the prescribed ordinary two-tori as its r ̸= 0 surface fibres.

Proof. 1. We first use the exact marked blowdown of 22.27. The exceptional curve of the single
  generic Hopf blow-up meets the persistent elliptic axis transversely at

                                    [v = −q] ∈ Ea(q) = C∗ /a(q)Z .

   All modifications in 22.43 are disjoint from that axis. The intersection section in the modified
   family is therefore still
                                             p(s) = [−s12 ].                                (22.35)
   The units a(q) obey 0 < |a(q)| < 1. Choose a holomorphic logarithm on the full parameter
   disc and put
                                                   log a(s12 )
                                          τ (s) =              .
                                                      2πi
   Then Es = C/(Z + τ (s)Z) and Im τ (s) > 0. The maps (x, y, s) 7→ [x + yτ (s)], with (x, y) ∈
   R2 /Z2 , give a smooth trivialization of the elliptic family. A logarithmic lift of (22.35) is

                                                   log(−s12 )
                                          z(s) =              .
                                                      2πi
   On a positive loop around zero, τ returns to itself and z changes by 12. Thus the loop of
   the section has class (12, 0) ̸= 0 in the integral first homology of this trivialized family. A
   continuous section over the disc would fill that loop. Hence p has no continuous, and therefore
   no holomorphic, extension. A meromorphic section from a nonsingular curve would extend
   holomorphically: its proper graph is generically degree one over the curve, and normalization
   gives a finite degree-one map to that normal base. This is equally impossible. A finite base
   change of degree d > 0 multiplies the winding to (12d, 0) and does not change the conclusion.

2. Suppose an analytic divisor Z in K∗ , proper over the disc, restricted over the punctured
   disc to the union of the Cs . Its horizontal irreducible part does not contain E, since the
   generic intersection is the one transverse point (22.35). Both are Cartier locally in the smooth
   threefold, so their intersection is an analytic curve, proper over the disc. Its reduced horizontal
   part has generic degree one. An irreducible horizontal analytic curve cannot have a positive-
   dimensional fibre without being contained in that fibre. Hence its normalization is finite
   of degree one over the disc and is isomorphic to the disc. It extends p(s), a contradiction.
   Vertical components of the intersection have no effect on this horizontal component.

3. If an additional finite proper modification admitted a proper analytic closure, its proper image
   would give such a Z, by the proper mapping theorem; the image has dimension two and
   the same generic exceptional curves. The horizontal exceptional locus of a relative proper
   holomorphic blowdown likewise gives Z. For a meromorphic contraction with proper analytic
   graph, resolve the graph and apply the same argument to its horizontal exceptional locus and
   its proper image in K∗ . This is a direct marked-intersection proof of a familiar nonproperness
   phenomenon for exceptional curves in GSS surface deformations; see Dloussky and Teleman
   (2012, arXiv version 2, Section 1.2, PDF pp. 3–5) for the primary context.

                                                235
4. Write C = Cs0 and S = K ∩ {Q = Q0 }. Near this curve, S is a smooth surface and C is its
   exceptional curve, so
                                   NC/S ≃ OP1 (−1).
   The base coordinate Q is submersive on K near C. Because C misses every other central
   branch, the reduced function r is a local defining function for K near C and its normal
   derivative is nowhere zero. Consequently the differential of (Q, r) gives the exact normal
   sequence
                                                       (dQ,dr)
                           0 −→ OP1 (−1) −→ NC/Y −−−−−−→ OP⊕2
                                                            1 −→ 0.                         (22.36)
   Its extension class vanishes because H 1 (P1 , O(−1)) = 0. Hence

            NC/Y ≃ O(−1) ⊕ O⊕2 ,         H 1 (C, NC/Y ) = 0,     h0 (C, NC/Y ) = 2.         (22.37)

   Moreover (22.36) induces an isomorphism on global sections, since both H 0 (O(−1)) and
   H 1 (O(−1)) vanish.
5. Kodaira’s embedded-deformation theorem therefore gives a smooth two-dimensional local
   parameter space T of compact embedded deformations of C, with tangent space H 0 (C, NC/Y ).
   In precisely this relative surface setting one may apply Dloussky and Teleman (2012, arXiv
   version 2, Proposition 2.3 and its proof, PDF pp. 6–7): after shrinking the neighbourhood of
   C, (Q, r) is a holomorphic submersion of relative dimension two, and C is a compact simply
   exceptional divisor of its fibre. The general completeness theorem is due to Kodaira; we use
   the exact statements in Merkulov (1995, Section 1, p. 71, and Section 3.1, p. 74). Shrink this
   family so its curves remain in the chosen neighbourhood. Their genus remains zero, so all
   are isomorphic to P1 . The functions Q, r are constant on every compact connected curve and
   thus define a holomorphic map
                                               T −→ C2 .
   Its derivative at [C] is precisely the isomorphism on sections induced by (22.36). The
   holomorphic inverse function theorem shows that the map covers a neighbourhood of (Q0 , 0).
   In particular the nearby fixed pairs with r ̸= 0 contain rational curves. A holomorphic map
   from P1 to a complex torus lifts to its vector-space universal cover and is constant. Thus
   those fibres cannot be the prescribed ordinary two-tori.
6. The conductor condition is essential. For example, if a further central component meets K along
   the persistent elliptic axis, then its intersection number with C is one and NK/Y |C ≃ O(−1).
   At the conductor intersection dr vanishes on the normal fibre of C, so (dQ, dr) is not the bundle
   epimorphism of (22.36). This computes precisely where that normal-sequence argument uses
   the conductor-disjoint hypothesis.




22.11    The associated logarithmic torsor at the missing origin

   contraction cannot have two equal distinct positive powers. Hence there are infinitely many
   resonances qN → 0 with the first value in (22.49).
3. For each N the resonance function is nonzero at q = 0, so is not identically zero. Its zeros in
   the punctured disc are discrete. The countable union of these discrete sets cannot contain an
   open disc. There are therefore also nonresonant points arbitrarily near zero, with the second
   value in (22.49).
4. Coherent direct images forbid this pattern. Suppose first that a proper completion π : X → ∆
   has a smooth connected total threefold and agrees with (22.45) over ∆∗ . Put L = KX−1 . On
                                                         −1
   each nonzero fibre, adjunction identifies L|Xq with KH  q
                                                             , because the normal direction is the
   trivial base direction. Grauert’s proper direct-image theorem gives coherent sheaves
                                    M = π∗ L,          N = R1 π∗ L
   on the disc (Grauert, 1960, Section 6, Hauptsatz I, p. 59). Multiplication by a nonzero base
   function is injective on L, and hence on M , since the total space is smooth and the map is
   nonconstant. Thus M is locally free of a fixed rank on the disc. The torsion subsheaf of N is
   coherent with locally finite support. After shrinking, it has no support in ∆∗ .
5. For any a ∈ ∆∗ , apply the direct-image long exact sequence to
                                           q−a
                                 0 −→ L −−−→ L −→ L|Xa −→ 0.
  At a its beginning yields
          0 −→ Ma /(q − a)Ma −→ H 0 (Xa , L|Xa ) −→ ker(q − a : Na → Na ) −→ 0.            (22.50)
                                               −1
  The last term vanishes. Therefore h0 (Ha , KH  a
                                                   ) = rank M for every sufficiently small a ̸= 0.
  This contradicts (22.49) and the accumulating resonances. The displayed coherent direct-image
  exact sequence proves the required local constancy on the punctured disc.
6. Now suppose an arbitrary proper analytic completion Z → ∆ exists. Pass to its reduction
   and retain the unique irreducible component containing the connected smooth punctured
   total space. This is a closed analytic component, remains proper over the disc, and dominates
   the disc. Its restriction over ∆∗ is exactly the given family. Resolve this component by a
   proper analytic resolution chosen to be an isomorphism on its already nonsingular locus; see
   Bierstone and Milman (1997, Theorem 1.6 and the following noncompact extension, p. 215).
   All singular points lie over zero, so the resolution is an isomorphism over the entire punctured
   family. Properness of the composition is preserved. Near the compact central fibre, local
   finiteness of the analytic resolution permits one shrinking of the disc; its dominating smooth
   component is a smooth proper total threefold as in the preceding paragraph. Its map to the
   disc is nonconstant, so the base function is a non-zero-divisor on this dominating component.
   The preceding contradiction applies. Reduction also shows that nilpotent structure supported
   at zero cannot evade it.
7. Finally, a finite base change replaces α by a holomorphic function of some positive vanishing
   order and replaces β by a unit whose value at zero still has modulus strictly between zero and
   one. The same proof applies verbatim.

22.12     A necessary vertical fibre over the missing origin
Proposition 22.49 (Every origin component is a threefold). [tag 030V]
    Suppose the partial family of 22.41 has a proper analytic completion f : Z → ∆q × ∆r with
smooth pure four-dimensional total space, with r ◦ f flat, and with its prescribed identification
over the punctured bidisc. The map to this fixed bidisc is assumed holomorphic. Then every
irreducible component of f −1 (0, 0) has dimension three. In particular, there is no equidimensional
completion, and no completion having even one two-dimensional component of the origin fibre.
    The stated map to the bidisc includes a holomorphic extension of q. Proposition 22.54 excludes
completions of this fixed partial family, including the displayed vertical-component geometry;
Theorem 18.6 excludes proper fillings of the global family.

Proof. 1. We first prove the finite-multisection consequence of the log-torsor obstruction of
  Proposition 22.46. Make the normalized finite base change q = Q12 . The resulting space Z ′ is
  normal and pure four-dimensional. Its restrictions to the two punctured axes have the explicit
  normalized fan presentations used in 22.46. Write

                 B = ∆Q × ∆r ,     Bq = ∆∗Q × ∆r ,      Br = ∆Q × ∆∗r ,         U = Bq ∩ Br .

2. Assume there is a finite surjective map p : V → B of positive generic degree d, together
   with a holomorphic map V → Z ′ over B. We may normalize V and retain any collection
   of components dominating B; its degree remains a positive integer. A normal surface is
   Cohen–Macaulay; finite over the smooth bidisc, it is flat. Thus the finite holomorphic trace
   and the degree-d sum with multiplicities are available also at branch points. On the ordinary
   locus, sum the d points of this multisection, with multiplicity, in each of the two axial group
   origins of 22.46. This gives two local expressions for the trace in the Jacobian group. We
   show that they extend as log-torus sections on Bq and Br .

3. Ramification away from the axes. Over the ordinary locus the torus family is a smooth
   holomorphic group family. Near a branch point, choose small neighbourhoods of the finitely
   many preimages in V and local Lie lifts of their maps to the torus. The trace of these
   holomorphic functions under the finite map is holomorphic, and its exponential is the ordinary
   sum. Changes of lifts add periods, which disappear in the group quotient. Thus the ordinary
   trace extends across the ordinary branch locus. Equivalently this is the usual addition map
   on the relative symmetric power, applied to the finite multisection.


                                                  241
4. The explicit norm at an axis. After shrinking B, every component of the finite cover’s branch
   divisor which is not an axis meets each punctured axis nowhere: its intersection with either axis
   is an isolated analytic germ at the origin. At a point of a punctured axis choose coordinates
   (x, y), with x the normal coordinate to that axis. Locally the normal finite cover is a disjoint
   union of covers
                                          x = te ,   y = y,                                  (22.51)
   including e = 1 sheets. Indeed the complement of the axis in a small polydisc has cyclic
   fundamental group; each connected unramified finite cover is the displayed root cover there,
   and its normal finite extension is unique.
5. The map from such a root polydisc into the prescribed fan model gives a section of its
   associated log-torus sheaf. It has a local bounded multiplicative log lift. This can also be seen
   directly in a toric chart: the pulled-back characters are meromorphic functions with zeros
   and poles supported on t = 0, hence are tk u(t, y) with k ∈ Z and u a holomorphic unit. The
   quotient by the period lattice causes only the period ambiguity already retained in 22.46.
6. The multiplicative norm of a character on (22.51) is explicitly
                           e−1                                          e−1
                                 (ζej t)k u(ζej t, y) = (−1)k(e−1) xk                        (22.52)
                           Y                                            Y
                                                                              u(ζej t, y).
                           j=0                                          j=0

  The last product is a holomorphic unit in (x, y). Thus the norm has an integral ghost vector
  and is a log character on the base. It is bounded in the required sense: on the r axis the
  first character has zero normal order and the second is unrestricted; on the Q axis both are
  unrestricted. These are precisely the bounded-character conditions for (22.38). Multiplication
  of lifts corresponds to addition in the log torus. Changing a lift by a period changes its norm
  by an integral period, so the resulting quotient section is independent of the lift. Summing
  over the finitely many covers (22.51), whose degrees add to d, proves the claimed extension
  along that axis.
7. The local extensions agree on overlaps because they agree on the ordinary locus. Lift locally
   to log characters: agreement there is an equality up to a locally constant Y -period, and that
   meromorphic equality extends across the axis. We have therefore obtained sections hq of A
   on Bq and hr on Br . To fix the sign, write zr = ζ − σ for the cusp group coordinate. The
   comparison map of 22.39 gives the rotating coordinate zq = ζ − σ + F = zr + F . Summing
   over the d points, with multiplicity, therefore gives

                                                hq − hr = dF                                 (22.53)

   on U . The ghost proof of 22.46 forbids (22.53): its r-loop Y -component is dγ =
                                                                                  ̸ 0. Thus no
   such finite multisection can exist.
8. A two-dimensional fibre germ would supply one. Suppose an origin point of Z has local
   fibre dimension two. Finite base change and normalization are finite maps and preserve that
   local fibre dimension at points lying above it. At a resulting point of Z ′ , choose two generic
   local linear sections in an analytic embedding. Their intersection with the fibre is isolated.
   Intersecting with Z ′ gives a two-dimensional analytic germ whose map to B is finite. This
   is the local finite-projection criterion from Weierstrass preparation; see also Demailly (2012,
   Chapter II, Proposition 8.2 and its proof, pp. 116–117). Choose a component through the
   point. Its finite image has dimension two and is therefore the whole base germ. A finite
   representative of this germ, after shrinking the bidisc, is finite and surjective over the entire
   smaller bidisc. Its normalization is still finite and maps to Z ′ , giving exactly the forbidden
   multisection of positive degree. Properness of this finite representative prevents loss of sheets
   at its boundary.

                                                     242
9. Every fibre component of a dominant map from a pure fourfold to a smooth surface has
   dimension at least two. If a two-dimensional irreducible component existed, a generic point on
   it would have local fibre dimension two, which we have excluded. Flatness over r makes r = 0
   a Cartier divisor of pure dimension three, so the origin fibre has no component of dimension
   greater than three. All its irreducible components consequently have dimension three, as
   asserted.




22.13    The obstruction survives modifications of the base
Proposition 22.50 (Logarithmic torsors under point blowups). [tag 030W]
    Let B = ∆Q × ∆R , with q = Q12m and r = Rn , where m, n are positive integers. Let

  of the two coordinate axes. The reduced total boundary is normal crossing. Every Ei is a

                                  ai = ordEi (Q),        bi = ordEi (R)                      (22.55)

2. The exact bounded-character subsheaf. The period pairing remains (22.38), pulled back to S.
   By the base-change lemma (Kajiwara et al., 2008b, Lemma 1.2.9, pp. 80–81) it defines AS .
   More explicitly its bounded multiplicative-character sheaf is
                                            (Y )

   Indeed the first character is bounded by powers of q, and therefore has zero order on DR . It

3. Cohomology of the blown-up bidisc. For a point blowup p of a smooth surface, p∗ O = O
