Proposition 22.51 (Maximal monodromy with trivial central dualizing bundle). [tag 030X]
    Let p : X → ∆ be a proper holomorphic map from a smooth complex threefold, smooth over ∆∗ ,
whose nonzero fibres are complex two-tori. Suppose that D = p−1 (0) is a reduced normal-crossing
divisor and that ωD ≃ OD . If its monodromy on H1 (Xt , Q) satisfies

                                          rank(T − 1) = 2,                                     (22.64)

then every normalization component of D is a smooth rational toric surface, its conductor is its
toric boundary, and the dual complex of D is a topological two-torus. In particular all normalized
components are Kähler.
    The trivialization of ωD in the hypotheses is the central section used in the residue and
nearby-period arguments below.

Proof. 1. Write Vi for the compact smooth normalization components and Ci for their reduced
  conductor divisors. Adjunction gives

                                             KVi + Ci ∼ 0.                                     (22.65)

   If D is smooth, the map is a proper submersion near its compact central fibre and its
   monodromy is trivial. Otherwise every Ci is nonempty, by connectedness. Adjunction on a
   conductor branch says that it is either a smooth elliptic curve disjoint from the other branches,
   or a rational curve with two boundary points, counted on its normalization. The rational
   branches form cycles, including the nodal irreducible and two-component cases.

2. Nonnegative Euler contributions. A nonempty effective anticanonical divisor makes every
   pluricanonical system empty: multiplying a nonzero pluricanonical section by the appropriate
   power of the anticanonical section would give a nonzero holomorphic function with a nonempty
   zero divisor. Thus the surface has Kodaira dimension −∞. Its minimal model is rational,
   ruled, or of class VII. We spell out the consequences for the reduced anticanonical pairs here.

3. On a rational surface, the conductor is connected, by 0 → KV → OV → OC → 0 and
   H 1 (KV ) = 0. For a rational cycle, the charge identity and positivity are

    e(V \C) = 12−C 2 −#{cycle components} ≥ 0,             e(V \C) = 0 ⇐⇒ (V, C) is toric. (22.66)

   Here e denotes compactly supported Euler characteristic. This includes the nodal irreducible
   convention: Friedman (2016, arXiv version 2, Section 1, p. 3; Definition 1.1 and Lemma 1.2,
   pp. 4–5; Lemma 2.2, p. 11; Lemma 2.7, p. 14). For a smooth elliptic anticanonical curve,
   e(V \ C) = 2 + b2 (V ) > 0 instead.

4. On a nonrational ruled minimal model, a conductor component dominating the base has degree
   at most two and genus at most one. The base is therefore elliptic. The minimal conductor is
   two disjoint elliptic sections or one unramified elliptic bisection. Its Euler contribution is zero.
   The two section squares sum to zero, and the bisection has square zero, also directly from
   KV + C ∼ 0 and KV2 = 0.



                                                 245
 5. A minimal class-VII surface with b2 = 0 and a curve is a Hopf surface. Its elliptic curves have
    square zero, and a reduced anticanonical divisor has at most two elliptic components. For this
    last assertion the exact sequence 0 → KV → OV → OC → 0 gives h0 (OC ) ≤ 1 + h1 (KV ) = 2.
    The Euler contribution is zero. This also covers secondary Hopf surfaces.

 6. For a minimal class-VII surface with b2 > 0, the reduced anticanonical divisor is a numer-
    ically anticanonical divisor whose coefficients are all one. Dloussky (2006, arXiv version 3,
    Corollary 2.25, pp. 16–17; Lemma 2.26, p. 17; Proposition 2.27, pp. 17–19) imply that it is
    parabolic Inoue or Inoue–Hirzebruch. Half-Inoue has only a nontrivially twisted anticanonical
    divisor and cannot satisfy (22.65). The remaining possibilities are hyperbolic Inoue with two
    disjoint rational cycles, or parabolic Inoue with one rational cycle and a disjoint elliptic curve.
    If n = b2 > 0, there are n rational cycle components and e(V ) = n, so the contribution is zero.
    In the parabolic case the elliptic curve has square −n. The curve configurations, anticanonical
                                                2
    identities and underlying (S 1 × S 3 )#nP topology are recorded in Fujiki and Pontecorvo
    (2010, Sections 3.2–3.3, pp. 20–22).

 7. These assertions extend to nonminimal pairs. An exceptional curve outside C meets it once,
    transversely at a smooth point, since −KV · E = 1; its contraction reverses an interior blow-up.
    An exceptional curve in C meets the rest at two points and its contraction reverses a corner
    blow-up. The reduced anticanonical condition is preserved. Interior blow-up increases e(V \ C)
    by one, whereas corner blow-up leaves it unchanged. Thus every contribution is nonnegative.
    Equality permits only toric rational pairs, minimal elliptic ruled or Hopf pairs, and corner
    blow-ups of hyperbolic or parabolic Inoue pairs. For these Inoue pairs the cycle count and
    b2 increase together, and the fundamental group stays Z. Corner blow-ups do not touch the
    parabolic elliptic curve, whose square remains strictly negative.

 8. The local nearby fibre at a multiplicity-k stratum of a reduced normal-crossing divisor retracts
    to (S 1 )k−1 . Euler integration consequently gives

                                       0 = e(Xt ) =        e(Vi \ Ci ).                        (22.67)
                                                      X

                                                       i

    Every summand is nonnegative and therefore zero. Rational components with a smooth
    elliptic conductor, and all interior blow-ups, are excluded.

 9. Elliptic normal-degree balance. An elliptic double curve contains no triple point. The local
    model p = xy gives opposite degrees to its two normal lines. Sum these degrees over all elliptic
    conductor branches. The total is zero. An elliptic ruled or Hopf component contributes zero;
    a parabolic Inoue component contributes the strictly negative degree of its sole elliptic branch.
    No rational component with elliptic conductor remains. Hence there are no parabolic Inoue
    components.

10. By connectedness, all conductors are now elliptic or all are rational: no remaining component
    has both types. In the elliptic case there are no triple points and every vertex of the dual
    graph has valence at most two. The graph is a segment or circle, allowing a loop or multiple
    edges. In this case
                                 rank(T − 1) ≤ b1 (dual graph) ≤ 1.                        (22.68)
    To prove this, remove small tubes about the disjoint double curves. The remaining compact
    cores extend as smooth submersions over the whole disc and can be trivialized there. Mon-
    odromy is then a product of the annular twists xy = t. A passage of a loop across one neck
    adds its oriented normal-circle class, with coefficient the signed crossing number of that edge.
    Core loops have zero change. Crossing numbers of a closed loop form a cycle of the dual
    graph. Thus T − 1 factors through its rational cycle space. The normal-circle rotation exists
    on the circle bundle of the normal line. This proves (22.68) and excludes the elliptic case.

                                                 246
11. Hyperbolic components contradict a nonzero nearby period. The remaining possibilities are
    toric rational pairs and corner blow-ups of hyperbolic Inoue pairs. Suppose one component is
    of the latter kind. A boundary of a small neighborhood of either rational conductor cycle,
    lying in Vi \ Ci , is a torus mapping torus MA , whose monodromy on its fibre lattice is

                                        A ∈ SL2 (Z),          | tr A| > 2.                     (22.69)

    Here is the exact marking needed. In Oda (1978, Section 15, Theorem 15.1 and the following
    paragraph, retypeset pp. 130–131), the universal toric construction has lattice N and deck
    action given by multiplication by a nontrivial totally positive unit of a real quadratic field.
    This is the hyperbolic matrix A. The complement of the two cycles is R times the compact
    angular-torus bundle over a circle. A path in the logarithmic absolute-value space from a
    point to its image by A realizes this mapping torus. The point can be chosen in a node cone
    arbitrarily near a conductor node. Its two adjacent primitive rays form a lattice basis, so
    the angular fibre is exactly the Clifford torus in the corresponding local coordinates (x, y).
    Corner blow-ups are toric star subdivisions; they alter neither the dense torus nor A, only this
    unimodular coordinate basis. Thus the same marked mapping torus exists for every corner
    blow-up allowed above.

12. Choose a compact such MA in the smooth open stratum. A neighborhood of this compact set
    extends as a smooth submersion over the full parameter disc. Transport gives an embedding
    MA → Xt for all small t, with the same marked fibre Lt ≃ (S 1 )2 . In the abelian group
    H1 (Xt , Q), the mapping-torus relations give

                                          (A − 1)H1 (Lt , Q) 7−→ 0.

    Since A − 1 is invertible over Q, both angular generators map to zero. The cohomology ring
    of a complex two-torus is the exterior algebra on H 1 . It follows that the map H 2 (Xt , Q) →
    H 2 (Lt , Q) is zero and hence
                                       [Lt ] = 0 in H2 (Xt , Q).                           (22.70)

13. On the other hand, h0 (D, ωD ) = 1, since D is compact and connected, and the corresponding
    dimension on every nearby two-torus is also one. Grauert’s cohomology and base-change
    theorem applied to the invertible relative dualizing sheaf supplies a relative section extending
    the chosen nonzero central generator; see Bănică and Stănăşilă (1976, Chapter III, Theo-
    rem 4.12(ii), pp. 134–135). Evaluation is nonzero at every point of D. Compactness and
    shrinking make this section nonvanishing near the entire fibre. Write it as Ω. At the conductor
    node just used, the total family has coordinates xyz = t and
                                                    dx dy
                                Ωt = U (x, y, z)      ∧ ,          U (0, 0, 0) ̸= 0.           (22.71)
                                                    x  y
    The angular torus can be transported specifically as |x| = ϵ1 , |y| = ϵ2 , z = t/(xy). This agrees,
    up to isotopy, with its compact-core transport. If U = aijk xi y j z k in a small polydisc, direct
                                                            P

    integration of the convergent series gives
                          Z
                                Ωt = (2πi)2         akkk tk −→ (2πi)2 U (0, 0, 0) ̸= 0.        (22.72)
                                              X
                           Lt                 k≥0

    For small t this contradicts (22.70), because the holomorphic two-form Ωt is closed. This
    excludes every hyperbolic Inoue component.

14. The dual complex. All normalization pairs are now rational toric pairs. Every vertex link is one
    circle and every edge has two incident faces, because each rational double curve has two triple
    points. Thus the finite dual complex K is a connected closed topological surface. It is oriented:

                                                       247
    the iterated residues of a trivialization of ωD are nonzero at every triple point, and the residue
    theorem on each rational double curve makes its two coefficients opposite, with the gluing
    sign for the two branches. These coefficients form a nowhere-zero two-cycle on K. Constancy
    of coherent Euler characteristic in the proper flat analytic family (Bănică and Stănăşilă, 1976,
    Chapter III, Theorem 4.12(iii), pp. 134–135), and the alternating normalization resolution,
    give
                                            0 = χ(OD ) = χ(K).                                 (22.73)
    The surface therefore has genus one.

15. For self-crossings, use the finite local-branch incidence cell structure; the link of a normalized
    toric component is its circular boundary. Over the normalization P1 of a double curve,
    the two-branch cover extends unramified over its triple-point ends by local normal-crossing
    coordinates and hence splits. Subdivision displays the same closed surface and the residue
    signs. The alternating normalization resolution uses these branch signs and gives the same
    Euler count. The hyperbolic-link argument took place in the open normalization stratum,
    which embeds in D, and is unchanged by self-identification of boundary branches.



 Remark 22.52 (Vertical divisors and component adjunction). [tag PT05] For a proper semistable

 22.14    What invariant forms do not control
 Proposition 22.53 (Full-rank periods do not bound an affine comparison). [tag 030Y]
     There is a proper semistable family of two-dimensional complex tori over a disc, with smooth
 total threefold and rank-two unipotent monodromy on H 1 , and a fibre-preserving automorphism
 over the punctured disc with the following properties. It acts identically on all relative invariant
 one- and two-forms and on the Gauss–Manin variation. Their coherent extensions supplied by the
 proper family therefore give the same lattices under this identification. An absolute holomorphic
 canonical form extending across the centre is also unchanged. Nevertheless, the automorphism
 has no meromorphic extension to the total family.
     Thus these invariant-form and connection data do not alone control an affine origin or a
 marked total-space comparison, even in the presence of a proper smooth semistable cap.

 Proof. 1. A proper full-rank example. Let E → ∆t be the standard Tate family with ordinary
   fibre
                                      Et = C∗ /tZ  (t ̸= 0)
    and reduced nodal rational central fibre. Its proper analytic model and node chart xy = t are
    the explicit example in Kajiwara et al. (2008b, Sections 1.1.1–1.1.3, pp. 73–74). Form E ×∆ E.
    Its only total-space singularity is the product of the two nodes, with local equations

                                   xy = t,      uv = t,      xy = uv.



                                                 248
   Blow up the ideal (x, u) in this conifold and take its strict-transform charts. They are
                                     u = xA,      y = Av,           t = xAv
  with smooth coordinates (x, A, v), and
                                    x = uB,       v = By,           t = uBy
  with smooth coordinates (u, B, y). This is the standard proper small resolution, an isomorphism
  away from the conifold point. Glue it to the identity on the complement of that point. The
  resulting p : Y → ∆ is proper, has smooth total threefold, and has reduced normal-crossing
  centre: its displayed equations are products of distinct coordinates. The resolution does not
  alter the ordinary fibres Et × Et .
2. For each elliptic factor choose period cycles wi , ui with ui 7→ ui + wi around t = 0. On the
   direct sum the logarithm of monodromy has rank two and square zero. The same rank holds
   on dual H 1 . Thus this example has the full-rank weight-one unipotent degeneration stated
   above.
3. The nonextending translation. On the punctured disc use multiplicative coordinates (Z, W )
   for the two factors and put
                           Th (Z, W, t) = e2πih(t) Z, W, t ,            h(t) = 1/t.        (22.75)
                                                                

  This is a holomorphic automorphism of the punctured family. The zero section e(t) = ([1], [1])
  extends to the smooth torus locus of the central normalization. For positive integers j tending
  to infinity,
                                 tj = 1/j,      t′j = 1/(j + 1/2)
   lie in the disc and tend to zero, whereas
                          Th (e(tj )) = ([1], [1]),         Th (e(t′j )) = ([−1], [1]).
   In the Tate model these approach the distinct central smooth points with multiplicative
   coordinates (1, 1) and (−1, 1). The small resolution is an isomorphism near both points.
   Hence Th ◦ e has no continuous extension to the centre.
4. This also excludes a meromorphic total extension. If such an extension existed, let Γ → Y be
   its proper meromorphic graph and pull it back along e : ∆ → Y. The resulting analytic space
   is proper over the disc and has a single point in each noncentral fibre. Its unique component
   dominating the disc is a proper analytic curve, generically of degree one. After normalization
   it is finite of degree one over the normal disc, hence is the disc itself. Its map to the target
   Y would extend Th ◦ e holomorphically. This contradicts the two distinct limits just found.
   Vertical components in the pulled-back graph do not affect this dominating curve.
5. Relative forms and their coherent extensions. On the ordinary locus the invariant relative
   one-forms are
                           ω1 = dZ/Z,      ω2 = dW/W      (mod dt).
  They and ω1 ∧ ω2 are unchanged by every Th . The holomorphic forms of a compact torus are
  invariant, so this accounts for all relative holomorphic one- and two-forms on the ordinary
  fibres. The relative log forms extend in the Tate model. Ordinary coherent relative forms also
  give finite-order extensions: for example tω1 , tω2 , and t2 ω1 ∧ ω2 extend as ordinary relative
  forms. In the first resolution chart the first two are explicitly
                               tω1 = Av dx,            tω2 = Av dx + xv dA;
   the other chart gives the analogous regular expressions. At an isolated Tate node the same
   identity is t dx/x = y dx.

                                                      249
 6. More generally, take the torsion-free image of each coherent direct image of relative forms in
    its bundle on the punctured disc. Under the two punctured identifications id and Th , these
    are identical coherent lattices, since the induced map on the entire ordinary relative-form
    bundle is the identity. Coherence therefore gives no bound on h in this example.

 7. Gauss–Manin and an absolute form. Every fibre translation is homotopic to the identity
    and acts identically on integral cohomology. Consequently Th induces the identity on the
    flat Gauss–Manin bundle, its connection, and its Hodge subbundle. The logarithmic period
    growth and regular singularity of that connection are unchanged.

 8. The absolute form
                                                 dZ dW
                                         Ω = dt ∧    ∧      .                                (22.76)
                                                  Z      W
    descends under both Tate period actions, since their extra differentials are multiples of dt. In
    the first small-resolution chart it is
                                           dx d(xA)
                                d(xAv) ∧     ∧      = dv ∧ dx ∧ dA,
                                           x   xA
    and in the other chart it is dy ∧ dB ∧ du. Thus Ω extends as a nonvanishing holomorphic
    canonical form on the smooth total space. Translation adds 2πih′ (t)dt to dZ/Z, which vanishes
    in (22.76), so Th∗ Ω = Ω.

 9. The horizontal term of an absolute differential. On a local multiplicative chart, an absolute
    lift of the first relative form transforms by

                                   Th∗ (dZ/Z) = dZ/Z + 2πih′ (t)dt.                          (22.77)

    This horizontal term is erased both on passing to relative forms and on wedging with the base
    differential. It is not controlled by the linear Gauss–Manin connection. The stronger choice
    h(t) = e1/t makes that term essential, while leaving all the preceding relative and canonical
    calculations unchanged. For this choice the two sequences tj = 1/ log j and t′j = 1/ log(j + 1/2)
    give the same two distinct central limits.

10. Both markings belong to the same proper family. Their relative invariant forms and their
    absolute canonical form agree by the displayed pullbacks, while the two limits of the translated
    zero section are distinct. A common translation cancels in a difference of two sections.




 22.15    Noncompletion of the prescribed partial filling
 Proposition 22.54 (Noncompletion of the fixed partial filling). [tag 0310]
    The partial filling of 22.41 has no proper Hausdorff complex-analytic completion over its
 missing base point. This remains true after finite coordinate roots of the two base coordinates
 and allows arbitrary additional three-dimensional components of the origin fibre.

 Proof. 1. Every finite coordinate-root cover is dominated by one with q = Q12m and r = Rn ,
   where m, n > 0; proper pullback reduces to this case. Suppose such a completion exists.
   Retain and normalize its reduced dominating component, resolve it, and principalize the
   inverse image of the two axes, as in the proof of Theorem 18.6. These proper modifications
   preserve the given family on the complement of the axes and the smooth open parts of the
   two prescribed axial models. The resulting proper map to the bidisc has connected fibres: its
   finite Stein factor is generically one sheet and the bidisc is normal.


                                                 250
2. We identify the axial markings with the standard specialization of Theorem 18.2, namely
   (l0 , l1 , l2 ) = (0, 1, −1) and a = b = 1. In the notation of Proposition 22.46, one has U = −12κ0 .
   The two origins in Theorem 18.2 equal the two origins there plus 6ve, where e = Πc δb = (0, 1)t .
   Translation by 6ve acts on the character W as W 7→ r−6 W . It shifts the twelve-chain index
   by six and extends, with its inverse, across the parameter axis; along the cusp axis r ̸= 0 it is
   multiplication by a holomorphic unit. Thus this is an explicit comparison of the prescribed
   axial models. It changes meridian labels only by multiples of δb and leaves their γb coefficients
   unchanged.

3. In the commuting lifts of Theorem 18.6, an axis component has orders (αi , βi ) and γb meridian
   coefficient κi . The same group calculation gives

                                   (mαi + nβi )κj = (mαj + nβj )κi

   for intersecting components. Every denominator mαi +nβi is positive, including for exceptional
   components over the origin. Hence the ratio κi /(mαi + nβi ) is constant on the incidence
   graph of components meeting the corner.

4. The prescribed parameter-axis model has an extending ordinary origin. Its positive parameter
   loop has zero lattice label in that origin, so the strict parameter component has ratio zero. The
   prescribed cusp-axis origin has ratio a = 1, by the exact covered origin formulas (18.4)–(18.5)
   and the commuting lift Qo = T−mbγ Q. Both strict components meet the corner by properness.
   The compact connected corner fibre makes the incidence graph connected, exactly as in the
   proof of Theorem 18.6. Its ratios would therefore be both zero and one. This contradiction
   proves noncompletion for every pair of positive root degrees and for all additional corner
   components.




22.16     Global elliptic monodromy constrains every central meridian
Proposition 22.55 (The global meridians have only the prescribed toric direction). [tag 0311]
    Suppose g : Z → ∆r is any proper complex-analytic filling of a finite parameter cover of
the six-sphere family. Retain its reduced main component, normalize and resolve it, extend its
intrinsically marked map to P1 by 18.3, resolve the graph, and resolve the support of its central
divisor. Denote the resulting smooth proper modification by Z,e and its holomorphic marked map
by h. All modifications can be chosen to be isomorphisms over r =   ̸ 0. The central divisor has
normal-crossings support and positive integral component multiplicities.
    There is a finite subset Σ ⊂ P1 , containing 0, 1, ∞, with the following property. For every
q ∈ B ◦ := P1 \ Σ, every local angular vanishing circle of the r-central normal-crossings divisor,
viewed in the homology of the nearby ordinary two-torus, lies in

                                          Zδb ⊂ H1 (Xq,r ; Z).                                  (22.78)

The same conclusion holds for the image of the entire local angular torus at a higher crossing
over B ◦ . Here δb is the primitive cycle in the fixed period marking. The conclusion is unaffected
by any further finite cover of the degeneration parameter.

Proof. 1. The global model and the finite exceptional set. The punctured total family is connected
  and smooth, hence irreducible. Its closure is the unique reduced main component dominating
  the parameter disc. Retain this component, normalize it, and resolve it properly, without
  changing its smooth punctured part. The resulting total space is a smooth connected fourfold,
  proper over the disc. The parameter is a nonzero divisor, so its map to the disc is flat.


                                                  251
  The torsion-free coherent bi-anticanonical pencil and labelled critical-value argument of 18.3
  apply to this smooth model. Its marked graph is therefore a proper modification. Further
  analytic resolution and principalization of the central ideal give the stated smooth model and
  normal-crossings support; the complex-analytic scope, including locally finite resolution, is
  explicit in Bierstone and Milman (1997, Theorems 1.6 and 1.10, pp. 215–216, including the
  noncompact extension after Theorem 1.6). Properness over a smaller parameter disc allows
  us to work over a compact central fibre throughout. The modifications have their centres over
  r = 0, so neither the punctured family nor its marked map changes. Flatness over r persists
  because r is a nonzero divisor in the smooth local rings; all central multiplicities are kept in
  the local monomial equations.

2. For possible self-crossings use the finite closed spaces of ordered local branch intersections,
   with each local component normalized. Locally these are the coordinate intersections of the
   central branches. In particular, the double-branch spaces are compact smooth surfaces and
   the triple-branch spaces are compact smooth curves, even when two branches belong to one
   global component. There are finitely many such components.

3. Add to Σ the images of all branch-intersection components on which h is constant and
   the critical values of h on every remaining branch-intersection component, including the
   normalizations of the single branches. These sets are finite. Indeed the maps are proper; on
   a component mapping nontrivially to the curve P1 their critical image is a proper analytic
   subset of that curve. Zero-dimensional deeper strata contribute only finitely many further
   values.

4. Thus, over B ◦ , the closed double-branch spaces form proper smooth families of compact curves.
   The connected components of their fibres form finite covering spaces of B ◦ : this follows either
   from proper submersion trivializations, or from their finite Stein factorizations. Removing
   the finitely many triple points from one connected smooth curve leaves it connected. Branch
   orderings, central multiplicities, and these connected fibre components therefore constitute
   finite discrete data over B ◦ .

5. The local angular circles, including multiplicities. At a point of an open double-branch stratum,
   the submersion condition for h gives coordinates in which q = h is a tangential coordinate and

                                        r = xa y b ,     a, b > 0.                          (22.79)

  A holomorphic unit has been absorbed in one coordinate on this small chart. Put d = gcd(a, b).
  Each connected component of the local nonzero fibre has the primitive angular circle

                           θ 7−→ x0 ei(b/d)θ , y0 e−i(a/d)θ ,        0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π,            (22.80)
                                                           


  where xa0 y0b = r. There are at most d choices of the connected monomial-fibre component.
  Interchanging the ordered branches can reverse the circle’s orientation. These are only finite
  choices.

6. Move the chosen base point along a path in the same open double-curve fibre. Local product
   charts and the normal line bundles transport the annular circle continuously. Changes of
   normal frame rotate its parameter and do not add a tangential one-cycle. Equivalently, this is
   the fibre circle of the normal circle bundle along that path. If a based loop is used, changing
   the path changes it by conjugation, which does not affect its class in H1 . Consequently, for
   fixed small nonzero r and fixed q, each of the finitely many branch-component data determines
   only finitely many homology classes, including signs.

7. The same local formula proves monodromy invariance in the r direction. Continuing around
   r = 0 permutes the finitely many connected components of xa y b = r; after a positive power it

 22.17    The radial-loop class of every global cap
Proposition 22.56 (Vanishing of the normalized radial-loop defect). [tag 0312]
    Suppose a proper complex-analytic filling of a finite parameter cover of the six-sphere family
exists. Make the modifications in 22.55 and delete its finite exceptional set from the marked base.
Use the ordinary local origins of 22.41 as reference. There is a well-defined normalized radial-loop
defect of a local extending cap section,

                                         λ ∈ V := Λ ⊗ Q /Qδ.                                     (22.86)
                                                            
                                                          b

It is independent of the section, of the finite parameter root needed to obtain that section, and
of the modifications used. It patches to a flat section of the local system V over the remaining
ordinary base, and this section is zero.
     In particular, let t be the trace of an extending finite multisection of degree d, and let o be the
reference ordinary origin. The radial-loop defect of t − do in V is zero. The same holds for an
origin obtained from multiplied such traces by bounded logarithmic differences along r = 0.

 Proof. 1. Use the smooth marked model of Theorem 18.3 and remove the finitely many base
   values which are images of vertical central components or critical values of the maps on the
   central branch strata. Every central component above the remaining ordinary base dominates
   the original P1 . Its positive normal meridian has zero lattice class in Λ/Zδb by Theorem 18.5.

    K = t4 /(t − 1)3 and v = log r/(2πi). The parameter descent of Theorem 18.1 is H = −k,

    Proposition 22.41. On an overlap, k changes by an integer, and the resulting radial label is an
    integral multiple of δ.
                         b The finite-root cancellation and the cusp comparison in that proposition
    have the same property. Thus the splitting used in Theorem 18.5 computes precisely the
    radial-loop defect relative to the stated ordinary origins.

 3. For completeness, the connecting map is the endpoint period of a continued additive lift. With
    Tr = I − mE, E = δb ⊗ γ and E 2 = 0, changing the lift adds (Tr − I)Λ ⊂ Zδ, b so its image νr
    in V is well defined. Under r = Re its label changes by

Remark 22.57 (A zero loop class with a nonextending translation). [tag PT07] In Proposi-
tion 22.53, the additive lift of the translation is h(t) = 1/t. It is single-valued on the punctured
disc, so its radial deck difference and loop class are zero. Its translated zero section has the
two distinct central limits computed there, and hence the translation has no meromorphic
extension. The loop class and the affine comparison are related by the endpoint-period map used
in Proposition 22.56; this example has zero image under that map.



23     Other logarithmic transformations and finite covers
23.1    Comparison under logarithmic transformation
Proposition 23.1 (The relative cohomology comparison). [tag 01S3]
    Fix the period family and cusp filling. Let X ′ be obtained by any admissible translation twists
and multiplicities m1 = 3k, m2 = 4l, where k, l are positive integers. Write D′ = W + S1′ + S2′
and
                                 E ′ = Ω1X ′ (log D′ )/f ′∗ Ω1B (log Σ).
The identity on the common smooth family induces isomorphisms on B

                    Rq f∗ OX ≃ Rq f∗′ OX ′ ,      Rq f∗ E ≃ Rq f∗′ E ′   (0 ≤ q ≤ 2).

These isomorphisms identify the logarithmic connecting maps κq . They also hold when the cusp
collar is changed by an admissible translation.

Proof. 1. We construct the comparison at every point. Over B \ Σ the two families are identified,
  and a translation acts trivially on H q (F, OF ) and H q (F, Ω1F ) for a complex torus F . For the

                                                   255
   second assertion, translation fixes the invariant holomorphic one-forms, and the first follows
   either from invariant Dolbeault forms or the exterior algebra H • (F, OF ) = • H 1 (F, OF ).
                                                                                 V

   These are statements about the induced maps on cohomology, including their holomorphic
   variation.

2. At a point with original order d = 3 or 4, let fe : T → ∆z be the smooth proper torus model
   with coarse coordinate q = z d . The new model is its pullback by z = se , where m = de,
   followed by the free cyclic quotient of order m. Smooth proper base change identifies the
   higher direct images upstairs with the pullbacks of those for T . The relative logarithmic
   cotangent bundle upstairs is precisely Ω1T /∆z pulled back: the base logarithmic direction is
   killed in the quotient defining E ′ . The derivative of a translation contributes only a multiple
   of ds; it consequently acts on this quotient as ordinary translation on relative forms.

3. Average over the cyclic action and choose holomorphic eigenframes. If a frame for H q (O)
   or H q (Ω1 ) has character ζd−a , 0 ≤ a < d, its original invariant extension is z a O∆q . On the
   order-m cover its character is ζm  −ea , and its invariant extension is sea O
                                                                                 ∆q = z O∆q . Taking
                                                                                       a

   invariants is exact in characteristic zero; hence the map s v 7→ z v, with z = se , identifies
                                                                  ea       a

   the extensions inside the common punctured-disc bundle. A translation twist induces the
   identity on the cohomology just used and changes none of these lattices. This proves the
   comparison at both finite points, including the full nonreduced fibres.

4. At the cusp the relative logarithmic forms have the global toric frame d log x1 , d log x2 , modulo
   d log q. A toric gluing has the form xi 7→ ci (q)q bi xi and therefore changes d log xi by (qc′i /ci +
   bi )d log q. It induces the identity on the relative logarithmic quotient. The structure-sheaf
   comparison is also the identity on the normalization cochain complex. This verifies the cusp
   extension and the assertion about translated collars.

5. The logarithmic cotangent exact sequences are isomorphic on the smooth base, so their
   connecting maps agree there under these comparisons. Their source and target sheaves are
   locally free by the local calculations in cited result 12.4 and proposition 12.6 and the eigenframe
   calculation above. A holomorphic map between vector bundles on a reduced curve which is
   zero on a dense open set is zero everywhere. Thus the connecting maps agree globally.



Proposition 23.2 (All admissible twists have the same Hodge numbers). [tag 01S4]
    For every family in 23.1 whose cusp is the one-component hexagonal filling, the direct images
of the absolute cotangent sheaves are

|12l0 − 4l1 − 3l2 | = 1 has the Hodge diamond of proposition 12.15.

Proof. 1. 23.1 identifies the logarithmic direct images and their connecting maps. By propo-
  sitions 12.10 and 12.13, the cokernel of κ0 is Cp1 ⊕ Cp2 , and κ1 is surjective with kernel
  O ⊕ O(−1)2 . These statements therefore hold for X ′ . The residue sheaf of its normalized

                  R0 f∗′ OD
                          e ′ = Cp 0 ⊕ Cp 1 ⊕ Cp 2 ,     R1 f∗′ OD
                                                                 e ′ = Cp 1 ⊕ Cp 2 ,   R2 = 0.

   Indeed the finite reductions are bielliptic, and the cusp normalization is rational. The base
   logarithmic residue is evaluation with weights (1, m1 , m2 ); its kernel is O(1)(−Σ) = O(−2).

   On H 1 the residue of the invariant class γ 0,1 is mj γ 0,1 |Sj′ ̸= 0. The other eigenline has zero
   residue. The local rank-one image of κ0 is its kernel, as follows either from the residue diagram
   of proposition 12.14 or from the eigenframe calculation in 23.1. Thus the two finite skyscrapers
   cancel exactly. This proves the first row, with no surviving torsion.
2. The proper flat map is Gorenstein of relative dimension two. Relative duality for F = Ω1X ′ ,
   using F ∗ ⊗ ωX ′ /B = Ω2X ′ ⊗ f ′∗ O(2), gives the second row because all sheaves in the first row
   are locally free. Coherent Leray on P1 gives every Hodge number. In particular hp,0 = 0 for
   p > 0 follows from these direct images and duality, as the degree-zero entries and their duals
   show.

Proof. 1. The cited proposition supplies exactly the free cyclic quotients used in 23.1; its Theorem

Proposition 23.7 (Connected cyclic covers and the cusp comparison). [tag 01S7]
    For an admissible (3, 4) member with n = |12l0 − 4l1 − 3l2 | > 1, let π : Y → X be the universal
cover and g = f π. It is a finite étale holomorphic map of degree n. Every fibre of g is connected;
its finite reductions are bielliptic, its multiplicities are 3, 4, and its cusp Wn normalizes to a
disjoint union of n copies of dP6 . For EX of Definition 12.3 and the identical quotient EY on Y ,
pullback induces isomorphisms
                            Rq f∗ OX ≃ Rq g∗ OY ,           Rq f∗ EX ≃ Rq g∗ EY .
Proof. 1. We first derive the fundamental-group presentation from the fillings. The smooth
  family over the punctured base has zero section, so its fundamental group is Λ ⋊ ⟨x, y⟩, where
  x, y are the analytic peripheral generators fixed by the root-deck convention and act by
  A1 , A2 . On a finite filling the lifted affine generator has mj th power translation by vj : its mj
  translations add to vj because Aj vj = vj . Thus filling the normal disc imposes x3 = tv1 and
  y 4 = tv2 , with the signs fixed by the clockwise convention on the first page.
2. The toric covering space of the cusp tube is simply connected. Indeed its dense torus has
   cocharacter lattice Z3 ; a loop may be perturbed into that torus, and the normal discs of the
   three rays (0, 1), (e1 , 1), (e2 , 1) kill a basis of this lattice. This argument applies also to the
   infinite fan, since a compact loop and a homotopy meet only finitely many of its locally finite
   charts. The same conclusion holds for the small tube: if a loop in |tc | < ϵ bounds a disc in
   the toric space, the torus action (x1 , x2 , tc ) 7→ (x1 , x2 , atc ) for a sufficiently small positive a
   moves that compact disc into the tube, and the scaling homotopy of its boundary stays in
   the tube. The cusp quotient therefore has fundamental group Λ/Λtor , and its toric meridian
   bounds the normal disc at fixed x1 , x2 . A translated collar makes this meridian tµ y −1 x−1 ,
   where γ(µ) = l0 . Van Kampen consequently kills Λtor and imposes xy = tµ .

                                                     259
3. The normal closure of Λtor in the fibre lattice is ker γ: it contains ŵ, δ̂ and A1 ŵ + ŵ = û,
   and all these relations lie in ker γ. The remaining generator c, the image of γ̂, is central
   because γAj = γ. The presentation is thus ⟨c, x, y | c central, xy = cl0 , x3 = cl1 , y 4 = cl2 ⟩.
   Eliminating y makes it abelian, with relation matrix
                                                 !
                                      3    −l1
                                                 ,       det = −p.
                                      4 l2 − 4l0
   Its first Smith divisor is one because its entries include three and four; hence the group is
   Z/|p|. After imposing c = 1 the quotient has x3 = x4 = 1, so it is trivial. Thus the image of
   the regular-fibre lattice, containing c, generates the entire group Z/n. The same is true of
   each reduced special fibre. At a finite point the cyclic model is a smooth torus family over
   a disc, with a free affine finite-group action. An equivariant smooth trivialization, obtained
   by averaging a horizontal connection, contracts the disc to its centre and descends to a
   deformation retraction of the local total space onto Sj . Thus the image of the regular-fibre
   lattice in the local fundamental group is contained in the image of π1 (Sj ); the same holds
   after mapping to π1 (X). At the cusp γ̂ survives in Λ/Λtor . The explicit normal-crossing
   contraction of the tube onto W in Lemma 23.6 identifies their fundamental groups, so the
   same generator is in the image of π1 (W ). The covering-space criterion therefore makes the
   inverse image of every fibre connected. Admissibility gives 3 ∤ l1 and odd l2 , so gcd(n, 12) = 1.
   The étale cover preserves fibre multiplicities. On a finite reduction it cannot kill the nontrivial
   order-3 or order-4 linear holonomy, since the covering degree is prime to it; the resulting finite
   torus quotient is again bielliptic.
4. Normalization commutes with the finite étale base change Y → X. The pullback of the simply
   connected normalization dP6 is its trivial degree-n cover. The double curves and triple points
   also pull back étale, and their incidence maps are the lifts of the original incidence maps. The
   lifted incidence maps therefore make the dual complex a degree-n covering of the original
   real two-torus. It is connected because Wn is connected. The normalization resolution for
   OWn has acyclic components, double curves and point strata. Its global cochain complex is
   consequently the cellular cochain complex of this dual torus, with n, 3n, 2n cells. Thus its
   coherent cohomology is (1, 2, 1), and pullback from W is an isomorphism over C: on a finite
   cover of real tori it is induced by a full-rank map of their integral first cohomology lattices.
5. Modulo d log q, the two toric forms d log xi are invariant under all cusp gluings as computed in
   23.1. Hence EX |W = OW  2 and E |
                                    Y Wn = OWn , and the same pullback argument applies to their
                                              2

   cohomology. Over a regular fibre, an isogeny of complex tori induces isomorphisms on H q (O)
   and H q (Ω1 ) over C. At a finite fibre, make the cyclic base change. The map is an isogeny of
   the smooth torus families and induces isomorphisms of their cohomology bundles. Taking
   the same cyclic invariant eigenspaces descends these isomorphisms, including all nilpotent
   layers of the scheme fibre. Grauert base change at the cusp, and this explicit calculation at
   the finite points, prove the asserted bundle maps are isomorphisms on all of B.

23.4    CM and torsion
Cited result 23.10 (The CM torsion fibres). [tag 000U]
   There is no t ∈ C \ {0, 1} for which Et has complex multiplication and Pt is torsion. On the
smooth models at t = 0, 1 after base change of orders 3, 4, respectively, the limiting points have
orders 3, 2. Thus these are the only CM torsion points on the completed family.

Proof. Theorem 4.15(a) of (Bourdon et al., 2017, arXiv v3, p. 23) applies to an elliptic curve
with CM by any imaginary quadratic order over F = Q(j(E)). Its torsion group is one of
0, Z/2, Z/3, Z/4, Z/6, (Z/2)2 . Here F = Q(t) because j = 1728t, and the equation and section of
definition 2.6 are defined over F . On the smooth base, ψ2 (P ) and ψ3 (P ) are nonzero. Thus only
orders four and six remain.
    The order-four value has j = 55296/5. The order-six values have irreducible monic polynomial
                                        10395648    24461180928
                               X2 −              X+             .
                                           11           11

                                                 263
None is an algebraic integer. The integrality of singular moduli for every imaginary quadratic
order (Sutherland, 2023, Theorem 20.12 and Corollary 20.13, Lecture 20, p. 6) therefore excludes
CM in all these cases.
   At zero, the changes t = s3 , x = s4 X, y = s6 Y give

                  Y 2 = X 3 − 34 s(s3 − 1)X + 41 (s3 − 1)2 ,             Ps = (0, (s3 − 1)/2).

The central equation is Y 2 = X 3 + 1/4, and the limiting point (0, −1/2) has order three by its
horizontal tangent. At one, t = 1 + s4 , x = s2 X, y = s3 Y give

                Y 2 = X 3 − 34 (1 + s4 )3 X + 14 (1 + s4 )4 s2 ,         Ps = (0, (1 + s4 )2 s/2).

The central equation is Y 2 = X 3 −3X/4, and (0, 0) has exact order two. Both central discriminants
are nonzero. Their CM orders are Z[ρ] and Z[i], and their norm values are those of proposition 4.3.

Proof. 1. Apply the analytic maximum theorem 6.6 at every embedding and substitute into

3. Theorem 1.1 of DeMarco and Mavraki (2020, arXiv v2, p. 2) applies with K = Q, B = P1 ,
   the displayed elliptic surface and rational section, since the generic height is positive. It
   equips this divisor with continuous adelic semipositive metrics whose associated height is
   exactly hb O (Pt ). Comparing with the usual height for (∞)/12 gives the bounded difference.
   This is the specialization here of the variation theorem of Tate, with the local refinements of

                                                    267
   Silverman reproduced in DeMarco and Mavraki (2020, Theorems 2.2–2.3, arXiv v2, pp. 7–8):
   outside finitely many places the local correction is zero, and at each remaining place it extends
   continuously after subtracting its prescribed logarithmic singularity. Our inequality is an
   explicit archimedean estimate with constant 12 log 2.

4. The same generic coefficient appears in (Call and Silverman, 1993, Theorem 4.1 and the
   following remark, pp. 183–184): for T = P1 and [2]∗ (O) ∼ 4(O), the specialization ratio tends
   to 1/12. The bounded remainder used here is the adelic-height conclusion applied in the
   preceding step.

24.1    Ranks, saturation, and central derivatives
Remark 24.8 (The real period and diagonal height pairing). [tag IA26] Write Ei for the eleven
minimal models in proposition 24.4. The full real period and the height relative to (O) are
those of definition 2.6. Pullback of the normalized Poincaré bundle along the diagonal gives
[2]∗ O(O) ⊗ O(O)−2 ≃ O(2O). Consequently the diagonal Néron–Tate pairing used in the
leading-term formula is 2hbO.

7. The exact root numbers are +1 for i = 1, 8 and −1 otherwise. All points are nontorsion by
   cited result 23.10. For a CM curve, the Coates–Wiles theorem, in the form Rubin (1999,
   Theorem 10.1, p. 47), says that a nonzero central Hecke L-value forces the Mordell–Weil
   group over the CM field to be finite. Rubin (1999, Proposition 5.3, p. 15) supplies, for
   a nonmaximal CM order, an isogenous curve with maximal order: the quotient is by the
   Galois-stable subgroup attached to the conductor ideal. The isogeny induces an isomorphism
   on Mordell–Weil groups tensored with Q and on their rational Tate modules, preserving ranks
   and local L-factors. Since L(E/K, s) = L(E/Q, s)2 for the CM field K, nontorsion therefore
   forces L(E, 1) = 0. This proves the needed central vanishing also in the two sign-+1 cases.
   The functional equation then forces L′ (E, 1) = 0 for those two curves. The positive first or
   second derivatives just evaluated prove exactly the asserted analytic ranks.

Proof. 1. Gross–Zagier’s theorem applies because each curve is modular and L(Ei , 1) = 0. CM
  modularity follows from its Hecke-character theta series. Their Theorem I.7.3 (Gross and
  Zagier, 1986, Chapter I, Theorem 7.3, preprint p. 12) gives a rational point R and a nonzero
  rational factor relating L′ (E, 1) to its canonical height times the real period. The differentials
  in the two conventions are rational multiples: write ω ′ = aωE with a ∈ Q∗ . A primitive real
  period for ω ′ is |a|Ωi /nR , where nR ∈ {1, 2} is the number of real components. Thus the
  change to the full real period multiplies the rational factor by |a|/nR . As L′ (Ei , 1) > 0, R has
  infinite order. Primitivity gives R = mPi + T , m ̸= 0, T torsion; its height is m2 h(P b i ). This
  proves (24.9), including positivity.

Remark 24.15 (Ordinary CM leading-term theorems). [tag IA05]
    The applicable ordinary CM results concern a prime p at which E has good ordinary reduction,
equivalently p splits in the CM field. One formulation of Rubin’s rank-one formula is Bertolini
et al. (2012, Theorem 1, p. 262): for a curve over Q with CM by the maximal order, an ordinary
prime prime to the conductor, and a simple central zero, an appropriate Katz p-adic L-value
is, up to a nonzero algebraic factor, the square of a formal logarithm of a nontorsion rational
point divided by a p-adic period. The analytic-rank-one input holds by proposition 24.11. The
formal logarithm, Katz value and period in this formula are the p-adic quantities specified in
that theorem.
    For the p-part of the real leading-term formula, a modern precise version is Castella (2025,
Theorem A, p. 2 of the author version). In addition to analytic rank one it requires full CM,
abelian torsion field over the CM field, p ∤ 6hK , splitting of p, conductor prime to p, and that
the different of K divide the Hecke conductor exactly. For the maximal odd-discriminant cases
here, the latter follows from the exponent two of the ramified prime in the rational conductor.
The nonmaximal cases of discriminant −12 and −28 can be passed through a 2-isogeny at
p > 3. The discriminant −16 case requires care: the direct application of this version has a
different-conductor hypothesis at 2 that fails, so this formulation does not apply directly to that
case.
                                        √
    For the last curve, 3 is inert in Q( −163) and is excluded by the stated p > 3 hypotheses.
The exact analytic quotient Q11 = 9 is proved in proposition 24.16; the remaining group-order
question is recorded in section D.

Proposition 24.25 (Torsion equidistribution). [tag 001K]
   Let Dn be the divisor, with intersection multiplicity, of parameters t ∈ P1 \ {0, 1, ∞} for which
nPt = O. Then
                      n2                1                              1
           deg Dn =      + O(1),           [Dn ] −→ mP ,                   [Dn ] −→ 12mP
                      12                n2                          deg Dn
weakly as n → ∞ through indices for which Dn ̸= 0. For any nonrepeating sequence of individual
algebraic torsion parameters, their Galois-orbit probability measures likewise converge to 12mP .
The factor 12 normalizes the mass to one.

                                                   285
Proof. 1. We apply DeMarco and Mavraki (2020, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2, arXiv v2, p. 2).
  Their hypotheses are a number field, a smooth projective base curve, an elliptic surface and
  a rational section of nonzero generic canonical height. Here they are Q, P1 , the displayed
  rational elliptic surface, and P , whose generic height for (O) is 1/12 by 24.6. At a torsion
  specialization the canonical height is zero. Corollary 1.2 consequently gives convergence of
  every nonrepeating sequence of Galois-orbit probability measures.

2. The limiting measure is the curvature of the height metric divided by the degree of its line
   bundle. In our normalization, 24.24 computes the curvature as mP , and 24.6 computes that
   degree as 1/12. Hence the probability measure is 12mP . The total mass is one because
   12 P1 mP = 1.
     R


3. The surface height formula, with our half-self-pairing convention, reads

                            b O (Q) = χ(OE ) + (Q · O) −   1X
                            h                                  contrv (Q).
                                                           2 v

   Here χ = 1, and the finitely many fibre corrections are bounded as Q = nP varies, because they
   depend only on its component. Since h  b O (nP ) = n2 /12, it follows that (nP · O) = n2 /12 + O(1).
   Removing the singular fibres changes this by O(1): the local intersection at each such fibre is
   bounded as n varies in characteristic zero. One can see this in the formal group after a fixed
   multiple enters it; multiplication by a nonzero integer is a local analytic isomorphism over the
   residue field C. Thus deg Dn = n2 /12 + O(1).

4. At any fixed smooth torsion parameter t0 , of exact order d, the multiplicity in Dn is zero
   unless d | n, and is constant when d | n. Indeed the formal parameter of nP = [n/d](dP ) has
   first term (n/d) times that of dP , with nonzero constant coefficient. Fix a continuous test
   function and ε > 0. Corollary 1.2 implies that all but finitely many distinct Galois orbits of
   torsion parameters have average within ε of the limiting integral; otherwise a countersequence
   would violate it. The total weighted contribution of the finitely many exceptional orbits
   is bounded independently of n, by the multiplicity observation. Divide by deg Dn and let
   n → ∞. This proves the probability convergence for Dn , and the degree asymptotic proves
   the unnormalized version.

Proposition 25.6 (The critical points and global level curves). [tag 001P]
   For every zero µ of ℘τ , the zero sets of the two critical factors are exactly
                                       W =0       ⇐⇒      τ ∈ SL2 (Z){i, ρ},
                         3W ℘′τ (µ) − 2g2 = 0     ⇐⇒      τ ∈ SL2 (Z)ρ.
On the coarse t-plane the function L has no critical point away from t = 1. The point t = 0
             √ C point, with Lt (0) = 7/384. The point t = 1 is the unique global maximum,
is a noncritical    1

of value log 2, and has the fractional-power local maximum described in proposition 5.3. In
particular there is no saddle in 0 < t < 1. On the root charts, h = 0 over t = 1 is a nondegenerate
maximum, while δ = 0 over t = 0 is a degenerate critical point with nonzero harmonic cubic
leading term and three alternating ascending and descending sectors. These are all critical points
on the root charts.
                                                                                        √
    For every angle√  θ, r 7 → L(1  +  reiθ ) is strictly decreasing for r > 0, from log 2 to −∞.

For each c < log 2, the level set {L = c} is one Jordan curve, strictly star-shaped about 1.
Its bounded complement is {L > c}; its unbounded complement is {L < c}. The curve is real
analytic except possibly at t = 0 when c = 14 log 3, where it is C 1 with nonzero tangent. The
closed superlevel sets form nested topological discs. At the maximum the level set is the single
point 1, and above it the level set is empty. The corresponding statements for Dpart follow by its
increasing affine change from L.

Proof. 1. Take a representative in the closed
                                            √ standard modular fundamental region. If T ≥ 7/5,
  25.4 applies. Otherwise |ℜτ | ≤ 1/2 and 3/2 ≤ T ≤ 7/5. For fixed ℜτ , the function
                                                (ℜτ )2 + (T − 1)2
                                       |χ|2 =
                                                (ℜτ )2 + (T + 1)2
   has its maximum on this interval at an endpoint and increases with (ℜτ )2 . The two endpoint
   bounds are r02 and 41/601 < r02 . Thus 25.5 covers the entire remaining region. We conclude
   |1 − X| < 1 for every t ̸= 1. Equations (25.2) now prove strict radial monotonicity, including
   t = 0 by continuity. They also exclude both critical equations W = 0 and 3W p − 2g2 = 0
   on the ordinary base. The elliptic points must be checked on their root charts: at ρ, the
   nonzero coarse derivative already given rules out a critical point; at i, W = p = 0 but
   3W p − 2g2 = −2g2 ̸= 0, and proposition 5.3 gives the strict maximum. At ρ, W = g2 = 0 and
   p ̸= 0, so both displayed factors vanish. This proves their exact zero sets, including the elliptic
   orbits. In particular the vanishing of both factors at ρ in the τ coordinate is a ramification
   effect, not a saddle on the coarse base. More explicitly, on the root chart at ρ,
                                              7

26     Arithmetic periods and compact subgroups
Definition 26.1 (Algebraic period coordinates). [tag IA10] Use an algebraic Weierstrass equation
and invariant differential as in definition 2.6. Write Λ = Zω1 + Zω2 with ℑ(ω2 /ω1 ) > 0,
ζ(z + ωj ) = ζ(z) + ηj , and extend η : Λ → C real-linearly. The discriminant is that of the
equation in this differential. For a homothety Λ 7→ cΛ, u 7→ cu,

              σcΛ (cu) = cσΛ (u),       ηcΛ (cu) = c−1 ηΛ (u),        ∆(cΛ) = c−12 ∆(Λ).

These formulas cancel the factors in (26.2), so N has the same value in the transported coordinates.

Proposition 26.2 (The sigma expression and third-kind period). [tag 0017]
   Let P ∈ E(Q), with P ̸= O and 2P ̸= O, and let u be an elliptic logarithm of P . Then
                       1
      2 log N (P ) =     log |∆| + ℜ{Λ1 + u(ζ(u) − η(u))},       Λ1 = 2 log σ(u) − uζ(u).    (26.1)
                       6
For a fixed elliptic logarithm u, changing the branch of log σ(u) changes the expression inside
the real part by an integer multiple of 4πi. Put B(u) = Λ1 + u(ζ(u) − η(u)). Under a lattice
translation,

           B(u + ω) − B(u) ≡ uη(ω) − ωη(u) + 2 log χ(ω)          (mod 4πiZ),        ω ∈ Λ,

where χ(ω) ∈ {1, −1} is the sigma semicharacter. This difference is purely imaginary, so the
displayed real part is independent of both choices. There is an extension GP of E by Gm ,
defined over Q and corresponding, under the principal polarization, to P , for which Λ1 , modulo
a logarithm of an algebraic number, is the negative of a relative period of [Z → GP ]. Changing
the third-kind differential while retaining its simple poles and residues adds an algebraic multiple
of u. Adding an exact algebraic differential to a relative-integral representative adds algebraic
endpoint differences when both endpoints are regular.

Proof. 1. The sigma–theta product, or its divisor and automorphy law together with its derivative
  at zero, gives
                                                          1
                                                                  
                           N (P ) = |∆|1/12 |σ(u)| exp − ℜ(uη(u)) .                        (26.2)
                                                          2
                                                                           2
  To check the constant, for Λ = Z + τ Z one uses σ(z) = eη1 z /2 ϑ1 (z, τ )/(2πη(τ )3 ), ∆ =
  (2π)12 η(τ )24 , and η(z) = η1 z − 2πiℑz/T . Substitution gives exactly the defining Gaussian
  in N . Homogeneity gives the general lattice formula. Taking logarithms proves (26.1). The
  automorphy law σ(u + ω) = χ(ω)eη(ω)(u+ω/2) σ(u) and real-linearity of η give the stated lift
  transport. Explicitly, writing u = aω1 + bω2 with a, b ∈ R and ω = mω1 + nω2 with m, n ∈ Z,
  Legendre’s relation gives uη(ω) − ωη(u) = 2πi(bm − an). This also proves that the transported
  difference is purely imaginary.

2. We make the period identification explicit. Put

   OE ((−P ) − (O)); this fixes the sign of the extension class. The apparent 0/0 at z = u has a

26.1    Motivic groups from the point and extension data
Remark 26.4 (The motivic dimension formula). [tag IA11] Bertolin et al. (2022, Construction 3.4,
p. 12, and Lemma 3.5, p. 13, arXiv v2) compute the motivic group from its abelian point and
extension data and the central Weil-pairing bracket. For the 1-motives used here, let B be the
smallest abelian subvariety generated by these data, and let Z(1) be the central torus obtained
from that bracket and the remaining algebraic lift. Their dimension formula is

                      dim Gmot (M ) = dim Gmot (A) + 2 dim B + dim Z(1).                    (26.6)

The bracket is described in their Section 6.1, pp. 26–27, and their corrected Table 2, p. 29, with
the correction on p. 28, gives unipotent dimension three in the dependent nondeficient case.

Proposition 26.5 (The motivic groups of the diagonal data). [tag 001C]
    Let P be nontorsion and let R be any algebraic lift above P in GP . Put MR = [Z → GP ],
1 7→ R. Its connected motivic group is, after a choice of Levi subgroup, the semidirect product
of Gmot (E) and the three-dimensional Heisenberg group attached to H1 (E) and its principal
polarization. Its dimension is 5 for CM and 7 without CM.
    For a non-real embedding put M = MR ⊕ MR . If E and Ē are not isogenous, its dimension
is 13. If they are isogenous, choose an isogeny ϕ : Ē → E of degree d and write Q = ϕ(P̄ ). Let r
be the dimension over F = End(E) ⊗ Q of the span of P, Q, modulo torsion. Then

                              case     dim B dim Z          dim Gmot (M)
                         r = 2, E CM     2     2                  8
                       r = 2, E not CM   2     2                  10
                         r = 1, E CM     1   1+e                5+e
                       r = 1, E not CM   1   1+e                7 + e.

Here e is either zero or one: it is zero precisely when the algebraic lift in the one-dimensional
quotient of the two central tori by the bracket torus is torsion. This criterion is independent of
the choices made modulo isogeny. In the real case we use the single motive MR .

Proof. 1. All curves, polarizations, points, and lifts are algebraic over Q, as required by Con-
  struction 3.4 and Lemma 3.5. For MR the smallest abelian subvariety containing (P, P ) is the
  diagonal B = E, since P is nontorsion. If ψ is the polarization pairing, the bracket on this
  diagonal is
                           [(x, x), (y, y)] = ψ(x, y) − ψ(y, x) = 2ψ(x, y).
   It is nonzero and spans Q(1). Hence Z ′ = Z = Gm . The pure group is GL2 without CM and
   ResF/Q Gm for the imaginary quadratic CM field. Their dimensions are four and two. This
   proves the single-motive assertion, including its Lie bracket and Levi action: the action on
   the centre is the polarization multiplier.




                                               296
2. For the direct sum only the two diagonal central coordinates occur. If the two elliptic curves
   are not isogenous, they cannot be CM conjugates. The pure group is {(g1 , g2 ) ∈ GL22 :
   det g1 = det g2 }, of dimension seven. The point data generate E × Ē, and the two brackets
   are independent, giving 7 + 4 + 2 = 13.

3. If the curves are isogenous, transport the second polarized factor through ϕ. Its polarization
   pairing becomes ψ/d. The smallest abelian subvariety has dimension r. For r = 2, independent
   variation in its two factors makes the two diagonal brackets span both central coordinates;
   thus Z ′ = Z = G2m . The unipotent group is the product of two Heisenberg groups, with the
   same pure group acting on both standard factors. For r = 1, after multiplying the points by a
   common integer we may write Q = aP , a ∈ F × . The bracket image is the one-dimensional
   line with proportional central coordinates

   where † is the Rosati involution. On an elliptic curve aa† is a positive rational number: a
   square in the non-CM case and the positive field norm in the CM case. Construction 3.4(3)

Proposition 26.8 (The CM multiplication law). [tag 001F]
   Let E/Q have complex multiplication by an order O, and use an algebraic invariant differential.

                                   θ(αz)2 = Fα (expE z)θ(z)2d .                              (26.10)

Its divisor and leading Laurent coefficient are

              div(Fα ) = 2[α]∗ (O) − 2d(O),         Fα (expE z) = α2 z 2−2d (1 + O(z 2 )).

Proof. 1. The Legendre relation gives the displayed real-linear decomposition of η. The sigma
  automorphy formula gives
                                             π ω̄

                   θ(z + ω) = ϵ(ω) exp            (z + ω/2) θ(z),      ϵ(ω) ∈ {1, −1}.

   For αΛ ⊂ Λ, the exponential multipliers of θ(αz)/θ(z)d cancel because αᾱ = d. Its remaining
   multiplier is a sign. Squaring therefore gives a meromorphic function on E, with the stated
   divisor. This divisor is defined over Q. The existence of a rational function with this divisor
   over C implies its existence over Q: the relevant one-dimensional Riemann–Roch space is
   obtained by extension of scalars. Normalize its leading Laurent coefficient, in the formal
   parameter of the algebraic differential, to α2 . This identifies it with the squared analytic
   quotient. The action of α on this differential is algebraic, so α2 is an allowed normalization.

2. Choose a nonreal α ∈ O. Since the normalized sigma series is σ(z) = z + O(z 5 ) with algebraic
   Laurent coefficients, the next coefficient of the squared quotient is

                                α2 z 2−2d {1 − s2 (α2 − d)z 2 + O(z 4 )}.

   the chosen field. At nontorsion u, none of the arguments αu is a lattice point; evaluating the
   identity proves the algebraicity implication. The injective map O → C, α 7→ αu, proves the
   rank assertion.

3. The qualification about rationality is necessary. For a square lattice, s2 = 0 and α = 1 + i give
   F1+i = 2i℘. The unsquared quotient has a simple zero at the nonzero point in ker(1 + i) and
   a simple pole at O, which is not a principal divisor on E; its square is the rational function
   just displayed.

26.3      Ordinary nonarchimedean heights
Cited result 26.12 (Nonzero ordinary heights). [tag 001H]
     Let E/Q have complex multiplication by the full ring of integers of an imaginary quadratic
field K of class number one. Assume that its functional-equation sign is −1, and let p > 3 be a
prime of good ordinary reduction, pOK = pp∗ . For a nontorsion P ∈ E(Q) the p-adic height and
the cyclotomic p-adic height of P over K, in the normalization of Agboola and Howard (2006,
Appendix A), are nonzero. In particular this applies to

                     E : y 2 + y = x3 − 38x + 90,       P = (0, 9),     p = 5.

Proof. Use Theorem A.1 and Lemma A.2 in Rubin’s appendix (Agboola and Howard, 2006,
Appendix A, p. 1043), with its standing CM, ordinary-prime and sign hypotheses. Theorem A.1,
attributed there to Bertrand, gives nonzero p-adic height for the nontorsion point over K. The
Galois-equivariance in (Mazur et al., 2006, Section 2.9, pp. 587–588; Remark 2.2, p. 588) makes
the anticyclotomic height of a rational point zero: complex conjugation fixes the point and acts by
−1 on that height space. Lemma A.2 says that vanishing of two of the cyclotomic, anticyclotomic
and p projections forces the third to vanish. Hence the cyclotomic height is nonzero.
    For the displayed curve, propositions 24.9 and 24.11 give nontorsion and analytic rank one,
hence sign −1. The CM order has discriminant −19 and is maximal. Its reduced positive binary
forms have the single class (1, 1, 5), so the class number is one. The minimal discriminant is −193 .
There are seven points over F5 , so a5 = −1, proving good ordinary reduction. Equivalently, −19
is a nonzero square modulo 5. These verify every stated hypothesis.

Remark 26.13 (The compact subgroup and the CM correction). [tag IA14]
    The complex holomorphic CM correction is θ of proposition 26.8; its exact relation to the real
norm includes exp(−π|u|2 /(2A)) as in (26.11). The height in cited result 26.12 has the ordinary
nonarchimedean normalization specified in its cited appendix.
    Bertrand (1995, Theorem 2.1, p. 147) constructs nontrivial multiplicative extensions with
nontorsion algebraic points in their maximal real compact subgroup. Its data include a Rosati-
antisymmetric endomorphism and a related nontorsion point over a real number field. For the
diagonal class here, N P = f (P ) with N > 0 and f + f † = 0 forces torsion: the endomorphism
N − f is an isogeny because (N − f )† (N − f ) = N 2 − f 2 is positive. The concrete antisymmetric
and diagonal extensions are compared by the maps in proposition 26.17. The vector-extension
statements (Bertrand, 1995, Theorem 3.1, p. 150) and (Bost and Künnemann, 2009, Theorem 3.1.2,
p. 386) use an algebraic connection, as described in remark 26.11.

Proof. 1. The torus is the maximal connected affine subgroup of Gq . Consequently every
  endomorphism of Gq induces multiplication by some n ∈ Z on Gm and an endomorphism α
  on E. Functoriality of extension classes gives
                                          α∗ q = nq    in E ∨ .                              (26.13)
   Here α∗ is the dual endomorphism. To make the convention explicit, choose a principal

   (α† − [n])Q0 = O. A nonzero endomorphism of an elliptic curve is an isogeny and has finite
   kernel. Since Q0 is nontorsion, α† = [n], hence α = [n] as well.
2. The difference between the given endomorphism and [n] has image in the torus and is trivial
   on the torus. It therefore factors through an algebraic-group homomorphism E → Gm .
   This homomorphism is zero, since a morphism from the proper connected curve E to the
   affine group Gm is constant and a group homomorphism preserves the identity. Thus the
   endomorphism is exactly [n]. Conversely all integer multiplications exist. This proves the first
   assertion.

   invariants and real u, ω1 make c real.
5. Suppose c were algebraic. Then ℓc would be an algebraic Lie subspace. Dividing the nonzero
   period ω1 (1, c) by a sufficiently large positive integer gives a vector in ℓc whose exponential
   is a nonzero torsion point of GQ , hence an algebraic point. The analytic subgroup theorem
   (Huber and Wüstholz, 2022, Theorem 6.1, arXiv v8, p. 43) supplies a positive-dimensional
   connected algebraic subgroup with Lie algebra contained in ℓc . Its dimension is one, and
   its projection to E is nontrivial. Such a subgroup must be an elliptic curve E ′ projecting
   isogenously to E: a connected one-dimensional affine algebraic group cannot map nontrivially
   to an elliptic curve. Its inclusion splits the pullback of GQ to E ′ . The dual of that isogeny
   would therefore kill the extension class λ(Q), forcing Q torsion. This contradicts 24.9. We
   conclude that c is transcendental. In particular the line is not defined over Q.

No proper connected algebraic subgroup of GQ projects onto E: as in the proof above, such a
subgroup would split the nontorsion extension after an isogeny. Every proper connected subgroup
is therefore contained in the torus, whereas expGQ f has nonconstant elliptic projection. Thus f
is GQ -nondegenerate in the subgroup condition (1.2) of Noguchi (2024, author preprint, p. 2).
Their Theorem 1.3 on the same page gives
                                                         Zar
                    dimC {(expGQ f (z), f (z)) : z ∈ C}        ≥ dim GQ + 1 = 3.

The graph is contained in GQ × ℓc , of dimension three, so equality holds. The graph therefore
has Zariski closure GQ × ℓc . This equality is the functional statement used here; the algebraicity
of the particular value RN = expGQ (u, cu) remains the question in section D.

The first torus coordinate of exp(Π− U ) is exactly the Gaussian exp(−πu2 /(2A)). The projector
is not the differential of an algebraic quasi-endomorphism. No sequence of rational polynomials
in B, even allowing inverses of isogenies, can converge to it as complex linear operators. At least

Proof. 1. Use the principal polarization to identify the two extension classes with Q and βQ.
  They are linearly independent over Q modulo torsion: any nonzero m + nβ is an isogeny,
  so (m + nβ)Q cannot be torsion. A character of G2m given by (m, n) ∈ Z2 extends to G
  exactly when the pushout extension has zero class, namely when mQ + nβQ = O. Hence the
  restriction of every homomorphism G → Gm to the torus is zero. Such a homomorphism then
  factors through E and is zero. This proves the asserted absence of characters. An isogenous
  semiabelian variety cannot acquire a nonzero character, because composing it with the isogeny
  would give a nonzero character of G.

2. The Rosati adjoint of β is −β. Pullback by β sends the ordered extension classes to (−βQ, dQ),
   exactly as does pushout by the displayed torus matrix. Equality of these extension classes
   provides the endomorphism B. It is unique because Hom(E, G2m ) = 0. Its square induces
   [−d] on the torus and on E, so the same uniqueness gives B 2 = [−d]. The map

                                End(G) ⊗ Q −→ End(E) ⊗ Q = Q(β)

   is injective: an endomorphism inducing zero on E has image in the torus, and the absence of
   characters makes it zero. Its image contains β, hence equals Q(β).

6. The two eigenspaces of dB have eigenvalues β and −β. Every algebraic quasi-endomorphism
   has differential a0 I + b0 dB for rational a0 , b0 , with eigenvalues a0 + b0 β and a0 − b0 β. The

   uniform obstruction to approximation. For arbitrary real a0 , b0 , put x = a0 + b0 β, so that its

                                                                1

   belong to the same endomorphism algebra and satisfy this bound.

7. Finally the image of Π− is the toric Lie line C(0, 1, β). It is not the Lie algebra of an algebraic
   subtorus: an algebraic one-dimensional subtorus of G2m has rational slope. Since u ̸= 0, the
   projected vector is nonzero. The analytic subgroup theorem in fact shows that its exponential
   cannot be an algebraic point of both torus coordinates. Indeed its nonzero logarithm lies in
   the algebraic line C(1, β), whereas a one-dimensional algebraic subtorus has a rational slope.
   The analytic subgroup theorem would put a positive-dimensional subtorus in that line for an
   algebraic exponential, contradicting these two slope computations.

Proof. 1. The real model and its algebraic differential give real sigma coefficients and a
  conjugation-stable lattice. In particular θ(z) = θ(z̄). The discriminant is −193 , so 26.2 gives
  the asserted diagonal identity. The sigma function and the exponential of the quadratic

                     θ(z + ω) = ϵ(ω)ekω̄(z+ω/2) θ(z),      ϵ(ω̄) = ϵ(ω) ∈ {1, −1}.

   exponent cancels the change of −kzw. This proves periodicity on all of C2 .

2. If αu + ω = 0, then [α]Q = O. Nontorsion of Q and the fact that a nonzero elliptic
   endomorphism is an isogeny imply α = 0, and then ω = 0. Thus the rank-two module Z[β]u
   and the rank-two period lattice are independent over Z. This proves the rank assertion.

3. For d = αᾱ, the squared CM law 26.8 gives the exact fixed-field identity

                              H(αu, ᾱu) = 191−d Fα (Q)Fα (Q)H(u, u)d .                       (26.18)

   All the endomorphisms and their normalized rational functions Fα are defined over a single

   CM order, and close it under conjugation. The uniqueness of the Laurent normalization in
   26.8 gives the same field of definition for every Fα . Writing that fixed number field as K,
   formula (26.18) places all values in K[H0 ]. The value for α = 0 is zero, and period shifts do
   not change it. Squaring was included because algebraicity of the individual positive square
   roots alone would not establish their membership in one fixed number field.

5. To prove k transcendental, recall the real period formula η1 = (s2 + k)ω1 . If k were algebraic,
   the nonzero period vector (ω1 , η1 ) of the algebraic universal vector extension of E would lie on
   the algebraic line of slope s2 + k. Dividing this period by a sufficiently large integer supplies a
   nonzero algebraic torsion exponential. The analytic subgroup theorem (Huber and Wüstholz,
   2022, Theorem 6.1, arXiv v8, p. 43) would give a one-dimensional algebraic subgroup with

                                                308
   that Lie line. Its projection to E is nonzero, so it splits the vector extension after an isogeny.
   The nonsplitting argument in cited result 26.9 excludes this: the coordinates here are exactly
   (z, w) with periods (ω, η(ω)) and algebraic charts t = w − ζ(z), tO = t − ℘′ (z)/(2℘(z)).

    Aα , Bα are algebraic. Since H = F 2 ,

    H(pα ) is nonzero because Q is nontorsion. At α = 1, a1 = 0, ℘(u) = 4 and s2 = −2, which
    give the last displayed formula in the statement.

 7. Differential and growth criteria. The differential criterion of Waldschmidt (2009, The-
    orems 3.6–3.7, author proof, pp. 21–22) requires a finite algebraically independent family
    whose partial derivatives belong to the polynomial ring generated by that family over one
    number field. Algebraic values of the full family then give algebraic values of all iterated
    partial derivatives. The calculation above gives the exact value-field obstruction: the field
    containing H(pα ) and its second directional derivative contains k as soon as the nonzero
    value is inverted. In particular its normalized second jet is transcendental. The issue persists
    although the first cancelling direction is algebraic; the direction also varies with α.

 8. Theorem 1 of (Waldschmidt, 1975, p. 24) uses d meromorphic functions on Cn , growth and
    arithmetic-size exponents ρ1 , . . . , ρd , and sampling sets of cardinality N ℓ−o(1) in a ball of
    radius O(N ), with separation at least N −λ−o(1) . Its strict numerical requirement is
                                              d

                                              X

    The theorem also requires all function values to belong to one number field and bounds on
    denominators in the entire representations of the meromorphic functions.

 9. The natural independent triple here is ℘(z), ℘(w), H(z, w), all of order at most two. The first
    two are algebraically independent. If H satisfied a polynomial over C(℘(z), ℘(w)), fix a generic
    pair (z, w) and translate only z by mω, with 0 ̸= ω ∈ Λ. The coefficients of the polynomial
    remain constant, whereas the absolute values of its proposed roots H(z + mω, w) grow as
    exp(k|ω|2 m2 + O(|m|)). This contradicts the finite set of roots of a nonzero polynomial. Thus
    the triple is independent.

10. The growth-order lower envelope is ρj = 2. Substitution of this envelope and n = 2, d = 3,
    ℓ = 4 into (26.19) gives the required inequality

    which fails even for λ = 0. Moreover, the ≍ N 4 points obtained by bounding the four integer
    coefficients lie in a ball of radius O(N ) in a real plane. Packing separated discs in that plane
    gives N 4 ≪ N 2+2λ+o(1) , hence λ ≥ 1. Removing the rank-two set of poles does not change
    this count. Larger growth exponents only worsen the inequality. Thus the stated rank and
    growth envelopes do not satisfy (26.19). The norm question is recorded in section D.

 (b) The height proof above applies with |m| ≤ Cn for any fixed C, changing only its constant. It

     polynomial evaluation inequality bounds their heights. Any removable zero or pole in these
     expressions lies in a fixed finite set and is handled by its specified model value. Taking the
     positive square root for a fixed complex-shifted norm divides height by two and costs at most
     a factor two in degree.
