  The sufficient inequality in Gramain–Mignotte–Waldschmidt (Gramain et al., 1986, Theorem 2.1,
  pp. 101–102) has the form

  On fixed nested discs the growth and geometric factors are constant. The scalar-model height
  envelopes are constant too. The numerical comparison of these envelopes is therefore dk+1 ≪ µk−1 .
  At denominator n the real group has O(n2 ) sample points, and through denominator N it has
  O(N 3 ). Substitution of the proved envelopes gives N 12 against N 3 for two functions and N 20
  against N 6 for three. These upper envelopes give the exponent comparisons 12 > 3 and 20 > 6.
  Verifying the sufficient inequality for these grids requires bounds sharper than these envelopes.
  For samples at λ = N0 , the base field is the displayed extension of Q(N0 ); its number-field status
  is exactly the unresolved algebraicity issue. Extra normalized translates remain in the function
  field of transcendence degree three proved above.

 (a) The arithmetic-germ criteria (Herblot, 2012, Theorem 6.1, pp. 31–32) (Gasbarri, 2010, Theo-
     rem 4.16, author preprint, p. 25) can be compared with the logarithmic tangent. At a real
     nontorsion division point z, the exact formula is
                                                 1 dg     ζ(z) − bz
                                                        =           .
                                                g(z) dx     ℘′ (z)
     Its numerator is transcendental by the period-line proof of 26.14, applied to this algebraic
     nontorsion point; its denominator is nonzero algebraic. A formal graph defined over Q would
     have an algebraic nonzero constant value and algebraic first derivative, contradicting their
     displayed ratio. The scalar change on the sampling group has not changed this exact tangent
     of the analytic graph.
 (b) For the Mahler system in (Adamczewski and Faverjon, 2017, Theorem 1.1 and system (1.2),
     p. 56), the needed algebraic Taylor coefficients and algebraic regular argument can be tested
     directly: the coefficient of z 3 in g is −δb/2, and b = s2 + k is transcendental by 26.19. The
     logarithm u is transcendental too: an algebraic u ̸= 0 would give an algebraic point (u, Q) on
     the diagonal Lie line of Ga × E; the analytic subgroup theorem would produce an algebraic
     one-dimensional subgroup projecting nontrivially to both factors, which is impossible since an
     elliptic curve has no nonconstant map to Ga and Ga has no nonzero group map to E. The
     duplication identity acts by the explicit elliptic multiplication map. The entropy identity in
     (Einsiedler et al., 2001, Theorem 5.1, author preprint, p. 9) uses the sequence built from the
     denominators of x(2n Q) with scale 4n .
 (c) Finally the period-refined rank comparison (Waldschmidt, 1988a, Theorem 4.1, pp. 385–386,
     and Corollary 4.3, p. 386) (Roy and Waldschmidt, 1993, main theorem, p. 363) has coefficient
     α(G) = 2 dim G − 2d0 (G) − d1 (G), where the last terms count additive and multiplicative
     quotients. Both vanish for GQ . An additive homomorphism vanishes on its torus and then
     on the proper quotient E; a nonzero torus character extending to GQ would kill a nonzero
     integer multiple of its nontorsion extension class. Thus α(GQ ) = 4.
 (d) The line ℓc has period rank one. A general period is (ω, ζ(u)ω − η(ω)u + 2πij). Writing
     ω = aω1 + dω2 , membership in ℓc gives du/ω1 ∈ Z by Legendre’s relation. Since u/ω1 is
     irrational, d = j = 0. The numerical rank bound in the cited theorem is (4−1) dim ℓc = 3. The
     period and the logarithm (u, cu) are independent over Q and span rank two; the algebraicity
     of the latter’s exponential remains exactly the point-algebraicity question in 26.14.

A      Parameter equivalence and deformations
Remark A.1 (Period and deformation comparison). [tag 02YS] For the fixed standard (3, 4, ∞)
data, the tangent cohomology (1, 1, 1, 0), smooth one-dimensional Kuranishi germ, automorphism
group C∗ , and equivalence Xc ≃ Xc′ ⇐⇒ c′ − c ∈ 2Z agree with the corresponding assertions
of Du et al. (2026a). Version 2, entitled Oka Geometry of Complex Six-Spheres, omits those
tangent-cohomology, miniversality, full-automorphism and exact-period assertions. Version 1,
submitted on 23 September 2026, states the exact 2Z equivalence as its Theorem 1.4.

Proof.     1. Use the same oriented triangle, ordered integral basis (γb , u
                                                                           b, w, b finite twists, and
                                                                              b δ),
      untranslated unit-square cusp fan as version 1. Its chosen function β0 and our β part
      obey the same affine transformation laws, and both β0 + τ and β part + τ extend over the
      cusp. Their difference descends to a holomorphic function on P1 , hence is the constant
      δ = β part −β0 . The exact parameter map and inverse are a = c+δ and c = a−δ: substitution
      gives Ωc+δ = Πc in the stated ordered basis. Writing M0 = sup(ℑβ0 − 6(ℑµ)2 /ℑτ ), our
      corresponding bound is Mpart = M0 + ℑδ, so this map also takes our admissible half-plane
      bijectively to version 1’s. The ordinary quotients, finite logarithmic maps, and cusp charts
      then identify by their identical marked periods and specified gluing data. In particular
      a′ − a = c′ − c. Its Theorem 1.4 therefore gives the displayed exact-period equivalence and
      the full automorphism group in this standard-data scope.

    2. Theorem 6.12 of version 1 gives the tangent-cohomology tuple, and Proposition 6.16 gives
       the smooth reduced Kuranishi germ and the locally miniversal parameter family. These are
       the four assertions compared with theorems B.2, C.4 and C.5 under that same parameter
       and marking.

    3. The second version retains the period construction and the Oka conclusions. Its displayed
       section list and its mathematical statements omit the first version’s logarithmic-deformation
       and classification sections and the four assertions just listed.

   At the cusp the relative canonical frame over Q is (dx1 /x1 ) ∧ (dx2 /x2 ) ∧ dtc . Extra dc terms
   in transition differentials vanish in relative forms. The finite determinant characters and the
   holomorphic units in the canonical calculation of proposition 7.2 are independent of c, since
   Rg , τ, µ are. Thus their coefficient identities hold jointly over Q. The evaluation exponents
   remain mj − 1 − aj = 0, 2. It follows by these transition functions and divisors that
                                                            −2
                          ωXQ /Q ≃ OXQ (−2S2 ),            ωX Q /Q
                                                                   ≃ F ∗ pr∗B OB (p2 ).             (A.14)

   Here the base identifications retain h = 1/(t − 1) and ηB = dt/(t − 1)2 from (7.3); these
   functions also do not depend on c. The joint transition identities prove (A.14) over the whole
   parameter disc.

6. For its complete degree-two system over the dual numbers, put A = C[ϵ]/(ϵ2 ), base-change by
                                                                 −2                −2
   c = c∗ + ϵ, write XA for the resulting deformation and LA = ωX A /A
                                                                       . For L∗ = ωX c∗
                                                                                        , flatness
   of the deformation and local freeness of LA give
                                                 ϵ
                                     0 −→ L∗ −−→ LA −→ L∗ −→ 0.                                     (A.15)

   The two sections of OB (p2 ) used in (7.6), namely σp2 and ℓ = A0 /(t − 1) + B0′ with A0 ̸= 0,
   pull back by (A.14) to sections s0 , s1 of LA whose reductions are a basis of H 0 (Xc∗ , L∗ ). This
   basis assertion is exactly the proved degree-two case of (7.4)–(7.6). Any section of LA reduces
   to a complex linear combination of these two reductions; subtract that lifted combination.
   Exactness of (A.15) then writes the remainder as ϵ times a section of L∗ , again a combination
   of that basis. Conversely, if an A-linear combination of s0 , s1 is zero, reduce modulo ϵ and
   then use the injective first arrow of (A.15) to see that all four complex coefficients vanish.
   Therefore
                                      H 0 (XA , LA ) = As0 ⊕ As1 .                              (A.16)
   The system is basepoint-free and its morphism is fA followed by the fixed coordinate map
   t 7→ [t − 1 : A0 + B0′ (t − 1)]. This is the base-change isomorphism for the complete degree-two
   system.

7. Nontriviality for the complete threefold. Suppose its first-order deformation were trivial, with
   an isomorphism XA ≃ Xc∗ × Spec A reducing to the identity. Intrinsic relative canonical
   bundles and their complete spaces of sections are preserved by that isomorphism. By (A.16),
   it would therefore identify fA with aA ◦ fc∗ for a projective linear change aA ∈ PGL2 (A)
   reducing to the identity.

8. This change fixes all three distinguished points even to first order. In the finite covering
                      m                                         m −1
   charts fA is tj = sj j , so its relative critical ideal is (sj j ), and its restriction to that critical
   scheme has tj = 0. The map from the parameter ring A to this critical scheme is injective; it
   contains a constant-parameter section given by sj = 0 and the zero section of the covering
   torus. At the cusp, in a chart containing a triple point, tc = z0 z1 z2 and the critical ideal

                                                     319
     is (z1 z2 , z0 z2 , z0 z1 ). Again tc = 0 in its ring and A injects, using z0 = z1 = z2 = 0. At a
     double chart the same assertion follows from tc = z0 z1 ; a smooth chart has no critical point.
     These critical ideals are intrinsic to the differential of the map over A, and the charts are
     local biholomorphisms onto XA . Away from the three distinguished base values the map is
     a submersion, so it has no critical point. Consequently the scheme-theoretic critical-value
     sections are exactly the three constant sections p1 , p2 , p0 . An automorphism reducing to the
     identity cannot permute these three distinct closed points. Its value at each is therefore the
     same point over A, not a nonzero infinitesimal displacement: such a displacement would be a
     nonzero element of ϵC in an injective copy of A on the just displayed critical chart.

 9. Write aA (t) = t + ϵ(b0 + b1 t + b2 t2 ). Fixing 0 gives b0 = 0, fixing 1 gives b0 + b1 + b2 = 0, and
    fixing infinity, in u = 1/t, gives b2 = 0. Hence aA is the identity. The proposed trivialization
    thus preserves f , and restricting it to any regular base value would trivialize the torus
    deformation (A.9). Its nonzero class (A.10) excludes this.

10. Finally, the zero Kodaira–Spencer class is precisely the condition for such a first-order
    trivialization. One may see the needed direction directly: choose local product charts for the
    holomorphic submersion π and differentiate their transition functions at c∗ . The resulting
    tangent-valued overlap functions form a Čech 1-cocycle. If its class vanishes, after refinement it
    is the coboundary of local holomorphic vector fields. Changing each chart by that vector field
    times ϵ cancels the first-order overlap terms, producing the identity-reducing trivialization.
    This is the usual Kodaira–Spencer connecting class (for the standard deformation-space
    interpretation see (McMullen, 1996, Section 67, p. 15)); the displayed conversion from the
    plus-graph convention in (A.10) changes its sign, not its vanishing. The contradiction proves
    the final assertion.




 B      Tangent cohomology and deformations
 B.1     Tangent direct images and local miniversality
Remark B.1 (The standard deformation theorem). [tag PI11] For the standard data (ℓ0 , ℓ1 , ℓ2 ) =
(0, 1, −1), the tangent dimensions and smooth reduced Kuranishi germ are given in (Du et al.,
2026a, Theorem 6.12, pp. 81–82; Proposition 6.16, p. 85). The weighted calculation also covers
the coprime multiplicities stated below, and the standard case includes the coarse tangent direct
images.

 Theorem B.2 (Tangent cohomology, direct images and miniversality). [tag 032U] Let k, l be
 positive integers with gcd(3k, 4l) = 1, and let X be a sphere member with multiplicities (3k, 4l) and
 the admissible logarithmic data of section 9.1. Put z = kl and d = 3k + 4l. On Bk,l = P(3k, 4l),

                                       E = O ⊕ O(−z),

vention κ(Φ) = (∂c Φ)Φ−1 , the Kodaira–Spencer class of ∂c is e ⊗ [γ], and the class of ∂u is
−(2πiu)−1 e ⊗ [γ]. Both classes are nonzero. The primary Kuranishi bracket vanishes, the
Kuranishi germ is a smooth reduced disc, and the fixed-data period family is locally miniversal.

   For the standard (3, 4) data, e = ξ and the coarse direct images are

              f∗ TX = O ⊕ O(−1),         R1 f∗ TX = O ⊕ O(−1)2 ,            R2 f∗ TX = O.       (B.1)

Proof. 1. The root lift, its proper flat Gorenstein charts, base change and relative duality are
  those of proposition 12.1. Write m = 3k and n = 4l. The finite root charts have the specified
  free affine cyclic actions, and the cusp charts are q = z0 z1 z2 .

2. Use weighted coordinates x, y of weights m, n, with coarse coordinate t = y m /(y m − xn ).
   The two root divisors have bundles O(n) and O(m), and the cusp has bundle O(mn). The
   root-forgetting morphism

                               r : Bk,l −→ B1,1 ,      (x, y) 7−→ (xl , y k ),

   uses the group homomorphism λ 7→ λkl on the weighted quotient. It is a holomorphic
   morphism of analytic stacks over B, with local maps s 7→ sk and s 7→ sl . In particular
   r∗ O(1) = O(z). The analytic Picard group of this root curve has the presentation ⟨H, R1 , R2 |
   mR1 = H, nR2 = H⟩: after subtracting the two stabilizer characters, a line bundle descends
   to the coarse projective line. Its only relations are the two defining root identities. The Smith
   form and gcd(m, n) = 1 identify this group with Z, with H = mnO(1), R1 = nO(1), and
   R2 = mO(1). This proves the analytic torsion-free Picard assertion used below. Translations
   have identity vertical derivative and act trivially on structure-sheaf cohomology. Thus the
   vertical bundle computed from the linear period factors is r∗ (O ⊕ O(−1)). The fixed vector
   gives a subline O; its extension splits because H 1 (O(z)) = 0.

3. Under the marked root-forgetting map in the preceding step, the constant lattice cocycle γ
   is unchanged. Its finite-chart representatives and its cusp edge values (0, −1, −1) therefore
   give the nowhere-zero cohomology line proved in proposition 12.2. The cusp resolution
   and cup-product pairing are those of proposition 12.1; pulling the linear period factors
   through r gives the quotient line O(−z). Relative duality gives R2 f¯∗ OX = O(−z) and
   det R1 f¯∗ OX = O(−z). The extension of that quotient by the specified [γ]-line splits because
   H 1 (O(z)) = 0, as computed in step 5. Connected fibres give f¯∗ OX = O. These maps prove
   the three structure-sheaf direct images.

4. The logarithmic tangent sequence is

                0 −→ V = f¯∗ E −→ T = TX (− log W ) −→ H = f¯∗ O(d − 12z) −→ 0.

   Its last map is the relative differential on smooth root charts and sends ai zi ∂zi to ( ai )q∂q
                                                                                 P          P

   at the cusp. It is surjective there. Since KB = O(−d), determinants give KX = f¯∗ O(z − d).

5. The two quotient charts x ≠ 0, y ̸= 0 are finite quotients of affine lines, and their overlap is a
   finite quotient of a punctured line. Finite averaging and Stein acyclicity compute coherent
   cohomology by this two-chart complex. Its homogeneous Laurent monomials give

                              h0 O(a) = #{(i, j) ∈ Z2≥0 : mi + nj = a},
                              h1 O(a) = h0 O(−a − d).

   The second equality identifies the remaining monomials x−i−1 y −j−1 .     The bundles
   O(−z), O(−2z) are acyclic.       Indeed a possible degree-one monomial would give

   hence 3A + 4B = a with A, B ≥ 1, which is impossible. Positive degree has no degree-one
   monomials, so H 1 O(z) = 0 as used above.

   deck cocycle is exactly its extending cocycle above. Its image under the two isomorphisms
   H 1 (V) ≃ H 1 (T ) ≃ H 1 (TX ) is e ⊗ [γ] ̸= 0. The chain rule gives the asserted u-class. With
                                   ¯
   the tangent-lift convention [∂h],    this class changes sign, as the explicit lift comparison in
   proposition A.3 shows. The parameter and the transition-arrow convention in the statement

9. Let α denote the nonzero tangent class just constructed. The holomorphic family gives a
   convergent deformation with this tangent. Differentiating its integrability equation gives
   ¯ 2 = −[α, α]/2. Thus the primary bracket vanishes; bilinearity and h1 (TX ) = 1 give
   ∂α
   vanishing on every pair.
   By (Douady, 1974, §VII.8, principal theorem, pp. 598–599; §VIII.1, Theorem 1 and its
   corollary, p. 600), there is a minimal versal analytic germ with tangent space H 1 (TX ). The
   identification of this tangent space uses tangent-valued Čech cocycles of transition maps, with
   changes of trivialization acting by coboundaries. Its local algebra is C{t}/I. The parameter
   family induces t 7→ g(c) with g ′ (c0 ) ̸= 0. By the analytic inverse function theorem, substitution
   by g is injective; it annihilates I, so I = 0. The classifying map is an isomorphism of germs.
   Pullback of the versal family realizes every sufficiently small deformation and proves local
   miniversality.

C.2    The full automorphism group
Theorem C.4 (The full automorphism group). [tag 02YQ]
  For every admissible twist of the (3, 4) construction,

Theorem C.5 (Integral torsor classes and the parameter period). [tag 02YR]
    For fixed admissible twist data, Xc ≃ Xc′ precisely when c − c′ ∈ 2Z. This fixes the integral
period of c; the construction still permits an additive choice of β part .
                                                                     −2
Proof. 1. The analytically computed complete linear system |ωX        c
                                                                        | is the marked map fc , by
  proposition 7.2. A biholomorphism preserves its canonical bundle, the complete space of
  sections, and its evaluation map. Consequently it induces α ∈ PGL2 (C) with fc′ F = αfc . The
  three special fibres have distinct intrinsic types: the cusp is reduced and nonnormal, while the
  other two have multiplicities three and four. All remaining fibres are smooth reduced tori.
  Thus α fixes p0 , p1 , p2 individually. In the marked coordinate, a fractional-linear map fixing
  ∞, 0, 1 has zero lower-left and upper-right entries and equal diagonal entries; hence α = idB .
  The centralizer computation of proposition A.2 then gives P = aI + bE41 with a = ±1 and
  b = a(c − c′ ). The root-fibre character calculation in that proposition excludes a = −1. Thus
  b = c − c′ is an integer.
2. Compute H 2 (B, H) with a pair of pants, two root discs, and a cusp disc. The pair of pants
   has cochains Λ → Λ2 with differential ((A1 − I), (A2 − I)). A root disc has the periodic cyclic
   resolution with alternating differentials Aj − I, Nj ; the cusp disc has ker(M0 − I) in degree
                            Aj −I
   zero. An annulus has Λ −−−→ Λ. The degree-one restriction from the pair of pants is

                               (x1 , x2 ) 7−→ (x1 , x2 , −M0 (x1 + A1 x2 )).

                                                  327
   The total-complex ranks in degrees zero through three are 14, 28, 20, 8. The resulting integer
   differentials have sizes 28 × 14, 20 × 28 and 8 × 20, and their consecutive products vanish by
   the restriction identities. Smith decompositions with unimodular changes of basis identify
   each integral kernel before quotienting by the preceding image, giving H 0 = Z, H 1 = 0,
   H 2 = Z ⊕ Z/2.

3. The degree-two presentation also reduces by hand. The invariant lattices have bases (δ,       b εj ),
   where ε1 = (1, 2, −4, 0) and ε2 = (1, 3, −3, 0). The five generators (δ1 , ε1 , δ2 , ε2 , hc ) have
   relations
                             δ1 = 0,   2δ2 = 0,      3ε1 = hc = 4ε2 .                             (C.5)
   For the constant sheaf Z, the same computation has generators z1 , z2 , hc and relations
   3z1 = hc = 4z2 ; its primitive generator is z1 − z2 . Inclusion Zδb → H sends it to the nonzero
   order-two class δ2 . The character γ sends εj to zj and kills δj .

4. Both H 1 (B, E) and H 2 (B, E) vanish, by ρ∗ E = O ⊕ O(−1) and the dimension of the coarse
   curve. Consequently (C.4) identifies compactified translation torsors H 1 (B, A) with H 2 (B, H).
   This identification takes logarithms of local translation transitions and their lattice-valued
   Čech coboundaries; the two vanishings also reverse that construction.

5. The cyclic norm of the translation vj /mj is vj , while the cusp collar has the opposite boundary
   orientation. Thus the torsor character is

                    l1 z1 + l2 z2 − l0 hc = (4l1 + 3l2 − 12l0 )(z1 − z2 ) = −p(z1 − z2 ).

   The shear Sb − I = bδb ⊗ γ changes its class by −bpδ2 . Freeness forces l2 odd and thus p odd.
   The class is preserved precisely for even b.

6. For an integral shear the Jacobian charts themselves identify: the period lattices differ by Sb ,
   and the bounded cusp matrix changes by an integer in its β entry. Every toric unit exp(2πiCλ)
   is therefore unchanged. The fan, lattice, and toric gluings are the same, and on root discs
   the basis change identifies the smooth Jacobian and its cyclic action. Equality of the torsor
   classes now gives a holomorphic isomorphism for the fixed sheaf A, which consists precisely of
   translations extending over the cusp. It extends on all three special charts. Conversely every
   isomorphism preserves the class, so forces b even.

D     Open arithmetic questions for the normalized norm
The arithmetic nature of N (P ) remains open for algebraic nontorsion points in this family. An
explicit instance is

       E : y 2 = x3 − 140x + 784,       P = (0, 28),       j = −3375,      N (P ) = 2e−hO (P ) .
                                                                                         b


The point is primitive modulo rational two-torsion, and h  b O (P ) = 0.46736568 . . .. The unresolved
assertion is transcendence of 2e−bhO (P ) . For the conductor-361 example y 2 + y = x3 − 38x + 90,
P = (0, 9), the corresponding exact formula is

                                                            L′ (E, 1)
                                                                   
                               N (P ) = e−hO (P ) = exp −             .
                                          b
                                                              4ΩE
Here every finite local contribution vanishes. The compact-point equivalence in proposition 26.3
and the explicit constructions in propositions 26.14 and 26.17 give precise group-theoretic forms
of this same unresolved value.
    The exact analytic leading quotients in remark 24.13 also leave group-order questions: the
orders of the Tate–Shafarevich groups are identified here for rows 3, 5, 7 only. In particular the
analytic quotient of row eleven is exactly 9; its identification with # Sha(E11 /Q), including its
3-primary part, remains open in the results of this paper.

D.1    The unresolved relative-period bound
The open lower-bound question is the Relative Semi-abelian Conjecture (Bertolin et al., 2022,
Conjecture 4.7, arXiv v2, p. 18) which asks whether algebraic lifts in the indicated semiabelian
varieties satisfy the bound

                   trdegQ(ΩG ) Q ΩG , R, R̄, log
                                              f (R, R̄) ≥ 2 dim BQ + dim Z(1).
                                                       
                                                 G

The full matrix ΩG includes the second-kind periods. This lower bound remains open for the
compact diagonal configuration at issue here. Its relation to Grothendieck’s period conjecture for
algebraic 1-motives is given in (Bertolin et al., 2022, Proposition 4.12, arXiv v2, pp. 19–20).
    The known calculations isolate the precise issue. For the algebraic motives of proposition 26.5,
projection from the point-extension variety to the extension-coordinate variety is an isogeny: the
point coordinates agree with the extension data under the stated polarizations. Equivalently,
(P, P̄ ) = (P, 0) + (0, P̄ ) in E × Ē. Formula (4.4), p. 19 of the same source therefore gives
dim BQ = 0. The remaining kernel of connected motivic groups is the weight-−2 vector group
Lie Z. After fixing the base periods its fibre is an affine torsor of dimension dim Z.
    In positive Tate coordinates the central action changes (v, v̄) by 2πi(c1 , c2 ). For an isogeny
ϕ : Ē → E of degree d, ϕt JE ϕ = dJĒ . Thus the dependent bracket line of proposition 26.5 has
coordinates (1, aa† /d) with positive second coordinate; in the independent case the bracket spans
both central coordinates. The functional (c1 , c2 ) 7→ c1 + c2 is nonzero on this central group,
including when there is a further quotient Tate direction. Accordingly, the compactness equation
(26.8) cuts a proper affine hyperplane. The unconditional period-field calculation is lemma 26.6;
the proposed lower bound needed to exclude an algebraic compact lift is the open step.
